items.control_description: With reference to ECC control 1-8-2, cybersecurity review and audit must be conducted periodically by independent parties outside the organization’s cybersecurity function as specified for each data classification level.

In addition to the subcontrols in the ECC control 1-9-3, cybersecurity requirements in human resources prior to employment, during employment and after termination/separation must include at least the following:
Screening and vetting candidates in jobs related to data handling.

A signed agreement by personnel pledging to not use social media, communication applications or personal cloud storage to create, store or share the organization’s data, with the exception of secure communication applications approved by relevant authorities.
In addition to the subcontrols in ECC control 1-10-3, the cybersecurity awareness program must cover topics related to data protection, including the following:
Risks of data leakage and unauthorized access to data during its lifecycle.
Secure handling of classified data while traveling and outside the workplace.
Secure handling of data during meetings (virtual and in-person).
Secure use of printers, scanners and copy machines.
Procedures for secure data disposal.
Risks of sharing documents and information through non-secure channels.
Cybersecurity risks related to the use of external storage media.
In addition to the subcontrols in ECC control 2-2-3, cybersecurity requirements for identity and access management must cover at least the following:

Strict restriction to allow only the minimum number of personnel accessing, viewing and sharing data based on lists of privileges limited to Saudi-national employees unless exempted by the Authorizing Official (the head of the organization or his/her delegate) and those lists are approved by the Authorizing Official.
Prohibiting the sharing of approved lists of privileges with unauthorized persons.
Managing identities and access rights to view data using Privileged Access Management systems.
In addition to ECC subcontrol 2-2-3-5, the approved lists of privileges and privileges used to handle data must be reviewed as specified for each data classification level.
In addition to the subcontrols in ECC control 2-3-3, cybersecurity requirements for Information System and Information Processing Facilities Protection must include at least the following:
items.subdomain_name: Information System and Information Processing Facilities Protection

items.control_description: Applying security patches and updates from the time of announcement on systems used to handle data as specified for each data classification level.
items.subdomain_name: Information System and Information Processing Facilities Protection

items.control_description: Reviewing the security configuration and hardening of systems used to handle data as specified for each data classification level.

items.control_description: Reviewing and hardening the default configuration (e.g., default passwords and backgrounds) of the technology assets used to handle the data.
items.subdomain_name: Information System and Information Processing Facilities Protection

items.control_description: Disabling the Print Screen or Screen Capture features on the devices that create or process documents.
items.subdomain_name: Information System and Information Processing Facilities Protection

items.control_description: In addition to the subcontrols in ECC control 2-6-3, cybersecurity requirements for mobile devices must cover at least the following:
Centrally managing the organization’s owned mobile devices using Mobile Device Management (MDM) system and activating the remote wipe feature.
Centrally managing BYOD devices using Mobile Device Management (MDM) system and activating the remote wipe feature.
In addition to the subcontrols in ECC control 2-7-3, cybersecurity requirements for data and information protection must cover at least the following:
Using Watermark feature to label the whole document when creating, storing, printing, on the screen and on each copy so that the symbol can be traced to the user or device level.
Using Data Leakage Prevention technologies and Rights Management technologies.

Prohibiting the use of data in any environment other than the production environment, except after conducting a risk assessment and applying controls to protect that data, such as: data masking or data scrambling techniques.
Using brand protection service to protect the organization's identity from impersonation.
In addition to the subcontrols in ECC control 2-8-3, cybersecurity requirements for cryptography must cover at least the following:

Using secure and up-to-date cryptographic methods and algorithms when creating, storing, transmitting data, and for overall network communication medium; as per the requirements of the “advanced level” in the National Cryptographic Standards (NCS-1:2020).

Using secure and up-to-date cryptographic methods and algorithms when creating, storing, transmitting data, and for overall network communication medium; as per the requirements of the “moderate level” in the National Cryptographic Standards (NCS-1:2020).
Cybersecurity requirements for secure data disposal must cover at least the following:
Identification of technologies, tools and procedures for the implementation of secure data disposal according to the data classification level.
When storage media is no longer needed, it must be securely disposed by using the technologies, tools and procedures identified in subcontrol 2-6-1-1.
When storage media needs to be re-used, data must be securely erased (secure erasure) in a manner it cannot be recovered.
Implementation of secure data disposal or   erasure operations referred to in sub-controls 2-6-1-2 and 2-6-1-3 must be verified.
Keeping a record of all secure data disposal and erasure operations that have been conducted.
The implementation of the secure data disposal requirements must be reviewed as specified for each data classification level.
Cybersecurity requirements for protecting printers, scanners and copy machines must be defined, documented and approved.

items.control_description: In addition to the controls in ECC subdomain 4-1, cybersecurity requirements for third-parties cybersecurity must include at least the following:
Screening or vetting third-party employees who have access to the data.

Requiring contractual commitment by third-parties to securely dispose the organization’s data at the end of the contract or in case of contract termination, including providing evidences of such disposal to the organization.
Documenting all data sharing operations within third-parties, including data sharing justification.

When transferring data outside the kingdom, the capability of the hosting organization abroad to safeguard data must be verified, approval of the Authorizing Official must be obtained and complying with related laws and regulations.
Requiring third-parties to notify the organization immediately in case of cybersecurity incident that may affect data that has been shared or created.
Reclassifying data to the least level to achieve the objective before sharing it with third-parties using data masking or data scrambling techniques.

In alignment with related laws and regulations, and in addition to the applicable controls in ECC and controls within DCC domain (1), (2), and (3); cybersecurity requirements when dealing with consultancy services that works on high-sensitivity strategic projects at the national level must cover at least the following:
Screening or vetting consultancy services employees who have access to the data.

Requiring contractual commitment by consultancy services including employees non-disclosure agreements and secure disposal the organization’s data at the end of the contract or in case of contract termination, including providing evidences of such disposal to the organization.
Documenting all data sharing operations within consultancy services, including data sharing justification.
Requiring consultancy services to notify the organization immediately in case of cybersecurity incident that may affect data that has been shared or created.
Reclassifying data to the least level to achieve the objective before sharing it with consultancy services using data masking or data scrambling techniques.
Dedicating a closed room for the consultancy services employees to perform their work, in addition to providing dedicated organization owned devices to share and process data.
Activating access control system to allow only authorized access to the closed room.
Preventing carrying out of devices, storage media and documents outside the closed room, as well as the entry of any other electronic devices.

items.control_description: All executable files and libraries belonging to the app are either encrypted on the file level and/or important code and data segments inside the executables are encrypted or packed. Trivial static analysis does not reveal important code or data.
items.remarks: Platform: iOS | MASVS: R | MSTG: MSTG-RESILIENCE-11 | Testing: File Integrity Checks (MSTG-RESILIENCE-3 and MSTG-RESILIENCE-11)

items.control_description: If the goal of obfuscation is to protect sensitive computations, an obfuscation scheme is used that is both appropriate for the particular task and robust against manual and automated de-obfuscation methods, considering currently published research. The effectiveness of the obfuscation scheme must be verified through manual testing. Note that hardware-based isolation features are preferred over obfuscation whenever possible.
items.remarks: Platform: iOS | MASVS: R | MSTG: MSTG-RESILIENCE-12

items.control_description: As a defense in depth, next to having solid hardening of the communicating parties, application level payload encryption can be applied to further impede eavesdropping.
items.remarks: Platform: iOS | MASVS: R | MSTG: MSTG-RESILIENCE-13

items.control_description: Conduct Search Engine Discovery and Reconnaissance for Information Leakage
items.evidence_reference: Google Hacking, Sitedigger, Shodan, FOCA, Punkspider
items.remarks: Tools: Google Hacking, Sitedigger, Shodan, FOCA, Punkspider | Desc: Use a search engine to search for Network diagrams and Configurations, Credentials, Error message content.

items.control_description: Fingerprint Web Server
items.remarks:
Tools: Httprint, Httprecon, Desenmascarame | Desc: Find the version and type of a running web server to determine known vulnerabilities and the appropriate exploits. Using
"HTTP header field ordering" and "Malformed requests test".

items.control_description: Review Webserver Metafiles for Information Leakage
items.remarks: Tools: Browser, curl, wget | Desc: Analyze robots.txt and identify <META> Tags from website.

items.control_description: Enumerate Applications on Webserver
items.evidence_reference: Webhosting.info, dnsrecon, Nmap, fierce, Recon-ng, Intrigue
items.remarks: Tools: Webhosting.info, dnsrecon, Nmap, fierce, Recon-ng, Intrigue | Desc: Find applications hosted in the webserver (Virtual hosts/Subdomain), non-standard ports, DNS zone transfers

items.control_description: Review Webpage Comments and Metadata for Information Leakage
items.remarks: Tools: Browser, curl, wget | Desc: Find sensitive information from webpage comments and Metadata on source code.

items.control_description: Identify application entry points
items.remarks: Tools: Burp proxy, ZAP, Tamper data | Desc: Identify from hidden fields, parameters, methods HTTP header analysis

items.control_description: Map execution paths through application
items.remarks: Tools: Burp proxy, ZAP | Desc: Map the target application and understand the principal workflows.

items.control_description: Fingerprint Web Application Framework
items.remarks: Tools: Whatweb, BlindElephant, Wappalyzer | Desc: Find the type of web application framework/CMS from HTTP headers, Cookies, Source code, Specific files and folders.

items.control_description: Fingerprint Web Application
items.remarks: Tools: Whatweb, BlindElephant, Wappalyzer, CMSmap | Desc: Identify the web application and version to determine known vulnerabilities and the appropriate exploits.

items.control_description: Map Application Architecture
items.remarks: Tools: Browser, curl, wget | Desc: Identify application architecture including Web language, WAF, Reverse proxy, Application Server, Backend Database

items.control_description: Test Network/Infrastructure Configuration
items.remarks: Tools: Nessus | Desc: Understand the infrastructure elements interactions, config management for software, backend DB server, WebDAV, FTP in order to identify known vulnerabilities.

items.control_description: Test Application Platform Configuration
items.remarks: Tools: Browser, Nikto | Desc: Identify default installation file/directory, Handle Server errors (40*,50*), Minimal Privilege, Software logging.

items.control_description: Test File Extensions Handling for Sensitive Information
items.remarks: Tools: Browser, Nikto | Desc: Find important file, information (.asa , .inc , .sql ,zip, tar, pdf, txt, etc)

items.control_description: Backup and Unreferenced Files for Sensitive Information
items.remarks: Tools: Nessus, Nikto, Wikto | Desc: Check JS source code, comments, cache file, backup file (.old, .bak, .inc, .src) and guessing of filename

items.control_description: Enumerate Infrastructure and Application Admin Interfaces
items.evidence_reference: Burp Proxy, dirb, Dirbuster, fuzzdb, Tilde Scanner
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, dirb, Dirbuster, fuzzdb, Tilde Scanner | Desc: Directory and file enumeration, comments and links in source (/admin, /administrator, /backoffice, /backend, etc), alternative server port (Tomcat/8080)

items.control_description: Test HTTP Methods
items.remarks: Tools: netcat, curl | Desc: Identify HTTP allowed methods on Web server with OPTIONS. Arbitrary HTTP Methods, HEAD access control bypass and XST

items.control_description: Test HTTP Strict Transport Security
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, curl | Desc: Identify HSTS header on Web server through HTTP response header. 
curl -s -D- https://domain.com/ | grep Strict

items.control_description: Test RIA cross domain policy
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Nikto | Desc: Analyse the permissions allowed from the policy files (crossdomain.xml/clientaccesspolicy.xml) and allow-access-from.

items.control_description: Test Role Definitions
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Validate the system roles defined within the application by creating permission matrix.

items.control_description: Test User Registration Process
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Verify that the identity requirements for user registration are aligned
with business and security requirements:

items.control_description: Test Account Provisioning Process
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Determine which roles are able to provision users and what sort of
accounts they can provision.

items.control_description: Testing for Account Enumeration and Guessable User Account
items.remarks: Tools: Browser, Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Generic login error statement check, return codes/parameter values, enumerate all possible valid userids (Login system, Forgot password)

items.control_description: Testing for Weak or unenforced username policy
items.remarks:
Tools: Browser, Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: User account names are often highly structured (e.g. Joe Bloggs
account name is jbloggs and Fred Nurks account name is fnurks)
and valid account names can easily be guessed.

items.control_description: Test Permissions of Guest/Training Accounts
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Guest and Training accounts are useful ways to acquaint potential users with system functionality prior to them completing the authorisation process required for access.Evaluate consistency between access policy and guest/training account access permissions.

items.control_description: Test Account Suspension/Resumption Process
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Verify the identity requirements for user registration align with business/security requirements. Validate the registration process.

items.control_description: Testing for Credentials Transported over an Encrypted Channel
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Check referrer whether its HTTP or HTTPs. Sending data through HTTP and HTTPS.

items.control_description: Testing for default credentials
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Hydra | Desc: Testing for default credentials of common applications, Testing for default password of new accounts.

items.control_description: Testing for Weak lock out mechanism
items.remarks:
Tools: Browser | Desc: Evaluate the account lockout mechanism’s ability to mitigate
brute force password guessing. Evaluate the unlock mechanism’s resistance to unauthorized account unlocking.

items.control_description: Testing for bypassing authentication schema
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Force browsing (/admin/main.php, /page.asp?authenticated=yes), Parameter Modification, Session ID prediction, SQL Injection

items.control_description: Test remember password functionality
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Look for passwords being stored in a cookie. Examine the cookies stored by the application. Verify that the credentials are not stored in clear text, but are hashed. Autocompleted=off?

items.control_description: Testing for Browser cache weakness
items.evidence_reference: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Firefox add-on CacheViewer2
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Firefox add-on CacheViewer2 | Desc: Check browser history issue by clicking "Back" button after logging out. Check browser cache issue from HTTP response headers (Cache-Control: no-cache)

items.control_description: Testing for Weak password policy
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Hydra | Desc: Determine the resistance of the application against brute force
password guessing using available password dictionaries by evaluating the length, complexity, reuse and aging requirements of
passwords.

items.control_description: Testing for Weak security question/answer
items.remarks: Tools: Browser | Desc: Testing for weak pre-generated questions, Testing for weak self-generated question, Testing for brute-forcible answers (Unlimited attempts?)

items.control_description: Testing for weak password change or reset functionalities
items.remarks: Tools: Browser, Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Test password reset (Display old password in plain-text?, Send via email?, Random token on confirmation email ?), Test password change (Need old password?), CSRF vulnerability ?

items.control_description: Testing for Weaker authentication in alternative channel
items.remarks: Tools: Browser | Desc: Understand the primary mechanism and Identify other channels (Mobile App, Call center, SSO)

items.control_description: Testing Directory traversal/file include
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Wfuzz | Desc: dot-dot-slash attack (../), Directory traversal, Local File inclusion/Remote File Inclusion.

items.control_description: Testing for bypassing authorization schema
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy (Autorize), ZAP | Desc: Access a resource without authentication?, Bypass ACL, Force browsing (/admin/adduser.jsp)

items.control_description: Testing for Privilege Escalation
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy (Autorize), ZAP | Desc: Testing for role/privilege manipulate the values of hidden variables. Change some param groupid=2 to groupid=1

items.control_description: Testing for Insecure Direct Object References
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy (Autorize), ZAP | Desc: Force changing parameter value (?invoice=123 -> ?invoice=456)

items.control_description: Testing for Bypassing Session Management Schema
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ForceSSL, ZAP, CookieDigger | Desc: SessionID analysis prediction, unencrypted cookie transport, brute-force.

items.control_description: Testing for Cookies attributes
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Check HTTPOnly and Secure flag, expiration, inspect for sensitive data.

items.control_description: Testing for Session Fixation
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: The application doesn't renew the cookie after a successfully user authentication.

items.control_description: Testing for Exposed Session Variables
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Encryption & Reuse of session Tokens vulnerabilities, Send sessionID with GET method ?

items.control_description: Testing for Cross Site Request Forgery
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy (csrf_token_detect), burpy, ZAP | Desc: URL analysis, Direct access to functions without any token.

items.control_description: Testing for logout functionality
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Check reuse session after logout both server-side and SSO.

items.control_description: Test Session Timeout
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Check session timeout, after the timeout has passed, all session tokens should be destroyed or be unusable.

items.control_description: Testing for Session puzzling
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: The application uses the same session variable for more than one purpose. An attacker can potentially access pages in an order unanticipated by the developers so that the session variable is set in one context and then used in another.

items.control_description: Testing for Reflected Cross Site Scripting
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Xenotix XSS | Desc: Check for input validation, Replace the vector used to identify XSS, XSS with HTTP Parameter Pollution.

items.control_description: Testing for Stored Cross Site Scripting
items.evidence_reference: Burp Proxy, ZAP, BeEF, XSS Proxy
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, BeEF, XSS Proxy | Desc: Check input forms/Upload forms and analyze HTML codes, Leverage XSS with BeEF

items.control_description: Testing for HTTP Verb Tampering
items.remarks: Tools: netcat | Desc: Craft custom HTTP requests to test the other methods to bypass URL authentication and authorization.

items.control_description: Testing for HTTP Parameter pollution
items.remarks: Tools: ZAP, HPP Finder (Chrome Plugin) | Desc: Identify any form or action that allows user-supplied input to bypass Input validation and filters using HPP

items.control_description: Testing for SQL Injection
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy (SQLipy), SQLMap, Pangolin, Seclists (FuzzDB) | Desc: Union, Boolean, Error based, Out-of-band, Time delay.

items.control_description: Testing for LDAP Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: /ldapsearch?user=*
user=*user=*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*
pass=password

items.control_description: Testing for ORM Injection
items.remarks: Tools: Hibernate, Nhibernate | Desc: Testing ORM injection is identical to SQL injection testing

items.control_description: Testing for XML Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Wfuzz | Desc: Check with XML Meta Characters
', " , <>, <!--/-->, &, <![CDATA[ / ]]>, XXE, TAG

items.control_description: Testing for SSI Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Presense of .shtml extension
• Check for these characters
< ! # = / . " - > and [a-zA-Z0-9]
• include String = <!--#include virtual="/etc/passwd" -->

items.control_description: Testing for XPath Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Check for XML error enumeration by supplying a single quote (')
Username: ‘ or ‘1’ = ‘1
Password: ‘ or ‘1’ = ‘1

items.control_description: IMAP/SMTP Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Identifying vulnerable parameters with special characters
(i.e.: \, ‘, “, @, #, !, |)
• Understanding the data flow and deployment structure of the client
• IMAP/SMTP command injection (Header, Body, Footer)

items.control_description: Testing for Code Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Liffy, Panoptic | Desc: Enter OS commands in the input field.
?arg=1; system('id')

items.control_description: Testing for Command Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Commix | Desc: Understand the application platform, OS, folder structure, relative path and execute OS commands on a Web server.
%3Bcat%20/etc/passwd
test.pdf+|+Dir C:\

items.control_description: Testing for Buffer overflow
items.remarks:
Tools: Immunity Canvas, Spike, MSF, Nessus | Desc: • Testing for heap overflow vulnerability
• Testing for stack overflow vulnerability
• Testing for format string vulnerability

items.control_description: Testing for incubated vulnerabilities
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, BeEF, MSF | Desc: File Upload, Stored XSS , SQL/XPATH Injection, Misconfigured servers (Tomcat, Plesk, Cpanel)

items.control_description: Testing for HTTP Splitting/Smuggling
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, netcat | Desc: param=foobar%0d%0aContent-Length:%200%0d%0a%0d%0aHTTP/1.1%20200%20OK%0d%0aContent-Type:%20text/html%0d%0aContent-Length:%2035%0d%0a%0d%0a<html>Sorry,%20System%20Down</html>

items.control_description: Analysis of Error Codes
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Locate error codes generated from applications or web servers. Collect sensitive information from that errors (Web Server, Application Server, Database)

items.control_description: Analysis of Stack Traces
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Invalid Input / Empty inputs
• Input that contains non alphanumeric characters or query syn
tax
• Access to internal pages without authentication
• Bypassing application flow

items.control_description: Testing for Weak SSL/TSL Ciphers, Insufficient Transport Layer Protection
items.remarks: Tools: testssl.sh, SSL Breacher | Desc: Identify SSL service, Idectify weak ciphers/protocols (ie. RC4, BEAST, CRIME, POODLE)

items.control_description: Testing for Padding Oracle
items.remarks:
Tools: PadBuster, Poracle, python-paddingoracle, POET | Desc: Compare the responses in three different states:
• Cipher text gets decrypted, resulting data is correct.
• Cipher text gets decrypted, resulting data is garbled and causes
some exception or error handling in the application logic.
• Cipher text decryption fails due to padding errors.

items.control_description: Testing for Sensitive information sent via unencrypted channels
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP, Curl | Desc: Check sensitive data during the transmission:
• Information used in authentication (e.g. Credentials, PINs, Session
identifiers, Tokens, Cookies…)
• Information protected by laws, regulations or specific organizational
policy (e.g. Credit Cards, Customers data)

items.control_description: Test Business Logic Data Validation
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Looking for data entry points or hand off points between systems or software.
• Once found try to insert logically invalid data into the application/system.

items.control_description: Test Ability to Forge Requests
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Looking for guessable, predictable or hidden functionality of fields.
• Once found try to insert logically valid data into the application/system allowing the user go through the application/system against the normal busineess logic workflow.

items.control_description: Test Integrity Checks
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: •Looking for parts of the application/system (components i.e. For example, input fields, databases or logs) that move, store or handle data/information.
• For each identified component determine what type of data/information is logically acceptable and what types the application/system should guard against. Also, consider who according to the business logic is allowed to insert, update and delete data/information and in each component.
• Attempt to insert, update or edit delete the data/information values with invalid data/information into each component (i.e. input, database, or log) by users that .should not be allowed per the busines logic workflow.

items.control_description: Test for Process Timing
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Looking for application/system functionality that may
be impacted by time. Such as execution time or actions that
help users predict a future outcome or allow one to circumvent
any part of the business logic or workflow. For example, not
completing transactions in an expected time.
• Develop and execute the mis-use cases ensuring that attackers
can not gain an advantage based on any timing.

items.control_description: Test Number of Times a Function Can be Used Limits
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Looking for functions or features in the application or system that should not be executed more that a single time or specified number of times during the business logic workflow.
• For each of the functions and features found that should only be executed a single time or specified number of times during the business logic workflow, develop abuse/misuse cases that may allow a user to execute more than the allowable number of times.

items.control_description: Testing for the Circumvention of Work Flows
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Looking for methods to skip or go to steps in the application process in a different order from the designed/intended business logic flow.
• For each method develop a misuse case and try to circumvent or perform an action that is "not acceptable" per the the business logic workflow.

items.control_description: Test Defenses Against Application Mis-use
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Measures that might indicate the application has in-built self-defense:
• Changed responses
• Blocked requests
• Actions that log a user out or lock their account

items.control_description: Test Upload of Unexpected File Types
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Review the project documentation and perform some exploratory testing looking for file types that should be "unsupported" by the application/system.
• Try to upload these “unsupported” files an verify that it are properly rejected.
• If multiple files can be uploaded at once, there must be tests in place to verify that each file is properly evaluated. 
PS. file.phtml, shell.phPWND, SHELL~1.PHP

items.control_description: Test Upload of Malicious Files
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: • Develop or acquire a known “malicious” file.
• Try to upload the malicious file to the application/system and verify that it is correctly rejected.
• If multiple files can be uploaded at once, there must be tests in place to verify that each file is properly evaluated.

items.control_description: Testing for DOM based Cross Site Scripting
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, DOMinator | Desc: Test for the user inputs obtained from client-side JavaScript Objects

items.control_description: Testing for JavaScript Execution
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Inject JavaScript code:
www.victim.com/?javascript:alert(1)

items.control_description: Testing for HTML Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Send malicious HTML code:
?user=<img%20src='aaa'%20onerror=alert(1)>

items.control_description: Testing for Client Side URL Redirect
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Modify untrusted URL input to a malicious site: (Open Redirect)
?redirect=www.fake-target.site

items.control_description: Testing for CSS Injection
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Inject code in the CSS context :
•  www.victim.com/#red;-o-link:'javascript:alert(1)';-o-link-source:current; (Opera [8,12])
•  www.victim.com/#red;-:expression(alert(URL=1)); (IE 7/8)

items.control_description: Testing for Client Side Resource Manipulation
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: External JavaScript could be easily injected in the trusted web site
www.victim.com/#http://evil.com/js.js

items.control_description: Test Cross Origin Resource Sharing
items.remarks:
Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Check the HTTP headers in order to understand how CORS is
used (Origin Header)

items.control_description: Testing for Cross Site Flashing
items.evidence_reference: FlashBang, Flare, Flasm, SWFScan, SWF Intruder
items.remarks: Tools: FlashBang, Flare, Flasm, SWFScan, SWF Intruder | Desc: Decompile, Undefined variables, Unsafe methods, Include malicious SWF (http://victim/file.swf?lang=http://evil

items.control_description: Testing for Clickjacking
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ClickjackingTool | Desc: Discover if a website is vulnerable by loading into an iframe, create simple web page that includes a frame containing the target.

items.control_description: Testing WebSockets
items.evidence_reference: Burp Proxy, Chrome, ZAP, WebSocket Client
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, Chrome, ZAP, WebSocket Client | Desc: Identify that the application is using WebSockets by inspecting ws:// or wss:// URI scheme.Use Google Chrome's Developer Tools to view the Network WebSocket communication. Check Origin, Confidentiality and Integrity, Authentication, Authorization, Input Sanitization

items.control_description: Test Web Messaging
items.remarks: Tools: Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Analyse JavaScript code looking for how Web Messaging is implemented. How the website is restricting messages from untrusted domain and how the data is handled even for trusted domains

items.control_description: Test Local Storage
items.remarks: Tools: Chrome, Firebug, Burp Proxy, ZAP | Desc: Determine whether the website is storing sensitive data in the storage. XSS in localstorage http://server/StoragePOC.html#

items.control_description: Step 1 - Conduct a criticality assessment for your organisation
Step 2 - Carry out a cyber security threat analysis, supported by realistic scenarios and rehearsals
Step 3 - Consider the implications of people, process and technology
Step 4 - Create an appropriate control environment
Step 5 - Review your state of readiness in cyber security response
Step 1 - Identify cyber security incident
Step 2 - Define objectives and investigate situation
Step 3 - Take appropriate action
Step 4 - Recover systems, data and connectivity
Step 1 - Investigate incident more thoroughly
Step 2 - Report incident to relevant stakeholders
Step 3 - Carry out a post incident investigation review
Step 4 - Communicate and build on lessons learned
Step 5 - Update key information, controls and processes
Step 6 - Perform trend analysis
There is a formal, documented, and current framework for the identification and prioritization of vulnerabilities.
There is a vulnerability identification process including scanning, penetration tests, and threat intelligence feeds.
There is an established vulnerability prioritization process.
There is a vulnerability remediation process, which includes patching, but also extends to work-arounds, configuration changes, and even risk acceptance.
Patching efforts are actively documented, tracked, analyzed, and communicated.
Remediation efforts are adequately deployed, assessed, and evaluated in a test environment before implemented organization-wide.
There is a formal process for the initiation and management of penetration testing, red teaming, and table top exercises.
There is a prioritization and remediation process when reviewing penetration test results.
There are vulnerability management metrics to provide oversight into the above bullet points.
There are defined roles and responsibilities for both patching and vulnerability remediation efforts.
A vulnerability management platform has been selected and implemented.
Internal and external intelligence publication standards and reporting procedures (alerts, reports, and briefings) have been formalized and documented.
There is a formalized inventory of approved intelligence collection sources (news, social media, internet, deep web, commercial vendors, ISACs, and internal security infrastructure).
There is a formalized intelligence vendor management program or policy that clearly documents and addresses vendor criteria.
Indicators of compromise such as hash values, IP addresses, domain names, and network/host artifacts are frequently collected by both internal and external sources.
There are defined intelligence ingestion and analysis processes within existing security functions and controls (Incident response, security operations, and vulnerability management).
There is a process to publish intelligence alerts, reports, and briefings to appropriate stakeholders.

Relationships are established between indicators, frequently targeted infrastructure, threat actors, threat actor capabilities, and potential victims to contextualize static IOCs and create unique internal IOCs.
Intelligence escalation protocol is been defined and the appropriate course of action is clearly established to address horizontal, vertical, and vendor escalation.
There is a formalized continuous improvement program in place that leverages feedback from intelligence consumers based on whether intelligence is actionable, informative, and insightful.
There are defined roles and responsibilities for the threat intelligence program.
An indicator of compromise collection and storage platform has been selected and implemented.
There is a formal, dedicated, and current security operations program budget.
There is a dedicated security operations sourcing strategy that clearly defines the specific sourcing criteria and applicable vendors.
There is a formalized and clearly defined security operations program strategy.
A tiered security operations methodology (tier 1 event monitoring, tier 2 incident response, tier 3 analysis and investigation) has been implemented.
Relevant data is preserved for an appropriate period of time within a centrally accessible database.
There is a formal process to ingest threat intelligence indicators with the security operation.
There is a formal process to ingest vulnerabilities and the respective CVEs within the security operation.
There is a formal process to escalate new and emerging threats to the appropriate stakeholders.
There is a formal process to create and deploy new signatures and correlation rules within security controls.
Event trending reports are produced and distributed to the necessary stakeholders on a periodic basis.
There is a dedicated team responsible for tuning sensors, updating firewalls and IDS/IPS SIEM technology, maintaining the IT infrastructure, and evaluating new security products.

Security operations staff have the necessary competencies and ongoing training to perform their responsibilities, e.g. correlation networking, log file analysis, deep packet analysis, and data analytics.
The security operations role has been  clearly defined as it relates to other teams such as incident response, threat intelligence, and vulnerability management.
Security controls have been deployed, documented, and are actively monitored  (SIEM, firewall, IDS/IPS, proxy, etc.).
Relevant security event data is stored in a centralized and accessible log server.
There is a formal, documented, and current framework for classifying and identifying incident severity.
Response procedures for specific incidents are documented in runbooks or playbooks and are frequently updated and evaluated.
Incident escalation protocol has been defined and the appropriate course of action is clearly established to address horizontal, vertical, and vendor escalation.
Security incident metrics are actively measured and tracked as benchmarks for future improvements.
There is a formalized post-mortem review and dedicated learning process for major security incidents.
There is a formalized public relations communication plan and process in the event of a major security incident.
There is a dedicated incident response team. Roles/responsibilities are defined, documented, and actively managed in a RACI charter.
There is a structured and actively communicated process for which end users can report incidents.
A centralized and easily accessible incident management or ticketing system is used to monitor incidents.
