items.control_description: Verify that symmetric keys used to verify submitted OTPs are highly protected, such as by using a hardware security module or secure operating system based key storage.
items.subdomain_name: Single or Multi Factor One Time Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that approved cryptographic algorithms are used in the generation, seeding, and verification of OTPs.
items.subdomain_name: Single or Multi Factor One Time Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that time-based OTP can be used only once within the validity period.
items.subdomain_name: Single or Multi Factor One Time Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that if a time-based multi-factor OTP token is re-used during the validity period, it is logged and rejected with secure notifications being sent to the holder of the device.
items.subdomain_name: Single or Multi Factor One Time Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify physical single-factor OTP generator can be revoked in case of theft or other loss. Ensure that revocation is immediately effective across logged in sessions, regardless of location.
items.subdomain_name: Single or Multi Factor One Time Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that biometric authenticators are limited to use only as secondary factors in conjunction with either something you have and something you know.
items.subdomain_name: Single or Multi Factor One Time Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that cryptographic keys used in verification are stored securely and protected against disclosure, such as using a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) or Hardware Security Module (HSM), or an OS service that can use this secure storage.
items.subdomain_name: Cryptographic Software and Devices Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that the challenge nonce is at least 64 bits in length, and statistically unique or unique over the lifetime of the cryptographic device.
items.subdomain_name: Cryptographic Software and Devices Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that approved cryptographic algorithms are used in the generation, seeding, and verification.
items.subdomain_name: Cryptographic Software and Devices Verifier Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that intra-service secrets do not rely on unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys or shared accounts with privileged access.
items.remarks: ASVS Level: LVL2: OS assisted, LVL3: HSM | CWE: 287 | NIST: 5.1.1.1

items.control_description: Verify that if passwords are required for service authentication, the service account used is not a default credential. (e.g. root/root or admin/admin are default in some services during installation).
items.remarks: ASVS Level: LVL2: OS assisted, LVL3: HSM | CWE: 255 | NIST: 5.1.1.1

items.control_description: Verify that passwords are stored with sufficient protection to prevent offline recovery attacks, including local system access.
items.remarks: ASVS Level: LVL2: OS assisted, LVL3: HSM | CWE: 522 | NIST: 5.1.1.1

items.control_description: Verify passwords, integrations with databases and third-party systems, seeds and internal secrets, and API keys are managed securely and not included in the source code or stored within source code repositories. Such storage SHOULD resist offline attacks. The use of a secure software key store (L1), hardware TPM, or an HSM (L3) is recommended for password storage.
items.remarks: ASVS Level: LVL2: OS assisted, LVL3: HSM | CWE: 798

items.control_description: Verify the application never reveals session tokens in URL parameters or error messages.
Verify the application generates a new session token on user authentication.
Verify that session tokens possess at least 64 bits of entropy.
Verify the application only stores session tokens in the browser using secure methods such as appropriately secured cookies (see section 3.4) or HTML 5 session storage.
Verify that session token are generated using approved cryptographic algorithms.
Verify that logout and expiration invalidate the session token, such that the back button or a downstream relying party does not resume an authenticated session, including across relying parties.

If authenticators permit users to remain logged in, verify that re-authentication occurs periodically both when actively used or after an idle period.
* L1: 30 days
* L2: 12 hours or 30 minutes of inactivity, 2FA optional
* L3: 12 hours or 15 minutes of inactivity, with 2FA

Verify that the application gives the option to terminate all other active sessions after a successful password change (including change via password reset/recovery), and that this is effective across the application, federated login (if present), and any relying parties.
Verify that users are able to view and (having re-entered login credentials) log out of any or all currently active sessions and devices.
Verify that cookie-based session tokens have the 'Secure' attribute set.
Verify that cookie-based session tokens have the 'HttpOnly' attribute set.
Verify that cookie-based session tokens utilize the 'SameSite' attribute to limit exposure to cross-site request forgery attacks.
Verify that cookie-based session tokens use "__Host-" prefix (see references) to provide session cookie confidentiality.

Verify that if the application is published under a domain name with other applications that set or use session cookies that might override or disclose the session cookies, set the path attribute in cookie-based session tokens using the most precise path possible.
Verify the application allows users to revoke OAuth tokens that form trust relationships with linked applications.
Verify the application uses session tokens rather than static API secrets and keys, except with legacy implementations.
Verify that stateless session tokens use digital signatures, encryption, and other countermeasures to protect against tampering, enveloping, replay, null cipher, and key substitution attacks.

Verify that relying parties specify the maximum authentication time to Credential Service Providers (CSPs) and that CSPs re-authenticate the subscriber if they haven't used a session within that period.
items.subdomain_name: Re-authentication from a Federation or Assertion

items.control_description: Verify that Credential Service Providers (CSPs) inform Relying Parties (RPs) of the last authentication event, to allow RPs to determine if they need to re-authenticate the user.
items.subdomain_name: Re-authentication from a Federation or Assertion

items.control_description: Verify the application ensures a valid login session or requires re-authentication or secondary verification before allowing any sensitive transactions or account modifications.
Verify that the application enforces access control rules on a trusted service layer, especially if client-side access control is present and could be bypassed.
Verify that all user and data attributes and policy information used by access controls cannot be manipulated by end users unless specifically authorized.

Verify that the principle of least privilege exists - users should only be able to access functions, data files, URLs, controllers, services, and other resources, for which they possess specific authorization. This implies protection against spoofing and elevation of privilege.

Verify that the principle of deny by default exists whereby new users/roles start with minimal or no permissions and users/roles do not receive access to new features until access is explicitly assigned.
Verify that access controls fail securely including when an exception occurs.

Verify that sensitive data and APIs are protected against Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) attacks targeting creation, reading, updating and deletion of records, such as creating or updating someone else's record, viewing everyone's records, or deleting all records.

Verify that the application or framework enforces a strong anti-CSRF mechanism to protect authenticated functionality, and effective anti-automation or anti-CSRF protects unauthenticated functionality.
Verify administrative interfaces use appropriate multi-factor authentication to prevent unauthorized use.

Verify that directory browsing is disabled unless deliberately desired. Additionally, applications should not allow discovery or disclosure of file or directory metadata, such as Thumbs.db, .DS_Store, .git or .svn folders.

Verify the application has additional authorization (such as step up or adaptive authentication) for lower value systems, and / or segregation of duties for high value applications to enforce anti-fraud controls as per the risk of application and past fraud.

Verify that the application has defenses against HTTP parameter pollution attacks, particularly if the application framework makes no distinction about the source of request parameters (GET, POST, cookies, headers, or environment variables).

Verify that frameworks protect against mass parameter assignment attacks, or that the application has countermeasures to protect against unsafe parameter assignment, such as marking fields private or similar.
Verify that all input (HTML form fields, REST requests, URL parameters, HTTP headers, cookies, batch files, RSS feeds, etc) is validated using positive validation (allow lists).

Verify that structured data is strongly typed and validated against a defined schema including allowed characters, length and pattern (e.g. credit card numbers or telephone, or validating that two related fields are reasonable, such as checking that suburb and zip/postcode match).
Verify that URL redirects and forwards only allow destinations which appear on an allow list, or show a warning when redirecting to potentially untrusted content.
Verify that all untrusted HTML input from WYSIWYG editors or similar is properly sanitized with an HTML sanitizer library or framework feature.
Verify that unstructured data is sanitized to enforce safety measures such as allowed characters and length.
Verify that the application sanitizes user input before passing to mail systems to protect against SMTP or IMAP injection.

Verify that the application avoids the use of eval or other dynamic code execution features. Where there is no alternative, any user input being included must be sanitized or sandboxed before being executed.
Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by ensuring that any user input being included is sanitized or sandboxed.

Verify that the application protects against SSRF attacks, by validating or sanitizing untrusted data or HTTP file metadata, such as filenames and URL input fields, and uses allow lists of protocols, domains, paths and ports.

Verify that the application sanitizes, disables, or sandboxes user-supplied Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) scriptable content, especially as they relate to XSS resulting from inline scripts, and foreignObject.
Verify that the application sanitizes, disables, or sandboxes user-supplied scriptable or expression template language content, such as Markdown, CSS or XSL stylesheets, BBCode, or similar.

Verify that output encoding is relevant for the interpreter and context required. For example, use encoders specifically for HTML values, HTML attributes, JavaScript, URL parameters, HTTP headers, SMTP, and others as the context requires, especially from untrusted inputs (e.g. names with Unicode or apostrophes, such as ねこ or O'Hara).
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that output encoding preserves the user's chosen character set and locale, such that any Unicode character point is valid and safely handled.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that context-aware, preferably automated - or at worst, manual - output escaping protects against reflected, stored, and DOM based XSS.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that data selection or database queries (e.g. SQL, HQL, ORM, NoSQL) use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from database injection attacks.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that where parameterized or safer mechanisms are not present, context-specific output encoding is used to protect against injection attacks, such as the use of SQL escaping to protect against SQL injection.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that the application protects against JavaScript or JSON injection attacks, including for eval attacks, remote JavaScript includes, Content Security Policy (CSP) bypasses, DOM XSS, and JavaScript expression evaluation.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that the application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities, or that specific security controls to prevent LDAP injection have been implemented.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that the application protects against OS command injection and that operating system calls use parameterized OS queries or use contextual command line output encoding.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that the application protects against Local File Inclusion (LFI) or Remote File Inclusion (RFI) attacks.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that the application protects against XPath injection or XML injection attacks.
items.subdomain_name: Output encoding and Injection Prevention Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that the application uses memory-safe string, safer memory copy and pointer arithmetic to detect or prevent stack, buffer, or heap overflows.
items.subdomain_name: Memory, String and Unmanaged Code Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that format strings do not take potentially hostile input, and are constant.
items.subdomain_name: Memory, String and Unmanaged Code Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that sign, range, and input validation techniques are used to prevent integer overflows.
items.subdomain_name: Memory, String and Unmanaged Code Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that serialized objects use integrity checks or are encrypted to prevent hostile object creation or data tampering.

Verify that the application correctly restricts XML parsers to only use the most restrictive configuration possible and to ensure that unsafe features such as resolving external entities are disabled to prevent XML eXternal Entity (XXE) attacks.
Verify that deserialization of untrusted data is avoided or is protected in both custom code and third-party libraries (such as JSON, XML and YAML parsers).
Verify that when parsing JSON in browsers or JavaScript-based backends, JSON.parse is used to parse the JSON document. Do not use eval to parse JSON.

Verify that regulated private data is stored encrypted while at rest, such as Personally Identifiable Information (PII), sensitive personal information, or data assessed likely to be subject to EU's GDPR.
Verify that regulated health data is stored encrypted while at rest, such as medical records, medical device details, or de-anonymized research records.

Verify that regulated financial data is stored encrypted while at rest, such as financial accounts, defaults or credit history, tax records, pay history, beneficiaries, or de-anonymized market or research records.
Verify that all cryptographic modules fail securely, and errors are handled in a way that does not enable Padding Oracle attacks.
Verify that industry proven or government approved cryptographic algorithms, modes, and libraries are used, instead of custom coded cryptography.
Verify that encryption initialization vector, cipher configuration, and block modes are configured securely using the latest advice.
Verify that random number, encryption or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers or modes, can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks.

Verify that known insecure block modes (i.e. ECB, etc.), padding modes (i.e. PKCS#1 v1.5, etc.), ciphers with small block sizes (i.e. Triple-DES, Blowfish, etc.), and weak hashing algorithms (i.e. MD5, SHA1, etc.) are not used unless required for backwards compatibility.

Verify that nonces, initialization vectors, and other single use numbers must not be used more than once with a given encryption key. The method of generation must be appropriate for the algorithm being used.
Verify that encrypted data is authenticated via signatures, authenticated cipher modes, or HMAC to ensure that ciphertext is not altered by an unauthorized party.
Verify that all cryptographic operations are constant-time, with no 'short-circuit' operations in comparisons, calculations, or returns, to avoid leaking information.

Verify that all random numbers, random file names, random GUIDs, and random strings are generated using the cryptographic module's approved cryptographically secure random number generator when these random values are intended to be not guessable by an attacker.

Verify that random GUIDs are created using the GUID v4 algorithm, and a Cryptographically-secure Pseudo-random Number Generator (CSPRNG). GUIDs created using other pseudo-random number generators may be predictable.
Verify that random numbers are created with proper entropy even when the application is under heavy load, or that the application degrades gracefully in such circumstances.
Verify that a secrets management solution such as a key vault is used to securely create, store, control access to and destroy secrets.
Verify that key material is not exposed to the application but instead uses an isolated security module like a vault for cryptographic operations.
Verify that the application does not log credentials or payment details. Session tokens should only be stored in logs in an irreversible, hashed form.
Verify that the application does not log other sensitive data as defined under local privacy laws or relevant security policy.
Verify that the application logs security relevant events including successful and failed authentication events, access control failures, deserialization failures and input validation failures.
Verify that each log event includes necessary information that would allow for a detailed investigation of the timeline when an event happens.

Verify that all authentication decisions are logged, without storing sensitive session identifiers or passwords. This should include requests with relevant metadata needed for security investigations.
Verify that all access control decisions can be logged and all failed decisions are logged. This should include requests with relevant metadata needed for security investigations.
Verify that the application appropriately encodes user-supplied data to prevent log injection.
Verify that all events are protected from injection when viewed in log viewing software.
Verify that security logs are protected from unauthorized access and modification.
Verify that time sources are synchronized to the correct time and time zone. Strongly consider logging only in UTC if systems are global to assist with post-incident forensic analysis.
Verify that a generic message is shown when an unexpected or security sensitive error occurs, potentially with a unique ID which support personnel can use to investigate.
Verify that exception handling (or a functional equivalent) is used across the codebase to account for expected and unexpected error conditions.
Verify that a "last resort" error handler is defined which will catch all unhandled exceptions.
Verify the application protects sensitive data from being cached in server components such as load balancers and application caches.
Verify that all cached or temporary copies of sensitive data stored on the server are protected from unauthorized access or purged/invalidated after the authorized user accesses the sensitive data.
Verify the application minimizes the number of parameters in a request, such as hidden fields, Ajax variables, cookies and header values.
Verify the application can detect and alert on abnormal numbers of requests, such as by IP, user, total per hour or day, or whatever makes sense for the application.
Verify that regular backups of important data are performed and that test restoration of data is performed.
Verify that backups are stored securely to prevent data from being stolen or corrupted.
Verify the application sets sufficient anti-caching headers so that sensitive data is not cached in modern browsers.
Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as HTML5 local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain sensitive data or PII.
Verify that authenticated data is cleared from client storage, such as the browser DOM, after the client or session is terminated.
Verify that sensitive data is sent to the server in the HTTP message body or headers, and that query string parameters from any HTTP verb do not contain sensitive data.
Verify that users have a method to remove or export their data on demand.

Verify that users are provided clear language regarding collection and use of supplied personal information and that users have provided opt-in consent for the use of that data before it is used in any way.
Verify that all sensitive data created and processed by the application has been identified, and ensure that a policy is in place on how to deal with sensitive data.
Verify accessing sensitive data is audited (without logging the sensitive data itself), if the data is collected under relevant data protection directives or where logging of access is required.
Verify that sensitive information contained in memory is overwritten as soon as it is no longer required to mitigate memory dumping attacks, using zeroes or random data.
Verify that sensitive or private information that is required to be encrypted, is encrypted using approved algorithms that provide both confidentiality and integrity.
Verify that sensitive personal information is subject to data retention classification, such that old or out of date data is deleted automatically, on a schedule, or as the situation requires.
Verify that secured TLS is used for all client connectivity, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.
Verify using online or up to date TLS testing tools that only strong algorithms, ciphers, and protocols are enabled, with the strongest algorithms and ciphers set as preferred.

Verify that old versions of SSL and TLS protocols, algorithms, ciphers, and configuration are disabled, such as SSLv2, SSLv3, or TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. The latest version of TLS should be the preferred cipher suite.

Verify that connections to and from the server use trusted TLS certificates. Where internally generated or self-signed certificates are used, the server must be configured to only trust specific internal CAs and specific self-signed certificates. All others should be rejected.

Verify that encrypted communications such as TLS is used for all inbound and outbound connections, including for management ports, monitoring, authentication, API, or web service calls, database, cloud, serverless, mainframe, external, and partner connections. The server must not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.
Verify that all encrypted connections to external systems that involve sensitive information or functions are authenticated.
Verify that proper certification revocation, such as Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Stapling, is enabled and configured.
Verify that backend TLS connection failures are logged.
Verify that a code analysis tool is in use that can detect potentially malicious code, such as time functions, unsafe file operations and network connections.

Verify that the application source code and third party libraries do not contain unauthorized phone home or data collection capabilities. Where such functionality exists, obtain the user's permission for it to operate before collecting any data.
Verify that the application does not ask for unnecessary or excessive permissions to privacy related features or sensors, such as contacts, cameras, microphones, or location.

Verify that the application source code and third party libraries do not contain back doors, such as hard-coded or additional undocumented accounts or keys, code obfuscation, undocumented binary blobs, rootkits, or anti-debugging, insecure debugging features, or otherwise out of date, insecure, or hidden functionality that could be used maliciously if discovered.
Verify that the application source code and third party libraries do not contain time bombs by searching for date and time related functions.
Verify that the application source code and third party libraries do not contain malicious code, such as salami attacks, logic bypasses, or logic bombs.
Verify that the application source code and third party libraries do not contain Easter eggs or any other potentially unwanted functionality.

Verify that if the application has a client or server auto-update feature, updates should be obtained over secure channels and digitally signed. The update code must validate the digital signature of the update before installing or executing the update.

Verify that the application employs integrity protections, such as code signing or subresource integrity. The application must not load or execute code from untrusted sources, such as loading includes, modules, plugins, code, or libraries from untrusted sources or the Internet.

Verify that the application has protection from subdomain takeovers if the application relies upon DNS entries or DNS subdomains, such as expired domain names, out of date DNS pointers or CNAMEs, expired projects at public source code repos, or transient cloud APIs, serverless functions, or storage buckets (autogen-bucket-id.cloud.example.com) or similar. Protections can include ensuring that DNS names used by applications are regularly checked for expiry or change.
Verify the application will only process business logic flows for the same user in sequential step order and without skipping steps.
Verify the application will only process business logic flows with all steps being processed in realistic human time, i.e. transactions are not submitted too quickly.
Verify the application has appropriate limits for specific business actions or transactions which are correctly enforced on a per user basis.
Verify the application has sufficient anti-automation controls to detect and protect against data exfiltration, excessive business logic requests, excessive file uploads or denial of service attacks.
Verify the application has business logic limits or validation to protect against likely business risks or threats, identified using threat modeling or similar methodologies.
Verify the application does not suffer from "Time Of Check to Time Of Use" (TOCTOU) issues or other race conditions for sensitive operations.

Verify the application monitors for unusual events or activity from a business logic perspective. For example, attempts to perform actions out of order or actions which a normal user would never attempt.
Verify the application has configurable alerting when automated attacks or unusual activity is detected.
Verify that the application will not accept large files that could fill up storage or cause a denial of service.
Verify that compressed files are checked for "zip bombs" - small input files that will decompress into huge files thus exhausting file storage limits.
Verify that a file size quota and maximum number of files per user is enforced to ensure that a single user cannot fill up the storage with too many files, or excessively large files.
Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are validated to be of expected type based on the file's content.
Verify that user-submitted filename metadata is not used directly by system or framework filesystems and that a URL API is used to protect against path traversal.
Verify that user-submitted filename metadata is validated or ignored to prevent the disclosure, creation, updating or removal of local files (LFI).

Verify that user-submitted filename metadata is validated or ignored to prevent the disclosure or execution of remote files via Remote File Inclusion (RFI) or Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.

Verify that the application protects against Reflective File Download (RFD) by validating or ignoring user-submitted filenames in a JSON, JSONP, or URL parameter, the response Content-Type header should be set to text/plain, and the Content-Disposition header should have a fixed filename.
Verify that untrusted file metadata is not used directly with system API or libraries, to protect against OS command injection.

Verify that the application does not include and execute functionality from untrusted sources, such as unverified content distribution networks, JavaScript libraries, node npm libraries, or server-side DLLs.
Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are stored outside the web root, with limited permissions, preferably with strong validation.
Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are scanned by antivirus scanners to prevent upload of known malicious content.

Verify that the web tier is configured to serve only files with specific file extensions to prevent unintentional information and source code leakage. For example, backup files (e.g. .bak), temporary working files (e.g. .swp), compressed files (.zip, .tar.gz, etc) and other extensions commonly used by editors should be blocked unless required.
Verify that direct requests to uploaded files will never be executed as HTML/JavaScript content.
Verify that the web or application server is configured with an allow list of resources or systems to which the server can send requests or load data/files from.
Verify that all application components use the same encodings and parsers to avoid parsing attacks that exploit different URI or file parsing behavior that could be used in SSRF and RFI attacks.
items.subdomain_name: Generic Web Service Security Verification Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that access to administration and management functions is limited to authorized administrators.
items.subdomain_name: Generic Web Service Security Verification Requirements

items.control_description: Verify API URLs do not expose sensitive information, such as the API key, session tokens etc.
items.subdomain_name: Generic Web Service Security Verification Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that authorization decisions are made at both the URI, enforced by programmatic or declarative security at the controller or router, and at the resource level, enforced by model-based permissions.
items.subdomain_name: Generic Web Service Security Verification Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that requests containing unexpected or missing content types are rejected with appropriate headers (HTTP response status 406 Unacceptable or 415 Unsupported Media Type).
items.subdomain_name: Generic Web Service Security Verification Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that enabled RESTful HTTP methods are a valid choice for the user or action, such as preventing normal users using DELETE or PUT on protected API or resources.
Verify that JSON schema validation is in place and verified before accepting input.

Verify that RESTful web services that utilize cookies are protected from Cross-Site Request Forgery via the use of at least one or more of the following: double submit cookie pattern, CSRF nonces, or Origin request header checks.
Verify that REST services have anti-automation controls to protect against excessive calls, especially if the API is unauthenticated.
Verify that REST services explicitly check the incoming Content-Type to be the expected one, such as application/xml or application/json.

Verify that the message headers and payload are trustworthy and not modified in transit. Requiring strong encryption for transport (TLS only) may be sufficient in many cases as it provides both confidentiality and integrity protection. Per-message digital signatures can provide additional assurance on top of the transport protections for high-security applications but bring with them additional complexity and risks to weigh against the benefits.
Verify that XSD schema validation takes place to ensure a properly formed XML document, followed by validation of each input field before any processing of that data takes place.
Verify that the message payload is signed using WS-Security to ensure reliable transport between client and service.

Verify that a query allow list or a combination of depth limiting and amount limiting is used to prevent GraphQL or data layer expression Denial of Service (DoS) as a result of expensive, nested queries. For more advanced scenarios, query cost analysis should be used.
items.subdomain_name: GraphQL and other Web Service Data Layer Security Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that GraphQL or other data layer authorization logic should be implemented at the business logic layer instead of the GraphQL layer.
items.subdomain_name: GraphQL and other Web Service Data Layer Security Requirements

items.control_description: Verify that the application build and deployment processes are performed in a secure and repeatable way, such as CI / CD automation, automated configuration management, and automated deployment scripts.

Verify that compiler flags are configured to enable all available buffer overflow protections and warnings, including stack randomization, data execution prevention, and to break the build if an unsafe pointer, memory, format string, integer, or string operations are found.
Verify that server configuration is hardened as per the recommendations of the application server and frameworks in use.

Verify that the application, configuration, and all dependencies can be re-deployed using automated deployment scripts, built from a documented and tested runbook in a reasonable time, or restored from backups in a timely fashion.
Verify that authorized administrators can verify the integrity of all security-relevant configurations to detect tampering.
Verify that all components are up to date, preferably using a dependency checker during build or compile time.
Verify that all unneeded features, documentation, samples, configurations are removed, such as sample applications, platform documentation, and default or example users.

Verify that if application assets, such as JavaScript libraries, CSS stylesheets or web fonts, are hosted externally on a content delivery network (CDN) or external provider, Subresource Integrity (SRI) is used to validate the integrity of the asset.
Verify that third party components come from pre-defined, trusted and continually maintained repositories.
Verify that an inventory catalog is maintained of all third party libraries in use.
Verify that the attack surface is reduced by sandboxing or encapsulating third party libraries to expose only the required behaviour into the application.
Verify that web or application server and framework error messages are configured to deliver user actionable, customized responses to eliminate any unintended security disclosures.
Verify that web or application server and application framework debug modes are disabled in production to eliminate debug features, developer consoles, and unintended security disclosures.
Verify that the HTTP headers or any part of the HTTP response do not expose detailed version information of system components.
Verify that every HTTP response contains a Content-Type header. text/*, */*+xml and application/xml content types should also specify a safe character set (e.g., UTF-8, ISO-8859-1).
Verify that all API responses contain Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="api.json" header (or other appropriate filename for the content type).
Verify that a Content Security Policy (CSP) response header is in place that helps mitigate impact for XSS attacks like HTML, DOM, JSON, and JavaScript injection vulnerabilities.
Verify that all responses contain a X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header.
Verify that a Strict-Transport-Security header is included on all responses and for all subdomains, such as Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=15724800; includeSubdomains.
Verify that a suitable "Referrer-Policy" header is included, such as "no-referrer" or "same-origin".

Verify that the content of a web application cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default and that embedding of the exact resources is only allowed where necessary by using suitable Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options response headers.

Verify that the application server only accepts the HTTP methods in use by the application/API, including pre-flight OPTIONS, and logs/alerts on any requests that are not valid for the application context.
Verify that the supplied Origin header is not used for authentication or access control decisions, as the Origin header can easily be changed by an attacker.

Verify that the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Access-Control-Allow-Origin header uses a strict allow list of trusted domains and subdomains to match against and does not support the "null" origin.
Verify that HTTP headers added by a trusted proxy or SSO devices, such as a bearer token, are authenticated by the application.
Determine and appoint a Data Protection Officer where required by the Regulations.
items.evidence_reference: DPO appointment letter; role mandate; org chart
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 30(2) | Q: Has the entity assessed whether a DPO is required, and appointed one with defined responsibilities?

items.control_description: Maintain Records of Processing Activities (ROPA) with the minimum required fields.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 31 | Q: Is a ROPA maintained covering contact details, purposes, data subject categories, recipients, transfers and retention periods?

items.control_description: Conduct data protection impact assessments for relevant products/services.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 22 | Q: Are impact assessments performed based on the nature of processing activities?

items.control_description: Bind staff and contractors to confidentiality, including after the relationship ends.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 41 | Q: Are all persons processing personal data under enforceable confidentiality obligations?

items.control_description: Cooperate with the Competent Authority and act on its requests.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 30(3) | Q: Is there a defined process to respond to SDAIA information requests and directions?

items.control_description: Register in the SDAIA national register where applicable.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 30(4)/33 | Q: Has the entity registered, or assessed its obligation to register, with SDAIA?

items.control_description: Establish an overarching data protection governance framework with clear ownership.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: General | Q: Is there an approved data protection policy and an accountable owner?

items.control_description: Obtain consent before processing, or before changing the purpose, unless an exception applies.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 5(1) | Q: Is valid consent captured before processing, with purpose-change controls?

items.control_description: Handle explicit-consent cases and legal-guardian consent for those lacking capacity.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 5(1) | Q: Are explicit-consent scenarios and guardian consent mechanisms in place?

items.control_description: Allow data subjects to withdraw consent at any time.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 5(2) | Q: Can a data subject easily withdraw consent, with downstream effect?

items.control_description: Document and validate any reliance on non-consent legal bases.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 6 | Q: Where processing relies on Art. 6 bases (legitimate interest, legal obligation, etc.), is each documented and justified?

items.control_description: Do not condition a service on consent unless directly related to that processing.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 7 | Q: Is consent free of improper bundling with unrelated services?

items.control_description: Collect directly from the data subject; use indirect collection only in permitted cases.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 10 | Q: Is data collected directly, with indirect sourcing limited to lawful exceptions?

items.control_description: Ensure collection purposes are linked to the controller's purposes and lawful.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 11(1) | Q: Are stated purposes legitimate and not contrary to law?

items.control_description: Limit collection to the minimum data necessary (data minimisation).
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 11(3) | Q: Is collected data limited to what is necessary, and reduced once the purpose is met?

items.control_description: Use clear, secure, fair collection methods free of deception.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 11(2) | Q: Are collection methods direct, secure and non-misleading?

items.control_description: Verify accuracy, completeness, timeliness and relevance before processing.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 14 | Q: Are data quality checks performed before processing?

items.control_description: Publish a privacy policy and make it available before collection.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 12 | Q: Is a privacy policy available to data subjects prior to collection?

items.control_description: Provide a collection notice with all mandated elements.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 13 | Q: Does the notice cover legal basis, purpose, mandatory/optional fields, recipients, transfers abroad, risks and rights?

items.control_description: Enable the right to be informed of legal basis and purpose.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 4(1) | Q: Can the entity inform subjects of the basis and purpose of collection?

items.control_description: Enable access requests, applying lawful restrictions correctly.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 4(2)/9 | Q: Is there an access-request process that also applies Art. 9/16 restrictions?

items.control_description: Provide data in a readable, clear format on request (portability).
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 4(3) | Q: Can subjects obtain their data in a clear, readable format?

items.control_description: Handle correction/completion/update and notify downstream recipients.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 4(4)/17 | Q: Are corrections processed and propagated to entities that received the data?

items.control_description: Handle destruction requests subject to retention rules.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 4(5)/18 | Q: Can subjects request destruction, with lawful retention exceptions applied?

items.control_description: Respond to data subject requests within the Regulation timeframes.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 21 | Q: Are DSRs tracked and answered within required timeframes?

items.control_description: Handle complaints, including escalation to the Competent Authority.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 34 | Q: Is there a complaints process for data subjects?

items.control_description: Disclose personal data only in permitted cases.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 15 | Q: Is disclosure restricted to the lawful situations in Art. 15?

items.control_description: Screen for prohibited-disclosure scenarios.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 16 | Q: Are disclosures checked against Art. 16 prohibitions (security, others' privacy, legal capacity, etc.)?

items.control_description: Destroy personal data without undue delay once the purpose ends.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 18(1) | Q: Is data destroyed promptly when no longer needed?

items.control_description: Document lawful retention beyond purpose (legal / judicial).
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 18(2) | Q: Are retention-beyond-purpose cases identified with a legal basis?

items.control_description: Ensure destruction renders data unreadable/irretrievable (or anonymised).
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 7 (def.) | Q: Are destruction/anonymisation methods irreversible per SDAIA guidance?

items.control_description: Implement organisational, administrative and technical safeguards.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 19 | Q: Are appropriate security controls implemented (mappable to NCA ECC / ISO 27001)?

items.control_description: Protect personal data during transfer.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 19 | Q: Are data-in-transit protections (e.g. encryption) in place?

items.control_description: Notify the Competent Authority of breaches per the Regulations.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 20(1) | Q: Is there a process to detect and notify SDAIA of breaches?

items.control_description: Notify affected data subjects where required.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 20(2) | Q: Are affected subjects notified when a breach harms their rights/interests?

items.control_description: Base transfers outside KSA on a permitted purpose.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 29(1) | Q: Are transfers abroad mapped to a lawful Art. 29(1) purpose?

items.control_description: Ensure adequacy, no prejudice to national interest, and data minimisation.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 29(2) | Q: Has a transfer assessment confirmed adequate protection and minimum data?

items.control_description: Use SDAIA Standard Contractual Clauses / binding common rules where needed.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Transfer Reg. | Q: Are approved SCCs or BCRs executed for relevant transfers?

items.control_description: Select processors that provide the necessary guarantees.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 8 | Q: Are processors assessed for adequate safeguards before engagement?

items.control_description: Bind processors by contract and monitor their compliance.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 8 | Q: Are processors under a data processing agreement and actively monitored?

items.control_description: Govern subsequent (sub-processor) contracts.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 8 | Q: Are sub-processing arrangements controlled and flowed down?

items.control_description: Apply additional Health Data controls and access minimisation.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 23 | Q: Is access to Health Data limited to the minimum necessary staff?

items.control_description: Apply additional Credit Data controls per the Credit Information Law.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 24 | Q: Is explicit consent obtained and the subject notified of disclosure requests?

items.control_description: Control research/statistical processing without consent.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 27 | Q: Is non-consent research processing de-identified per the rules?

items.control_description: Restrict copying of identifiable official documents.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 28 | Q: Is copying official documents limited to lawful cases?

items.control_description: Obtain prior consent and provide an opt-out for marketing/awareness messages.
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 25 | Q: Is prior consent captured and a clear opt-out mechanism provided?

items.control_description: Process marketing data only if collected directly with consent (excluding Sensitive Data).
items.remarks: PDPL Ref: Art. 26 | Q: Is marketing data collected directly with consent and free of Sensitive Data?

assessments.name: Digital Operations Maturity
assessments.file_name: Digital Operations Maturity Assessment_Questionnaire_2020_Rapid and Full      NEW ASSESSMENT.xlsx

items.control_description: 1. How do you feed and reconcile data from different systems?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Data ingestion along with quality assurance requires extensive manual efforts.  ||  Emerging: Data is mostly fed automatically for each supply chain area but requires manual maintenance and integration across functions. Local data storage.  ||  Advanced: Internal data is automatically fed into the system and screened from sources within each supply chain area and stored on connected databases.  ||  Differentiated: Internal and external data is automatically fed into the system and screened within each SC area and stored in a common data lake to make it accessible across the supply chain.  ||  Best In Class: Fully automatic ingestion of data from all supply chain areas, suppliers, partners and other external sources. Automated pre-processing of raw data and storage in data lakes. Machine learning is used to connect the data.

items.control_description: 2. How do you connect the data and information along the value chain and capture their relationships?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Data across the supply chain from raw material to customer and back is not connected across functions.  ||  Emerging: Some supply chain functions started to connect data across the supply chain but there is no E2E connection yet. Relationships are only partly captured.  ||  Advanced: All internal and external data from public data sources are connected to each other and their relationships are captured with some manual effort.  ||  Differentiated: All internal and external data from raw material to customer and back are captured, connected and the relationships are captured in a graph database (partially manual corrections needed).  ||  Best In Class: All internal and external data from raw material to customer and back are captured, connected and the relationships are captured in a graph database and automatically optimized through AI (e.g. machine learning algorithms).

items.control_description: 16. How well do current data structures support analytics requirements?
items.remarks: Basic: Current data structures are hierarchical or network models; important data stored in excel or access.  ||  Emerging: Individual business units create their own data models for reporting purposes.  ||  Advanced: Organization data model exists but business units create their own data marts for analytics.  ||  Differentiated: Organizational data warehouse exists for simple reporting capabilities.  ||  Best In Class: Organizational data lake exists; granular data is available together with denormalized tables for reporting as also XML support.

items.control_description: 17. What is the expected turnaround time to receive and process data?
items.remarks: Basic: Data processed daily is received with a 2 day delay; quarterly reports take over 2 weeks to generate.  ||  Emerging: Data processed daily is received with a 1 day delay; quarterly reports take 1-2 weeks to generate.  ||  Advanced: Data processed daily is received with a 1/2 day delay; quarterly reports take <1 week to generate.  ||  Differentiated: Data is processed daily in real-time; quarterly reports are generated in less than 3 days.  ||  Best In Class: There is real-time data warehousing and reporting.

items.control_description: 18. How many instances of the same data exist and how is data shared across the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: Multiple sources of the same data exist across the organization and within individual business units; understanding of attribute overlap is unclear.  ||  Emerging: Some data rationalization is conducted in silos within individual business areas but data is not shared across the organization.  ||  Advanced: A common organization-wide data model exists for some functions but business units still create additional siloed versions of information.  ||  Differentiated: An organization-wide data warehouse provides a single source of information to business units and only specific projects require business units to create their own data marts.  ||  Best In Class: There is a single source of data; the source is well defined and easy to find and meets almost all business requirements.

items.control_description: 19. What management practices and processes are in place to measure and control the quality of data collected by the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: No formal or informal processes exist to ensure or measure data quality.  ||  Emerging: Informal processes for ensuring or measuring data quality exist but there is little understanding and usage; data management is reactive in nature.  ||  Advanced: Formal processes and procedures for ensuring or measuring data quality exist with less than 50% usage across the organization; data management is proactive in nature for critical data only.  ||  Differentiated: Formal processes and procedures for ensuring or measuring data quality exist with greater than 50% usage across the organization; data management is proactive in nature.  ||  Best In Class: Processes and procedures for ensuring or measuring data quality are defined at the organization level and used across more than 90% of the organization.

items.control_description: How mature are your analysis capabilities (from descriptive to prescriptive)?
items.remarks: Basic: Data analytics mainly descriptive using excel and simple algorithms. No prescriptive analytics capabilities in place.  ||  Emerging: There are selected narrow topics for prescriptive analytics (e.g. isolated pilots).  ||  Advanced: The supply chain is run by artificial intelligence: it manages and optimizes all process across the whole supply chain where possible, without partner integration (e.g. suppliers delivering raw materials).  ||  Differentiated: The supply chain is run by artificial intelligence: it manages and optimizes all process across the whole SC and integrates partners for selected use cases.  ||  Best In Class: The supply chain is run by artificial intelligence: it manages and optimizes all process across the whole supply chain also integrating partner.

items.control_description: How do you apply prescriptive data analytics technologies (e.g. AI) in your company?
items.remarks: Basic: AI is not used.  ||  Emerging: There are selected narrow topics for AI within some functions (e.g. isolated pilots).  ||  Advanced: AI is used for process optimization and decision taking on selected topics within one supply chain step e.g. warehousing or logistics (silo) - Automation.  ||  Differentiated: AI used for process optimization and decision taking on selected topics across various supply chain steps e.g. warehousing and logistics etc. - Augmented intelligence.  ||  Best In Class: AI is taking decisions across all supply chain processes, self-learning and autonomous systems. External factors also taken into consideration - Autonomous intelligence.

items.control_description: Do you have the data analytics use cases clearly described along the end-to-end value chain?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Data analytics use cases are only defined for individual, narrow topics.  ||  Emerging: Each function across the supply chain has a data analytics roadmap but it is not connected across the E2E supply chain.  ||  Advanced: The data analytics use cases and roadmap are defined, aligned and implemented to a good extent across functions. There is one jointly prioritized roadmap based on the company's business needs.  ||  Differentiated: The data analytics use cases and roadmap are defined, aligned and partly implemented across functions and together with external supply chain partners. There is one jointly prioritized roadmap based on the company's and the partner's business needs.  ||  Best In Class: All key data analytics use cases are implemented together with the affected partners. There is an aligned roadmap for the remaining topics.

items.control_description: 12. What is the scale of impact of analytics projects in the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: The impact of analytics projects are limited to only a portion of a business unit.  ||  Emerging: At least one analytics project has an impact over an entire business unit.  ||  Advanced: Atleast one analytics project has an impact on more than one business unit.  ||  Differentiated: At least one analytics project has an impact over a half of the business units in the organization.  ||  Best In Class: There are multiple analytics projects that have an impact on the whole organization.

items.control_description: 13. What proportion of the overall personnel budget is allocated to analytics projects?
items.remarks: Basic: The personnel budget of all analytics projects is less than 1% of the total personnel budget.  ||  Emerging: The personnel budget of all analytics projects is between 1% and 5% of the total personnel budget.  ||  Advanced: The personnel budget of all analytics projects is between 5% and 10% of the total personnel budget.  ||  Differentiated: The personnel budget of all analytics projects is between 10% and 20% of the total personnel budget.  ||  Best In Class: The personnel budget of all analytics projects is greater than 20% of the total personnel budget.

items.control_description: 14. Are analytics algorithms used to make real-time business decisions?
items.remarks: Basic: Analytics algorithms are not used to make real-time business decisions.  ||  Emerging: Analytics algorithms are currently being experimented with for making a few real-time business decisions.  ||  Advanced: Analytics algorithms are used to make some but not important real-time business decisions.  ||  Differentiated: Analytics algorithms are used to make some important real-time business decisions.  ||  Best In Class: Analytics algorithms are extensively used to make many important real-time business decisions.

items.control_description: 20. How does the organization characterize the sensitivity of information and implement controls to prevent unwarranted access to data?
items.remarks: Basic: The organization does this through system access only.  ||  Emerging: Data classification exists at the table level.  ||  Advanced: Data classification exists at the column level but is only implemented at the business unit level.  ||  Differentiated: Development of a data classification scheme is implemented at the business unit level.  ||  Best In Class: Security is mapped to an organization-wide data classification supply chainheme; encryption exists as does row / column based access.

items.control_description: 15. What is the combined ROI of analytics projects?
items.remarks: Basic: The combined ROI of analytics projects is less than 100%.  ||  Emerging: The combined ROI of analytics projects is above 100%.  ||  Advanced: The combined ROI of analytics projects is greater than 200%.  ||  Differentiated: The combined ROI of analytics projects is greater than 500%.  ||  Best In Class: The combined ROI of analytics projects is greater than 1000%.

items.control_description: 21. What is the level of automation of data and analytics processes across the organization?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: The organization does not have analytics automation in place.  ||  Emerging: Analytics is predominantly manual in nature, with select automated processes established and utilized.  ||  Advanced: Periodic analytics projects (monthly, quarterly, yearly reporting, etc.) are automated to generate and report insights.  ||  Differentiated: Analytics is conducted and corresponding insights are built into business processes by automating them as business rules; no formalized processes have been established to change business rules based on findings.  ||  Best In Class: Analytics is conducted and corresponding insights are built into business processes by automating them as business rules; automated processes have been established to alter business rules due to human overrides or change triggers.

items.control_description: 22. Has the organization established standard processes for applying analytics?
items.remarks: Basic: The organization does not have standard processes for applying analytics.  ||  Emerging: The organization has defined standard processes for applying analytics in a few business processes.  ||  Advanced: The organization has defined standard processes for applying analytics to functions across two business units.  ||  Differentiated: The organization has defined standard processes for applying analytics to functions across three or more business units.  ||  Best In Class: The organization has defined standard processes for applying analytics for all kinds of analytics.

items.control_description: 26. How are analytics investment decisions made in the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: Analytics investment decisions are made in an ad hoc manner in the organization.  ||  Emerging: Analytics investment decisions follow informal processes.  ||  Advanced: Analytics investment decisions are made at the business unit level.  ||  Differentiated: Analytics investment decisions are optimized at the organization level.  ||  Best In Class: Analytics investment decisions are aligned with organization's strategic goals.

items.control_description: 27. How effectively does the culture of the organization provide a foundation for employing and sustaining analytics practices?
items.remarks: Basic: Information gathering is siloed across business units and there is no collaboration or data sharing in place; decisions are primarily based on anecdotal measures and intuition and decision making criteria vary greatly across the organization.  ||  Emerging: Information gathering is siloed across business units but there are short-term collaborative efforts on an ad-hoc basis for specific projects; decisions are primarily based on anecdotal measures and intuition and decision making criteria vary greatly across the organization.  ||  Advanced: Information is frequently shared across business units using informal processes and procedures. Specific business lines use information to drive decisions.  ||  Differentiated: There is widespread organizational data gathering and sharing with standardized collaboration processes; decision making is information driven.  ||  Best In Class: There is Information transparency and availability across the organization; information-driven decision making pervades the organization from front-line staff to the CEO.

items.control_description: 28. Do analytics initiatives get executive commitment?
items.remarks: Basic: Analytics initiatives do not receive executive commitment in the organization.  ||  Emerging: Analytics initiatives receive informal executive commitment from select managers without confirmed agreement from higher level executives in the organization.  ||  Advanced: Analytics initiatives receive executive commitment from a few select business units across the organization.  ||  Differentiated: Analytics initiatives receive executive commitment from a majority of business units across the organization.  ||  Best In Class: Analytics initiatives receive executive commitment from all CEO and C-1 level executives in the organization; information advantage is championed as being a key differentiator and success measure with respect to the competition.

items.control_description: 29. Do organization resources have the relevant business and technology skills to help implement advanced analytics?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: The required business and technical skills to implement advanced analytics do not exist within the organization and the organization is not aware of 'skills gaps'  ||  Emerging: The required business and technical skills to implement advanced analytics exist in silos across the organization; external sources are not sought to supplement skill gaps.  ||  Advanced: The required business and technical skills to implement advanced analytics exist in the organization but do not work in a coordinated fashion; there is minimal access to external sources.  ||  Differentiated: An organization-wide view of business and technical skills is present; there are efforts underway to build a robust analytics skills capability but the organization does not yet have it.  ||  Best In Class: Organization-wide business and technical skills exist and work in a coordinated fashion; external help is sought to fill 'skill gaps' or is not needed.

items.control_description: 30. Does the organization actively recruit analytics talent and does it clearly specify career paths?
items.remarks: Basic: The organization has no plans to recruit analytics talent.  ||  Emerging: The organization has started recruiting analytics talent.  ||  Advanced: A few business units are actively recruiting analytics talent with weakly defined career paths.  ||  Differentiated: Half of the business units are actively recruiting analytics talent and some units have clearly defined career paths.  ||  Best In Class: The whole organization is actively recruiting analytics talent and has defined clear career paths for them.

items.control_description: 31. How integrated are analytics processes in the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: Most analytics processes in the organization are isolated.  ||  Emerging: Analytics processes are integrated within a business unit but not across units.  ||  Advanced: Analytics processes are integrated across a few business units.  ||  Differentiated: Analytics processes are integrated across most business units.  ||  Best In Class: All analytics processes are fully integrated across the organization.

items.control_description: 6. Do you have a clear data governance strategy and structure for supply chain related data?
items.remarks: Basic: No data governance strategy, governance is driven by the various systems in place and only done in silos.  ||  Emerging: Mature data governance strategies per supply chain function exist, but an overarching strategy across all functions is still missing.  ||  Advanced: Overarching data governance strategy deployed across all supply chain functions.  ||  Differentiated: Data governance strategy aligned and commonly applied E2E with key supply chain partners (e.g. suppliers, logistics providers).  ||  Best In Class: E2E digital governance strategy and automated governance in place.

items.control_description: 23. Does the organization structure support and maximize the value of analytics initiatives?
items.remarks: Basic: The organization structure was not designed for analytics initiatives.  ||  Emerging: The organization structure has started evolving to adapt to analytics initiatives.  ||  Advanced: The organization has started to think about a Chief Analytics Officer (CAO) position.  ||  Differentiated: The organization has elevated the position and responsibilities of a CAO.  ||  Best In Class: The organization recognizes the CAO as one of the most important officers in the C-suite.

items.control_description: 24. How is data governed across the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: There are no data governance positions in the organization and employees have incentives that conflict with governance practices (e.g. employees are expected to get data quickly whereby they might avoid sound data governance practices).  ||  Emerging: Specific business units have informal data governance leads in place and employees are encouraged but not mandated to follow sound data governance procedures.  ||  Advanced: Data governance leads are in place across the organization; resources commit a percentage of their time to data governance in addition to their routine responsibilities and all employees are expected to follow sound data governance procedures but there is minimal liability for circumventing processes.  ||  Differentiated: A full-time data governance lead position is in place at a high level in the organization and there are incentives for employees to follow sound data governance procedures.  ||  Best In Class: A full-time data governance lead position is in place at a high level in the organization and the data governance organization includes a governance committee that has the power to make decisions; employees with governance duties are incented to employ sound data governance practices.

items.control_description: 25. How does the organization manage their data assets?
items.remarks: Basic: Data assets do not have owners in the organization.  ||  Emerging: Greater than 25% of data assets have an owner/ steward in the organization.  ||  Advanced: Greater than 50% of data assets have an owner / steward in the organization.  ||  Differentiated: Greater than 75% of data assets have an owner / steward in the organization.  ||  Best In Class: Each data asset has an owner / steward in the organization.

items.control_description: 32. Do you have a dedicated and clearly defined big data organization in place?
items.remarks: Basic: There are individual people across the company dealing with data analytics independently, no organization behind.  ||  Emerging: A silo-based data analytics organization is in place for individual supply chain functions. Further integration with other departments is work in progress.  ||  Advanced: There is a dedicated data analytics organization covering all key aspects of data analytics for e.g. data gathering, data reconciliation, data storage, data analytics, data systems, data governance, within the company. However the data analytics activities are not aligned with external partners.  ||  Differentiated: The data analytics organization collaborates with data analytics organizations of key supply chain partners (e.g. suppliers, 3rd party platforms, logistics providers). The roadmaps are aligned where it is of importance.  ||  Best In Class: The data analytics organization collaborates horizontally with external partners. Key workflows are automated. Data analytics is part of the company's customer solutions ecosystem and provided as a service on the market.

items.control_description: 7. KPI Measurement: How do you measure your KPIs?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: KPIs do not exists at all / somehow.  ||  Emerging: Rudimentary, manual tracking of select performance KPIs with a predefined cadence.  ||  Advanced: Semi-automated data collection and report creation at a predefined cadence for a comprehensive KPI set; visualization in excel-like sheets.  ||  Differentiated: Automated data collection and report creation on demand and at a predefined cadence for a balanced scorecard. Visualization in an interactive dashboard that allows to dynamically view the data, visual and email alerts inform staff about deviations from targeted performance level.  ||  Best In Class: Real-time, automated tracking of a balanced KPI scorecard; displayed in interactive “dashboards that matter” which are tailored to the user needs and behavior and allow to drill down into the information and issues. Automated alerts immediately inform staff about deviations from targeted performance levels and recommend counter actions.

items.control_description: 8. How do you measure your BPIs?
items.remarks: Basic: BPIs do not exists at all / somehow.  ||  Emerging: Rudimentary, manual tracking of select performance BPIs with a predefined cadence.  ||  Advanced: Semi-automated data collection and report creation at a predefined cadence for a comprehensive BPI set; visualization in excel-like sheets.  ||  Differentiated: Automated data collection and report creation on demand and at a predefined cadence for a balanced scorecard. Visualization in an interactive dashboard that allows to dynamically view the data, visual and email alerts inform staff about deviations from targeted performance level.  ||  Best In Class: Real-time, automated tracking of a balanced BPI scorecard; displayed in interactive “dashboards that matter” which are tailored to the user needs and behavior and allow to drill down into the information and issues. Automated alerts immediately inform staff about deviations from targeted performance levels and recommend counter actions.

items.control_description: 9. How do you measure your PPIs?
items.remarks: Basic: PPIs do not exists at all / somehow.  ||  Emerging: Rudimentary, manual tracking of select performance PPIs with a predefined cadence.  ||  Advanced: Semi-automated data collection and report creation at a predefined cadence for a comprehensive PPI set; visualization in excel-like sheets.  ||  Differentiated: Automated data collection and report creation on demand and at a predefined cadence for a balanced scorecard. Visualization in an interactive dashboard that allows to dynamically view the data, visual and email alerts inform staff about deviations from targeted performance level.  ||  Best In Class: Real-time, automated tracking of a balanced PPI scorecard; displayed in interactive “dashboards that matter” which are tailored to the user needs and behavior and allow to drill down into the information and issues. Automated alerts immediately inform staff about deviations from targeted performance levels and recommend counter actions.

items.control_description: 10. Do you conduct benchmarking?
items.remarks: Basic: No benchmarking is conducted.  ||  Emerging: Internal / External Benchmarking is done on demand.  ||  Advanced: Internal benchmarking is done within the network on a regular basis, external benchmarking is done on demand.  ||  Differentiated: Internal benchmarking is done in real time, external benchmarking with partners and suppliers is done on a regular basis.  ||  Best In Class: Internal benchmarking is done in real time, external benchmarking with partners and suppliers is done in real time.

items.control_description: 11. How does your CIP look like?
items.remarks: Basic: Continuous Improvement processes are either not established or their use is minimal in the ongoing operation of the supply chain management business.  ||  Emerging: Most departments within the SCM-Organization are participating in the continuous Improvement process. Some achievements have been made.  ||  Advanced: A formal, visible, and continuous Improvement process is in place. Most departments within the SCM-Organization as well as suppliers participate in these processes. Substantial improvements have been made in many areas.  ||  Differentiated: Continuous improvement has become a natural way of life for employees, suppliers and customers. Improved quality in both SCM and support functions, reduced costs, increased velocity and a focus on the customer has contributed to competitive advantage.  ||  Best In Class: Continuous improvement has become a natural way of life for employees, suppliers, customers and partners. Improved quality in both supply chain management and support functions, reduced costs, increased velocity and a focus on the customer has contributed to competitive advantage, use of machine learning algorithms for self-improving data lake, continuous improvement is supported by an integrated digital solution.

items.control_description: 1. How well defined and relevant is your overall business plan?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: The formal business plan links external factors to internal competencies. The process is embedded in a formal routine with at least an Annual Plan definition and quarterly results against plan reviews. Ad-hoc unilateral planning (occasionally, joint meetings).  ||  Emerging: A three to five year business plan is documented and supported by key departmental and area plans. Strategic progress is not measured / tracked in a rigorous way. Employees are aware to a limited extent of the strategic imperatives of the organization.  ||  Advanced: A three to five year business plan is documented and supported by key departmental and area plans. A balanced scorecard approach is used to measure strategic progress. Employees at all levels are aware of the strategic imperatives of the organization. Joint planning meetings but different plans in the end.  ||  Differentiated: Strategic planning is done a regular intervals with some limited collaboration between customers and strategic partners. Plans are regularly reviewed to ensure effectiveness and to compare results to goals. Operational measures are not fully linked to the strategic plan.  ||  Best In Class: Strategic planning is a continuous process that involves collaboration between customers and strategic partners including the subsidiaries and Division. Plans are regularly reviewed to ensure effectiveness and to compare results to goals. Operational measures throughout the organization are linked to the strategic plan and the mission, vision, and values. Consensus meetings. One cross-functional outlook (“one number”).

items.control_description: 33. How does supply chain meet with sales, market research and product development?
items.remarks: Basic: Manual data transfer is necessary.  ||  Emerging: Macros ensure integration of key data and limit manual data transfer.  ||  Advanced: Advanced tools such as Salesforce.com are integrated in ERP. Sales data and forecast can be automatically used.  ||  Differentiated: Advanced tools are used across functions, though multiple data sources still exist within some of the functions.  ||  Best In Class: Data is fully integrated with one single source of truth.

items.control_description: 2. How well understood is your business plan?
items.remarks: Basic: Employees know individual department goals but not conversant on key strategies of business plan. They are informed, at least on a quarterly basis, on how performance is against plan. There is minimal alignment between customers and strategic partners including the subsidiaries and division.  ||  Emerging: Employees understand the link between their department goals and delivering the business plan. Employees understand metrics and their basic relationship with the Business Plan goals. There is not a good understanding of how external parties fit into the strategy.  ||  Advanced: Employees understand the link between their department goals and delivering the business plan. Employees understand metrics and their basic relationship with the business plan goals. There is an understanding of metrics and the relationship between the company, customers and strategic partners for meeting the same business plan goals.  ||  Differentiated: Employees generally understand how their success contributes to department success and delivering the business plan Employees understand the longer-term business vision and strategic priorities. There is limited alignment of day to day choices consistent with strategic direction and influenced by performance through a relevant set of metrics.  ||  Best In Class: Employees actively participate in department’s portion of business plan. Employees fully understand how their success contributes to department success and delivering the business plan. Employees understand the longer-term business vision and strategic priorities, and make day to day choices consistent with strategic direction and influenced by performance through a relevant set of metrics. There is a clear line of sight between business plans of customers and strategic partners including subsidiaries and division.

items.control_description: 3. How well developed is your overall operations strategy?
items.remarks: Basic: No clear operations strategy in place.  ||  Emerging: Decisions are addressed informally or part of a functional strategy related to sales, purchasing or manufacturing.  ||  Advanced: Functional operations strategies are defined with partial integration with other functional areas. Some segmentation by products is in place.  ||  Differentiated: Integrated operations strategy in place. It is segmented by products and reviewed on a timely basis.  ||  Best In Class: Operations strategy is a fundamental building block of the supply chain strategy and is clearly defined by product segments.
