items.remarks: Basic: Limited engagement outside operations.  ||  Emerging: No formal SIOP leader and team.  ||  Advanced: Dedicated SIOP leader and their team drives activities.  ||  Differentiated: Extensive C-suite executive involvement.  ||  Best In Class: C-Suite views and operates SIOP as a competitive advantage.

items.control_description: 35. What cultural norms drive the S&OP process?
items.remarks: Basic: Culture is driven by individual functional leaders’ and legacy practices.  ||  Emerging: Culture norms and behaviors are established within each department.  ||  Advanced: Culture norms and behaviors shifting from departmental to group focused (e.g., Supply chain and operations).  ||  Differentiated: Culture of continuous improvement and innovation through teaming / collaboration.  ||  Best In Class: Culture focuses on continuous improvement through collaboration, rapid innovation, increasing agility and flexibility for mutual benefit for all participants.

items.control_description: 36. How are S&OP leads rewarded for process improvements and meeting KPI goals?
items.remarks: Basic: There is limited, enterprise-wide formal rewards and recognition system. Ad-hoc rewards and recognition linked mainly to each functional groups’ near-term goals.  ||  Emerging: A formal reward system is in place but not based on objective criteria and only loosely tied to individual and business performance.  ||  Advanced: Reward system linked to team and business’ performance.  ||  Differentiated: Recognition and rewards based on contributions and results that drive overall business and team performance.  ||  Best In Class: Rewards system measures contribution of internal and external teams (suppliers and business partners).

items.control_description: 37. How well are metrics used to drive decision-making and enterprise strategy?
items.remarks: Basic: Existing metrics are calculated at a business leader level and not communicated upward or across the organization.  ||  Emerging: Metrics are used as a measurement tool but not used in decision-making process.  ||  Advanced: Metrics are used to make and support business decisions at enterprise-level.  ||  Differentiated: Metrics are clearly aligned with the group’s business strategy and are regularly communicated.  ||  Best In Class: Metrics are clearly aligned with enterprise business strategy and communicated across the enterprise including key suppliers and channel partners.

items.control_description: 71. How embedded is decision-making into the S&OP process?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Decision making processes vary by function and focus more on tactically siloed execution rather than strategic priorities.  ||  Emerging: Beginning to prioritize decision making around strategic value and decision complexity.  ||  Advanced: Application of commercially available S&OP tools with pre-defined reports to support decision making.  ||  Differentiated: Advanced analytical and reporting capabilities support strategic decision making and drive additional opportunities.  ||  Best In Class: Decision making is focused on high strategic value and high decision complexity.

items.control_description: 72. How many different functions are active participants in S&OP?
items.remarks: Basic: S&OP is not cross- functional.  ||  Emerging: Different focuses and goals between S&OP cross-functional processes (single, consensus-driven plan) and finance (profitability) result in sub-optimal financial and operational performance.  ||  Advanced: Some key stakeholders and business units engaged in joint decision-making and execution (e.g., finance and operations).  ||  Differentiated: Mature S&OP capabilities that include key internal stakeholders, customers and key suppliers.  ||  Best In Class: Operational and financial performance goals tailored to measure achievement of strategic objectives.

items.control_description: 73. In S&OP, what is the alignment between supply chain / operations and finance?
items.remarks: Basic: Finance and supply chain are not aligned in S&OP.  ||  Emerging: Some process integration and limited data sharing in business planning, budgeting between some functional teams and business units.  ||  Advanced: Open line of communication between supply chain and finance organizations.  ||  Differentiated: A specific but limited set of operational and financial performance goals defined and flowed down across executive and management levels and all functional areas.  ||  Best In Class: Integrated finance and core operational management information reporting.

items.control_description: 82. How well is data and information used to drive planning activities?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: No structured data available for planning.  ||  Emerging: Taxonomy and hierarchy of data for products, customers and locations vary between functional areas and their disparate tools.  ||  Advanced: Some alignment / mapping of product and customer data and hierarchies between tools used by different functional groups. Updates to master data occurring but not fully synchronized and require alignment meetings.  ||  Differentiated: Data taxonomy and hierarchical relationships are aligned across planning groups and their systems. Changes to master data are automated and rapidly updated within the enterprise.  ||  Best In Class: Data taxonomy and hierarchical relationships are aligned across internal and key supplier / channel partner systems..

items.control_description: 83. How are KPIs and metrics used to drive the planning processes?
items.remarks: Basic: No metrics are available.  ||  Emerging: Functional oriented metrics; bias towards financial metrics.  ||  Advanced: Metrics indicating how effectively operations meets the sales plan.  ||  Differentiated: Key performance indicators / metrics are shared across functions including forecast accuracy, inventory turns / DOH, inventory aging, on-time delivery to commit / promise date, value of excess /obsolete, % fill rate (cycle service level).  ||  Best In Class: KPIs are used to drive planning process effectiveness and efficiencies as well as improve overall SIOP business objectives. Customized metrics dashboards are readily available at all levels of enterprise.

items.control_description: 88. How well are tax considerations built into the planning process?
items.remarks: Basic: Tax is not considered.  ||  Emerging: Tax function not well connected in the process from the outset.  ||  Advanced: Tax involved but not at all stages.  ||  Differentiated: Tax involved in all stages.  ||  Best In Class: Tax is involved in all stages and is an integral part of the planning process.

items.control_description: 89. What is the process for creating the organization's strategic plan?
items.remarks: Basic: There is no strategic plan.  ||  Emerging: Inconsistent approach to strategic planning across the organization.  ||  Advanced: Business units perform planning using different processes by location although a central timetable exists.  ||  Differentiated: Comprehensive central guidelines on the strategic planning process.  ||  Best In Class: Centrally defined output and timetable with proactive engagement from the finance function.

items.control_description: 90. What functions are involved in the creation of the strategic plan?
items.remarks: Basic: Senior management creates the strategic plan without the input from various functions.  ||  Emerging: Finance involved in the process but often after key decisions have been made by senior management.  ||  Advanced: Corporate strategy shared although changes continue to be made to the top level plan as the business develops its supporting plans leading to multiple iterations.  ||  Differentiated: Efficient strategic planning process in which finance is actively engaged.  ||  Best In Class: Efficient strategic planning process in which finance, operations and sales are actively engaged.

items.control_description: 91. With what frequency does the team monitor the variances of the financial budget and forecast?
items.remarks: Basic: Once created, no monitoring of forecast and budget.  ||  Emerging: Inconsistent monitoring against forecast and budget.  ||  Advanced: Reasonably consistent monitoring against forecast and budget.  ||  Differentiated: Consistent monitoring against forecast and budget.  ||  Best In Class: Instantaneous feeds that show monitoring of forecast and budget.

items.control_description: 92. How well established is the financial budgeting and forecasting process?
items.remarks: Basic: No process  ||  Emerging: Processes are different by location.  ||  Advanced: A centrally-defined process, but may not be followed by each location.  ||  Differentiated: Centrally defined output and timetable, with project management, although this may be hindered and manipulated by the business.  ||  Best In Class: Centrally defined output and timetable with strong finance lead project management.

items.control_description: 93. How readily available is the data used for financial planning?
items.remarks: Basic: Data is inconsistent across multiple IT systems and difficult to access.  ||  Emerging: Data captured by various processes.  ||  Advanced: Data captured by various processes although a central timetable exists.  ||  Differentiated: Comprehensive central guidelines on data capture, processes, assumptions and integration to be applied locally.  ||  Best In Class: Fully automated process using web based workflow and data capture and a central calculation and consolidation system / warehouse.

items.control_description: 94. How well does the organization report on financial results?
items.remarks: Basic: Little to no management information and scorecards.  ||  Emerging: Management information is limited, heavily financial biased and focused upon traditional BS and P&L with limited commentary.  ||  Advanced: Management reporting and analysis is mainly focused on financial with some operational elements.  ||  Differentiated: A reasonably well balanced scorecard in place allowing management across bot financial outcomes and the key drivers of performance operationally, commentary is therefore much improved.  ||  Best In Class: Balanced scorecard that integrates risk management information, financial and operational perspectives.

items.control_description: 4. What is the input for creating the demand plan?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Forecasting based on historical data.  ||  Emerging: Integrated S&OP planning tools including sales, production, purchasing.  ||  Advanced: Input from sales and market research and historical data.  ||  Differentiated: Input from sales and market research and historical data being fed into a data analytics engine for choosing the "best fit" forecast.  ||  Best In Class: Advanced use of data from e.g. social media, macroeconomic, product life-cycle statistical data, data from e.g. configurators for an advanced forecasting.

items.control_description: 5. How do you integrate external partners (e.g. suppliers, customers, 3rd party vendor platforms) into your Demand Planning process?
items.remarks: Basic: No integration of external (or internal) partners into demand planning.  ||  Emerging: No integration of external partners into demand planning. Demand planning only based on traditional interaction and communication with sales.  ||  Advanced: Key customers and suppliers integrated into demand planning. Demand planning only based on traditional interaction and communication with sales.  ||  Differentiated: Customer and supplier near-time integrated into demand planning. Data exchange for demand planning automated.  ||  Best In Class: External partners e.g. customer and supplier are integrated real-time into the planning platform.

items.control_description: 6. Do you perform demand sensing (incl. external and unstructured data, machine learning)?
items.remarks: Basic: There is no demand sensing (forecast method leveraging new mathematical techniques and near real-time information).  ||  Emerging: Automated consolidation of selected, mainly internal and structured, data sources but manual analysis based on experience for demand sensing.  ||  Advanced: Usage of structured internal and external data such as weather, logistics provider updates, TMS, device information, etc.  ||  Differentiated: Usage of structured and unstructured internal and external data such as weather, logistics provider updates, TMS, device information, social media, traffic situation, strikes, etc.  ||  Best In Class: Proactive alerting on different devices (e.g. via web, app, sms) based on dynamic ETA calculation incl. social media, traffic situation, strike, weather, logistics provider data etc..

items.control_description: 7. What is the frequency of updating the Demand Plan?
items.remarks: Basic: On a certain time period base independent of other internal business requirements (e.g. manufacturing, sales etc.).  ||  Emerging: On a monthly basis via excel sheets or with an independent tool analysis.  ||  Advanced: Planning frequency adopted to the production and sales variance requirements.  ||  Differentiated: Planning frequency adopted to the production, sales variance requirements and in collaboration with external partners.  ||  Best In Class: Near-time, continuously in collaboration with external partners.

items.control_description: 8. How do you plan promotions and integrate them into your demand planning process?
items.remarks: Basic: Promotions are planned on an ad-hoc basis, e.g. when expected sales are not met. Promotions are, if communicated, communicated via non-standardized channels and tools.  ||  Emerging: A standardized reporting tool is in place and widely used. The reporting tool facilitates an easy integration of the promotion and related sales effects into the forecasting / planning tool.  ||  Advanced: Promotions are centrally coordinated and communicated. All promotions are assessed and evaluated offline to support future forecasting. All promotions are integrated in a forecasting tool.  ||  Differentiated: Integrated tools allow advanced planning of promotions. The tool provides a good output of planned promotions based on certain input parameters.  ||  Best In Class: Promotions are defined by a system based on inventory levels, expected sales, market developments, expectations etc. Big data analytics recommends the kind of promotion, the necessary price reductions, etc..

items.control_description: 9. How do plan new product introductions (NPIs)?
items.remarks: Basic: Product (re)launches are not forecasted.  ||  Emerging: Forecasts for launches, re-launches, changes and phase outs are handled separately.  ||  Advanced: Launches, re-launches, changes and phase-outs are integrated into the demand planning processes.  ||  Differentiated: Launches, re-launches, changes and phase-outs are an integral part of the demand planning process and are systematically prepared (with assigned roles and responsibilities).  ||  Best In Class: NPIs are defined by system based on inventory levels, expected sales, market developments, expectations etc. Predictive data analytics recommends the kind of promotion, ramp-up speed, production volume etc..

items.control_description: 10. What external sources (causal data elements) are used to create the Demand Plan?
items.remarks: Basic: Historical data and limited external input are integrated into the demand plan.  ||  Emerging: An advanced forecast from sales based on SKU and regions, including promotions, are integrated into the Demand Plan.  ||  Advanced: Macroeconomic data, regulatory changes, product lifecycles and field wear and tear are all inputs into the demand plan.  ||  Differentiated: Online shops, configurators, product offerings and predictive maintenance data are all inputs into the demand plan.  ||  Best In Class: Social listening, data from industry portals, google, etc. are inputs into the demand plan.

items.control_description: 38. How are statistical forecasts generated?
items.remarks: Basic: Demand forecast is manually calculated using standalone spreadsheets, limited statistical analysis and less than three months of historical data.  ||  Emerging: Some statistical methods (e.g., coefficient of variation, bias, and forecast error) used to determine forecastability across different planning hierarchies.  ||  Advanced: Automated forecasting tools used to aggregate and analyze internal and external demand data.  ||  Differentiated: Use of advanced statistical methods (smoothing, multiple regression, time series) to develop the forecast.  ||  Best In Class: Use of multiple advanced forecasting algorithms with frequent optimization and tuning.

items.control_description: 39. How prevalent are demand planning metrics used?
items.remarks: Basic: No demand planning measurements exist.  ||  Emerging: Forecast accuracy and bias periodically measured. Forecast assumptions not tracked.  ||  Advanced: Increasing consistency in using MAPE, lag, and bias to calculate forecast accuracy.  ||  Differentiated: Forecast accuracy and variability tracked and methods continuously improved.  ||  Best In Class: Forecast accuracy and bias is measured at multiple levels and used to improve forecasts.

items.control_description: 40. How many functions are involved in the creation of the demand plan?
items.remarks: Basic: No cross-functional participation.  ||  Emerging: Limited cross-functional participation (e.g., sales, product management, marketing, engineering).  ||  Advanced: A single demand plan, resulting from a consensus demand planning meeting, is used to drive operations.  ||  Differentiated: Some inclusion of key customers and suppliers in the demand planning process.  ||  Best In Class: Open sharing of forecasts (and changes) with suppliers and customers. Formal collaborative planning process and cadence in use.

items.control_description: 74. Is the demand plan (& forecast) "dollarized" or valuated?
items.remarks: Basic: Forecast is in volume only, no valuation.  ||  Emerging: Offline valuation of the forecast.  ||  Advanced: Top line and bottom line valuation of the forecast.  ||  Differentiated: Automated top line and bottom line valuation of the forecast with limited scenario analysis.  ||  Best In Class: Automated top line and bottom line valuation of the forecast in monetary terms with advance scenario planning and gap identification.

items.control_description: 75. How are demand planning (& forecast) assumptions and drivers captured and recorded?
items.remarks: Basic: Forecast assumptions and volume drivers are not tracked.  ||  Emerging: Inconsistent tracking of forecast assumptions and drivers.  ||  Advanced: Tracking of some forecast assumptions and drivers.  ||  Differentiated: Tracking of forecast assumptions and volume drivers through all cycles.  ||  Best In Class: Forecast assumptions and value drivers are tracked and reported for continuous improvement.

items.control_description: 78. What is the objective of the demand planning process?
items.remarks: Basic: No demand planning process exists.  ||  Emerging: Develops an operational plan to run the business.  ||  Advanced: Conducts demand and supply balance.  ||  Differentiated: Manages demand to improve profitability.  ||  Best In Class: Shapes demand and drives profitable response.

items.control_description: 79. How is the forecast generated?
items.remarks: Basic: No inputs are used.  ||  Emerging: Use rudimentary forecast based on informal inputs and budgets.  ||  Advanced: Use statistical forecasting; links with products, sales, marketing established.  ||  Differentiated: Collaborates with key accounts to develop consensus forecast.  ||  Best In Class: Develops order-based demand management to eliminate short term forecast.

items.control_description: 80. How much visibility is there into demand data?
items.remarks: Basic: Little to no visibility.  ||  Emerging: Uses sales history as primary source of demand view.  ||  Advanced: Provides company wide visibility of changes to the forecast and order book.  ||  Differentiated: Develops full consensus forecast and agree at SKU level.  ||  Best In Class: Captures product demand by SKU as close as possible to point of consumption.

items.control_description: 81. How effective is the organization at shaping demand?
items.remarks: Basic: No demand shaping.  ||  Emerging: Order management is de-coupled from forecasting.  ||  Advanced: Order management is part of demand planning.  ||  Differentiated: Leverages order process to influence / change demand.  ||  Best In Class: Conducts explicit proactive demand shaping actions.

items.control_description: 84. How well does the planning team incorporate customer forecasts into the plan?
items.remarks: Basic: Customer forecasts are not considered.  ||  Emerging: Customer forecasts are reviewed, but are not incorporated into the plan.  ||  Advanced: Customer-generated (e.g., POS) forecasts are directly incorporated.  ||  Differentiated: Collaboratively developed forecast are shared with customers and suppliers automatically.  ||  Best In Class: Forecasts rapidly incorporate specific customers demand patterns.

items.control_description: 85. How does the organization collaborate to create a demand plan?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Demand Plans are not created.  ||  Emerging: Multiple demand plans created via different functions, informally, across different organizations.  ||  Advanced: Multiple demand plans created via different functions and consolidated into a single plan.  ||  Differentiated: Use of a centralized demand planning function to generate a single demand plan.  ||  Best In Class: A dedicated, centralized demand planning group owns the forecasting and demand planning process with all key functional areas and key customers contributing to forecasts and the final demand plan.

items.control_description: 11. How do you perform detailed scheduling, master production scheduling and dispatching?
items.remarks: Basic: Offline planning with no visibility into constraints.  ||  Emerging: Offline planning systems with visibility into capacity constraints pulled from spreadsheets or other offline systems.  ||  Advanced: Advanced online production planning and dispatching tools are used and vertically integrated across plant systems.  ||  Differentiated: Planning and dispatch tools are integrated across business processes and the end to end plant network. Tools are compatible across plants.  ||  Best In Class: The planning tool steers production to dispatch orders in real time across company's fully integrated planning tool..

items.control_description: 12. How often does the detailed schedule refresh?
items.remarks: Basic: On a daily / weekly basis.  ||  Emerging: Updated manually in near real-time (within the day) as orders arrive.  ||  Advanced: Updated automatically, mostly in real time, as orders arrive electronically and plant and material status (e.g. shortages, unplanned stops) changes.  ||  Differentiated: Updated automatically, mostly in real time, as logistics status changes. Reschedules across company network / external capacity automatically in near real-time.  ||  Best In Class: Real time updates from production across the plants, suppliers and customers.

items.control_description: 13. Are you able to predict impacts, using scenario analysis, of changes within your detailed scheduling system?
items.remarks: Basic: Evaluations on high level (not on the dispatching level) are possible. Accuracy is limited or dependent on how often the all systems are updated.  ||  Emerging: Evaluations on a high level (not on the dispatching level) are possible. Manual work needed to assess impacts on the detailed schedule.  ||  Advanced: Simulation down to the dispatching level can be conducted. Most critical vertical information about e.g. resources, asset configuration, quality, inventory levels, maintenance schedules are automatically included.  ||  Differentiated: Horizontal information e.g. delivery status of parts, capacity of key suppliers, etc. are included in the simulation.  ||  Best In Class: Planning tool enables "what if" simulations in real time. All horizontal and vertical data are precise. Scenarios are displayed and evaluated.

items.control_description: 54. What quality management systems are used in production planning / detailed scheduling?
items.remarks: Basic: No standardized quality management system exists.  ||  Emerging: Root – cause analysis, but not consistently rigorously applied.  ||  Advanced: The total internal chain is awar / feels responsible for total chain output / quality / effectiveness.  ||  Differentiated: Design for quality, statistical process control is consistently applied, supplier involvement in quality planning & control, lean / TQM principles implemented & documented in core functions (Andon, PDCA), manufacturing cells stop automatically upon predetermined number of occurrences of the same fail codes for operator resolution.  ||  Best In Class: Statistical process control (SPC) including Six Sigma techniques are widely used throughout the organization to ensure quality.

items.control_description: 55. How do IT systems help to manage the quality processes?
items.remarks: Basic: Product quality data is not captured.  ||  Emerging: Product quality data is manually captured and physically attached to a product as it moves through the manufacturing process.  ||  Advanced: Product quality data is captured electronically for all products.  ||  Differentiated: There is rapid feedback of process and quality information on product quality issues enabling learning effects in production but follow-up to suppliers takes times.  ||  Best In Class: On-line statistical process control allows dynamic evaluation of product quality and process performance.

items.control_description: 56. To what extent do cross-functional teams address quality?
items.remarks: Basic: Each operation only looks at own quality / output of own added value or process.  ||  Emerging: Authorize each operation to assess the output / quality of the previous operations.  ||  Advanced: The total internal chain is aware / feels responsible for total chain output / quality / effectiveness.  ||  Differentiated: Regular troubleshooting workshops are organized, taking the voice of the customer into account.  ||  Best In Class: Cross-enterprise root – cause and issue resolution in place.

items.control_description: 57. How well integrated are the detailed scheduling IT systems?
items.remarks: Basic: No system is in place.  ||  Emerging: Different, non-integrated IT systems are in use.  ||  Advanced: One integrated MES system for the whole plant.  ||  Differentiated: MES / ERP integration.  ||  Best In Class: Web-based access to plant scheduling status, collaborative data-sharing environment.

items.control_description: 58. How well are environmental, health and safety (EH&S) processes and tools integrated into the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: No EH&S controls.  ||  Emerging: Limited EH&S controls.  ||  Advanced: EH&S controls are partially integrated with MES or ERP systems.  ||  Differentiated: Integrated EH&S controls.  ||  Best In Class: Operator consoles are used to quickly monitor production, handheld functionality feeds all field and control room readings to operators. EH&S integrated in to daily operations using technology.

items.control_description: 59. How well does automated transactional data (production / process orders) drive the shop floor?
items.remarks: Basic: Production occurs without any formal order.  ||  Emerging: Production orders on paper.  ||  Advanced: Paperless production order and inventory tracking.  ||  Differentiated: Paperless production order and inventory tracking, including first tier supplier and/or customer information.  ||  Best In Class: Outsource manufacturing and work force augmentation providers connected to production schedules via the internet.

items.control_description: 60. How are work instructions communicated to the shop floor?
items.remarks: Basic: No work instructions.  ||  Emerging: Knowledge on work instructions only exists through experience / vocally.  ||  Advanced: Work instructions on paper.  ||  Differentiated: Digital work instructions available at production line.  ||  Best In Class: Work instructions are lively used and regularly updated by dedicated people.

items.control_description: 61. How does your organization use overall equipment effectiveness (OEE)?
items.remarks: Basic: Limited to no tracking of the performance of technical equipment or only output figures.  ||  Emerging: Registration of OEE.  ||  Advanced: Registration of OEE on machine level and fact-based problem solving based on data (Six Sigma).  ||  Differentiated: Benchmarking of OEE across factories.  ||  Best In Class: Benchmarking of OEE across industry peers.

items.control_description: 62. How are best practices and benchmarks used to improve the shop floor?
items.remarks: Basic: Best practices are not explicitly known / considered.  ||  Emerging: Sharing and replication of best practices are used in isolated functions in the organization.  ||  Advanced: Sharing and replication of best practices in the organization.  ||  Differentiated: Benchmarking and adopting best practices from other organizations.  ||  Best In Class: Implementing best practices through collaboration with other organizations.

items.control_description: 63. How is preventative maintenance integrated into the production planning processes?
items.remarks: Basic: Technical breakdowns are just solved on an ad-hoc basis, no structure in place to decrease downtimes.  ||  Emerging: Initial preventive maintenance plans based on experience and dedicated team for urgent technical breakdowns.  ||  Advanced: Preventive maintenance plans and spare part management based on historical performance.  ||  Differentiated: Collaboration with maintenance service providers and suppliers of technical equipment to improve production performance.  ||  Best In Class: Predictive analytics are used to proactively anticipate downtime.

items.control_description: 64. How is detailed capacity managed?
items.remarks: Basic: Capacity is unknown.  ||  Emerging: Inadequate capacity.  ||  Advanced: Inadequate capacity.  ||  Differentiated: High utilization.  ||  Best In Class: Capacity matched to demand.

items.control_description: 65. How is scrap and material loss managed?
items.remarks: Basic: No scrap / material loss analysis.  ||  Emerging: High level in / out material analysis used.  ||  Advanced: Informal tracking and pursuit of material losses.  ||  Differentiated: Material losses pursued regularly through fact driven analysis.  ||  Best In Class: Joint pursuit of material loss by supplier, manufacturer and customer.

items.control_description: 66. Once products are deemed ineffective or scrap, what process is used to analyze the defects?
items.remarks: Basic: Failed products are thrown away at the process step without further investigation  ||  Emerging: Failed products are removed from the process and inspected in non-quality zone.  ||  Advanced: Failed products are used for root cause analysis.  ||  Differentiated: Full transparency and internal coordination of rework cost.  ||  Best In Class: Costs of material non quality are reclaimed from or shared with suppliers.

items.control_description: 67. What level of training is provided to production personnel?
items.remarks: Basic: Each operator is specialized in / focused on specific areas or production lines.  ||  Emerging: Operators skilled in multiple operations.  ||  Advanced: Flexible operators with high utilization.  ||  Differentiated: Pro-active training program has been established to train people to become multi-disciplinary.  ||  Best In Class: Team based problem solving with maximum labor productivity.

items.control_description: 68. How do engineers measure labor activity?
items.remarks: Basic: Extremely basic or non-existent activity data.  ||  Emerging: Some activity analysis performed on an infrequent basis; focused primarily on direct labor.  ||  Advanced: Periodic activity analysis performed; data not always used to calculate or analyze staffing requirements.  ||  Differentiated: Active benchmarking and monitoring of activities and resourcing of direct / indirect personnel.  ||  Best In Class: Thorough data-based understanding of activities.

items.control_description: 69. How much cross-training is provided to employees?
items.remarks: Basic: Every person is responsible for his / her job, and does the job in his / her own way.  ||  Emerging: Every person is responsible to do his / her job according to documented Job standards.  ||  Advanced: Operators are empowered and capability training is provided.  ||  Differentiated: Provide continuous formal trainings to employees.  ||  Best In Class: An overall competence matrix / plan is available based on current / future needs.

items.control_description: 70. How are KPIs used to drive production planning activities?
items.remarks: Basic: No accurate performance measures and KPI reporting.  ||  Emerging: Monthly KPI reporting on department level (scrap expense, in-process failure rates, capacity utilization, WIP days of supply, etc.).  ||  Advanced: Monthly management reporting with long term actions.  ||  Differentiated: Monthly KPI reporting on department level (scrap expense, in-process failure rates, capacity utilization, WIP days of supply, etc.).  ||  Best In Class: Standardized KPI reporting across all entities and benchmarking.

items.control_description: 77. Are you able to successfully create frozen time periods in order to create a stable detailed schedule?
items.remarks: Basic: No frozen window.  ||  Emerging: Long frozen window.  ||  Advanced: A frozen window is accompanied by a slushy period.  ||  Differentiated: Lead time often broken into for a variety of reasons.  ||  Best In Class: Stable SKUs are locked in as far out as possible to stabilize production. Most SKUs follow frozen time, based on effective manufacturing lead times and breaks in the schedule occur only when profitable.

items.control_description: 14. How do you perform your inventory planning and optimization process?
items.remarks: Basic: Single echelon inventory management using stand-alone tools.  ||  Emerging: Multi-echelon inventory management using standalone optimization tools.  ||  Advanced: Company internally: Automated reduction of dead and slow moving stock based on real time integrated analytics.  ||  Differentiated: End to end (multi-echelon) inventory optimization.  ||  Best In Class: Automatic real time, multi-echelon inventory optimization including forecasts, logistics, costs, uncertainties… (all influencing factors) through the use of data analytics.

items.control_description: 15. How do you integrate external partners (e.g. suppliers, 3rd party vendor platforms) into your supply and inventory planning process?
items.remarks: Basic: There is no integration of external partners into supply and Inventory planning. Supply and inventory planning is only based on internal interaction and communication.  ||  Emerging: Key customers and suppliers are loosely integrated into Inventory Planning (inconsistent and manual data feeds). Supply planning is based on traditional interaction and communication.  ||  Advanced: Key customers and suppliers are integrated into Inventory Planning. Supply planning is based on traditional interaction and communication.  ||  Differentiated: Customers and suppliers are integrated, in near real-time, into supply and inventory planning. Some inputs may be manual.  ||  Best In Class: External partners e.g. customers and suppliers, are integrated, in real-time, into the planning platform.

items.control_description: 16. How quickly are you able to react to changes in the plan?
items.remarks: Basic: Any disruptions require high manual effort. Disruptions cannot be automatically handled with the existing systems.  ||  Emerging: Dedicated abnormalities can be handled with limited manual effort (e.g. increase in sale due to promotions).  ||  Advanced: Dedicated demand driven abnormalities can be handled automatically (e.g. increase in sale due to promotions).  ||  Differentiated: Dedicated supplier driven abnormalities can be handled automatically.  ||  Best In Class: Systems automatically react to any changes and provide a recommendation.

items.control_description: 20. To what extent do you directly link your planning results to execution processes (e.g. replenishment)?
items.remarks: Basic: Planning and execution processes only linked via regular traditional exchange processes (e.g. Excel sheets).  ||  Emerging: Planning and execution only partially linked within certain business processes.  ||  Advanced: Planning and execution partially linked in one region / area.  ||  Differentiated: Planning and execution linked also in collaboration with selected external partners.  ||  Best In Class: Planning and execution real-time linked in collaboration with external partners performed (e.g. production optimized based on real-time planning changes).

items.control_description: 22. How are supply and inventory planning roles and responsibilities shared and defined?
items.remarks: Basic: A dedicated person is responsible for managing the process of parameter changes and / or planning policy changes.  ||  Emerging: An internal team exists to manage inventory and is sufficiently empowered to impose decisions (e.g., like "like production frequency decisions) where required.  ||  Advanced: The internal team has sufficient support from top management to impose modifications in the tactics area (lot sizes, planning policies).  ||  Differentiated: The internal team has full support from top management to impose modifications.  ||  Best In Class: The responsible team includes key strategic suppliers and channel partners.

items.control_description: 41. How collaborative is the supply planning process?
items.remarks: Basic: Supply planning performed using spreadsheets and simple heuristics, by multiple operations groups with limited involvement from other groups.  ||  Emerging: Common approach to supply planning, coordinated by a central team with inputs from procurement, distribution and field services.  ||  Advanced: Select suppliers are directly involved with supply plan development.  ||  Differentiated: Supply plans beginning to span internal supply sources and some key suppliers of critical parts / materials and are critical to SIOP.  ||  Best In Class: A centralized supply planning team with active involvement and supply information from internal and external suppliers.

items.control_description: 42. What is the time horizon of the supply and inventory process?
items.remarks: Basic: Supply plans have a near-term (e.g., 3 month) focus to achieve production goals.  ||  Emerging: Short and medium-term (up to 12 months) planning horizons are part of supply planning focus.  ||  Advanced: Consistent tracking and root cause of demand and supply variability and feedback loop to reset inventory targets.  ||  Differentiated: Inventory status and targets are measured and adjusted monthly based on market, NPI / EOL needs, and forecast accuracy.  ||  Best In Class: Current on-hand inventory, safety stock and targets across the network are measured and adjusted weekly based on market, NPI / EOL needs, and forecast accuracy.

items.control_description: 43. What IT system is used to create supply and inventory plans?
items.remarks: Basic: Supply plans are created manually and multiple versions are created.  ||  Emerging: Supply plans detached from MRP systems.  ||  Advanced: MRP enabled methods being developed, but data is not robust.  ||  Differentiated: Using the IT tool, a central planning team manages the entire network to understand the market conditions.  ||  Best In Class: IT systems are integrated to quickly share / upload MRP and supply commits plans with vendors and contract manufacturers. IT systems also support collaborative supply planning, visibility and reporting.

items.control_description: 44. How are inventory planning strategies determined?
items.remarks: Basic: No criteria for determine planning strategies.  ||  Emerging: MTO / MTS is based on arbitrary criteria and gut feeling.  ||  Advanced: MTO/MTS decision is made per product group/category and its impact on service policy is assessed regularly.  ||  Differentiated: Order points, safety stock, MTO vs. MTS, and required capacity flexibility are calculated with relevant costs and associated risks to enable trade-offs throughout the product lifecycle.  ||  Best In Class: Regular analytical assessment of safety stocks, lot sizes and MTO / MTS classification.

items.control_description: 45. How are stocking levels determined?
items.remarks: Basic: Stock levels are infrequently reviewed against forecasts.  ||  Emerging: Stock levels are regularly reviewed against forecasts.  ||  Advanced: Supply variability measures are taken into account for calculating safety stocks.  ||  Differentiated: Service level targets balance customer service needs, and the costs and implications of stock outs.  ||  Best In Class: Stock buffer management is part of integrated optimization of stock along the supply chain.

items.control_description: 46. How integrated are the inventory planning systems?
items.remarks: Basic: No system is used for calculating inventory values.  ||  Emerging: A basic, PC-based tool, typically spreadsheets, is available to calculate safety stocks and lot sizes.  ||  Advanced: Use of a stand-alone system to manage product inventory across internal storage locations.  ||  Differentiated: Use of a partially integrated system to manage product inventory across internal storage locations that is tied to the shipping & production systems.  ||  Best In Class: Highly integrated system to manage product storage locations across key suppliers, channel partners and select end-customers.

items.control_description: 47. How are tools used to help manage the planning strategies?
items.remarks: Basic: No commercial off-the-shelf application used to support inventory planning / management.  ||  Emerging: No system support for material flow and inventory management. Totally manually system, not computerized.  ||  Advanced: A tool is available to support MTO / MTS decision making; The tool clearly calculates the impact of parameter changes on inventory level, responsiveness, operational efficiency, etc. The tool can optimize the parameters starting from a goal function taking into account all relevant constraints.  ||  Differentiated: The MTO / MTS tool is fit for / adapted to the environment; The tool is able to calculate capacity impact of MTO/MTS decisions. Exception management is used to identify the big changes. The tool facilitates scenario comparisons.  ||  Best In Class: Team has tools and processes to optimize inventory levels and change inventory management policies given current supply chain capabilities, leveraging production planning, statistical analysis and sophisticated advanced planning and optimization (APO) tools.

items.control_description: 48. How much visibility do you get into inventory holdings and movements?
items.remarks: Basic: Limited visibility to inventory aging by product family or SKU.  ||  Emerging: Inventory information (including unit volumes, value, aging) is available at the aggregate, product family and SKU levels.  ||  Advanced: Regular inventory updates (units, values, aging, consumption) are available on a daily basis from internal systems (or from 3PLs).  ||  Differentiated: Inventory addition and consumption data available on a near-real time basis across the entire enterprise network of stocking locations.  ||  Best In Class: Full real-time visibility of inventory positions, aging and movements (inbound, transfers, and outbound) both within the enterprise and across key suppliers and channel partners.

items.control_description: 49. Who owns inventory and how is that organization managed?
items.remarks: Basic: No one has responsibility for inventory.  ||  Emerging: A dedicated person is responsible for managing the process of parameter changes and / or planning policy changes.  ||  Advanced: An internal team exist to manage inventory and is sufficiently empowered to impose decisions (e.g., like "like production frequency decisions) where required.  ||  Differentiated: The internal team has sufficient support from top management to impose modifications in the tactics area (lot sizes, planning policies).  ||  Best In Class: The responsible team includes key strategic suppliers and channel partners.

items.control_description: 50. How do inventory metrics and benchmarks drive the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: The inventory person(s) and team are not guided by metrics or benchmarks.  ||  Emerging: Inventory managers are mainly concerned about their specific area; limited cross-functional collaboration.  ||  Advanced: Cross-functional project teams are common and have shared objectives and targets.  ||  Differentiated: Clear metrics are being used to monitor the performance with regards to the supply chain tactics process (timeliness, frequency, etc.).  ||  Best In Class: The goals defined in the supply chain strategy including specific inventory performance goals are realized.

items.control_description: 51. How well do the supply and inventory leads use teamwork to drive the strategy?
items.remarks: Basic: Culture is driven by individual functional leaders’ and legacy practices.  ||  Emerging: Teamwork is project focused within a single functional group. Frequent misalignments and redundant efforts across functional groups to achieve a similar goal.  ||  Advanced: Culture norms and behaviors shifting from departmental to group focused (e.g., Supply chain and operations).  ||  Differentiated: Teamwork and collaboration is the pervasive between operations / supply chain and other functional groups to drive supply chain and inventory performance improvements.  ||  Best In Class: Teamwork and collaboration extends internal and external groups including key suppliers, channel partners and key customers.

items.control_description: 52. How well are rewards used to drive the organization towards the strategic supply and inventory goals?
items.remarks: Basic: There is limited, enterprise-wide formal rewards and recognition system. Ad-hoc rewards and recognition linked mainly to each functional groups’ near-term goals.  ||  Emerging: A formal reward system is in place but not based on objective criteria and only loosely tied to individual and business performance.  ||  Advanced: Reward system linked to team and business’ performance.  ||  Differentiated: Recognition and rewards based on contributions and results that drive overall business and team performance.  ||  Best In Class: Rewards system measures contribution of internal and external teams (suppliers and business partners).

items.control_description: 53. How does your organization use KPIs and metrics to drive the supply and inventory organization?
items.remarks: Basic: Basic KPIs are in place.  ||  Emerging: Inventory targets are beginning to be defined, reported and managed.  ||  Advanced: Clear metrics are used to measure effectiveness and efficiency within client’s four walls. They include: inventory turns / days on hand, inventory balance ($ and units), service level, product availability, inventory aging profile, lot size impact on productivity, MTO lead times, etc.  ||  Differentiated: Clear metrics are used to measure effectiveness and efficiency across key suppliers and channel partners. They include: inventory turns / days on hand, inventory balance ($ and units), service level, product availability, inventory aging profile, lot size impact on productivity, MTO lead times, etc.  ||  Best In Class: All inventory performance goals are monitored, adjusted based on business needs and consistently achieved.

items.control_description: 76. How is capacity managed in supply and inventory planning?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: No visibility into capacity.  ||  Emerging: Capacity planning annually with yearly buckets; capacity constraints reviewed for following year.  ||  Advanced: Short and medium-term planning horizons and minimal production planning adjustments for a few market conditions. Demand forecast is manually sent to supply on an ad-hoc basis.  ||  Differentiated: Medium and long term planning horizons and limited production planning adjustments to all changing market conditions such as demand or prices. Suppliers receive regular results from the monthly planning process via EDI or web-based communications.  ||  Best In Class: Short, medium and long term planning horizons. Supply chain networks constantly updated to minimize lead times and ensure demand is met. Close collaboration with all vendors through advanced electronic functionality. Majority of strategic suppliers have automatic access to forecasts, usages, and inventory to drive planning systems on a weekly basis. Overflow handled through co-packing opportunities.

items.control_description: 86. How are inventory policies and procedures established and implemented?
items.remarks: Basic: No inventory policies are in place.  ||  Emerging: There is a process for defining inventory and planning parameters per facility.  ||  Advanced: Changes to inventory policy follow a clear, regularly scheduled process and are communicated internally.  ||  Differentiated: Sales and / or manufacturing are consulted appropriately in redefining planning and inventory parameters.  ||  Best In Class: Policy changes are verified with the market before implementation.

items.control_description: 87. Within your organization, who is held accountable for inventory management?
items.remarks: Basic: Accountability for inventory performance rests within operations groups managers only.  ||  Emerging: The team’s communication and decision-making workflows are clear. A RACI map is in place.  ||  Advanced: Rank and file personnel, in addition to functional managers, demonstrate understanding and accountability for inventory performance.  ||  Differentiated: Employees demonstrating accountability for enterprise-wide inventory performance.  ||  Best In Class: Culture focuses on continuous improvement through collaboration, rapid innovation, increasing agility and flexibility for mutual benefit for all participants.

items.control_description: 1. To which extent is your supply chain IT strategy aligned with your supply chain strategy and connected business priorities?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: The supply chain and IT strategy are mainly disconnected from each other.  ||  Emerging: The IT strategy is derived from the supply chain strategy. However, the IT strategy is executed on functional level and not integrated across supply chain functions.  ||  Advanced: The IT strategy is derived from the supply chain strategy and executed across all supply chain functions in an integrated way.  ||  Differentiated: The IT strategy is derived from the supply chain strategy and aligned with key supply chain partners.  ||  Best In Class: The IT strategy is derived from the supply chain strategy and synchronized internally as well as externally across functions and enterprises.

items.control_description: 2. Are your supply chain systems seamlessly integrated with each other through APIs?
items.remarks: Basic: The supply chain systems are not integrated with each other. There are system breaks that need to be solved through manual data extraction / integration.  ||  Emerging: The systems across supply chain functions are not integrated with each other. However, the systems are optimized within the function.  ||  Advanced: The supply chain systems within a company are integrated with each other through APIs. However, they are not externally connected.  ||  Differentiated: The supply chain systems within are integrated with each other through APIs across different enterprises.  ||  Best In Class: The supply chain systems are integrated through APIs and content is made available to many channels, internally and externally. APIs are standardized, but open.

items.control_description: 3. Is the integration of your supply chain systems driven by events and near real-time or batch information?
items.remarks: Basic: All supply chain systems are batch driven.  ||  Emerging: Some supply chain systems are driven by events near real-time.  ||  Advanced: All internal supply chain systems are driven by events in near real-time.  ||  Differentiated: External supply chain systems are connected through events near real-time.  ||  Best In Class: All internal and external supply chain systems are seamlessly integrated and contain near real-time data.

items.control_description: 4. Are your supply chain systems seamlessly integrated with other systems and platforms (e.g. PLM, MDM, PIM, CRM) through APIs?
items.remarks: Basic: The supply chain systems are not integrated with other platforms or systems.  ||  Emerging: The integration between supply chain systems and other platforms or systems occurs through manual interventions.  ||  Advanced: The internal systems are integrated with each other through APIs.  ||  Differentiated: Internal and external supply chain, MDM, PIM, PLM systems are connected through APIs.  ||  Best In Class: Internal and external supply chain, MDM, PIM, PLM systems are connected through APIs near real-time and optimized through machine learning algorithms.

items.control_description: 5. Do you have the capability to manage and enrich any kind of data (i.e. internal, external, structured & unstructured)?
items.remarks: Basic: The does mainly use internal and structured data to manage the supply chain.  ||  Emerging: Selected functions integrate and use external and unstructured data.  ||  Advanced: All internal supply chain functions use internal, external, structured and unstructured data.  ||  Differentiated: The company uses and exchanges all data types with external supply chain partners.  ||  Best In Class: The company uses and exchanges all data types with external supply chain partners on a real-time basis.

items.control_description: 6. How do your supply chain system foster collaboration through a compelling user interface and end-to-end workflows?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: The supply chain is driven by siloed workflows.  ||  Emerging: The supply chain is driven by functional workflows. Systems focus on functionality rather than usability.  ||  Advanced: There are seamless workflows across the internal supply chain functions with a good level of usability.  ||  Differentiated: There are seamless workflows across the internal and external supply chain functions with a good level of usability.  ||  Best In Class: Supply chain workflows are integrated across companies and optimized using machine learning / AI.

items.control_description: 7. How do you use collaboration tools based on automated end-to-end workflow to orchestrate your supply chain?
items.remarks: Basic: The supply chain is using "manual" collaboration options that are not workflow enabled.  ||  Emerging: Selected functions use workflow enabled and automated collaboration options.  ||  Advanced: All internal functions use workflow enabled and automated collaboration options.  ||  Differentiated: All internal and external supply chain partners use workflow enabled and automated collaboration options.  ||  Best In Class: Workflows and collaboration options are fully automated internally and externally.

items.control_description: 8. Has the organization established a big data platform?
items.remarks: Basic: The organization has not implemented a big data platform.  ||  Emerging: The organization has implemented at least one big data platform.  ||  Advanced: Some projects (25%) utilize big data platforms.  ||  Differentiated: 50% of projects utilize big data platforms.  ||  Best In Class: The organization is a leader in using big data platforms.

items.control_description: 9. What extraction, transformation and loading (ETL) tools does the organization use and how long do changes take?
items.remarks: Basic: The organization uses code based ETL tools; changes take >1 month.  ||  Emerging: The organization uses minimally scalable tools; changes take 3-4 weeks.  ||  Advanced: The organization uses moderately scalable tools; changes take 2-3 weeks.  ||  Differentiated: The organization uses highly scalable tools; changes take 1-2 weeks.  ||  Best In Class: ETL tools can be configured by the business; changes take <1 week.

items.control_description: 10. What reporting capabilities are available for data analysis?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: There are no reporting tools in place; excel / access are used across the organization  ||  Emerging: Informal reporting tools are used in specific business units.  ||  Advanced: Standardized organization-wide reporting tools provide regular reports and some ad-hoc capabilities.  ||  Differentiated: Standardized organization-wide reporting tools are actively used across all business units.  ||  Best In Class: Advanced reporting tools are actively used across the organization (for data visualization, advanced analytics, etc.).

items.control_description: 11. What analytics software platforms does the organization have?
items.remarks: Basic: The organization mainly has spreadsheets and flat files.  ||  Emerging: The organization has data warehouses or data marts.  ||  Advanced: The organization has reporting and analytics platforms but in a siloed mode.  ||  Differentiated: The organization has Hadoop or other big data platforms but in a siloed mode.  ||  Best In Class: The organization has a range of integrated software platforms.

items.control_description: 12. To what extent are AI and ML utilized?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: AI and ML are not utilized.  ||  Emerging: The organization is starting to experiment with AI and ML in a few projects.  ||  Advanced: AI and ML are utilized in a few business units.  ||  Differentiated: AI and ML are utilized in half of the business units.  ||  Best In Class: AI and ML are widely utilized to make organizational decisions.

items.control_description: 13. How well is the architect organization aligned with the business functions?
items.remarks: Basic: Minimal architecture - business interaction.  ||  Emerging: The business is involved in a few aspects of the architecture but not into business investment or acquisition strategy.  ||  Advanced: Architecture is integrated with the enterprise planning and budgeting process.  ||  Differentiated: Metrics are captured to measure the implementation of the business goals and objectives.  ||  Best In Class: The business is involved in the continuous improvement of the architecture.

items.control_description: 14. How well is the architect organization aligned with the delivery functions?
items.remarks: Basic: Architects have no visibility into project architecture.  ||  Emerging: Architecture is used as baseline for projects only.  ||  Advanced: Ongoing, but informal dialog between architects and project team; no penalty for variance.  ||  Differentiated: Trust and confidence achieved.  ||  Best In Class: Attained with customers and partners.

items.control_description: 15. How well is the architect organization aligned with the operations functions?
items.remarks: Basic: Minimal architecture-operations interaction.  ||  Emerging: Operations is involved informally with a few aspects of the architecture.  ||  Advanced: Architecture is integrated with the operations standards development and application portfolio management processes.  ||  Differentiated: SDLC identifies specific checkpoints for architectural review; variances must be justified and recorded.  ||  Best In Class: Operations is involved in the continuous improvement of the architecture.

items.control_description: 16. Level of integration architect practitioners have organizationally. Are they a group of individualists or are they a well integrated group that works using common processes, practices and goals?
items.remarks: Basic: No formal architecture governing body exists to enforce architecture policies.  ||  Emerging: Loose confederation of architects assembled, given new responsibility but little authority.  ||  Advanced: Formal architecture group defined independently of other IT areas; owns and manages key architecture processes.  ||  Differentiated: Greater architecture community established and collaborating regularly; clear ownership of architecture vision (i.e. blueprints).  ||  Best In Class: Architecture body seen as guiding force for IT and organization; broad skill sets enable them to contribute to both business and technical decisions.

items.control_description: 17. How well is the role and needed skills of an architect defined?
items.remarks: Basic: No formal architecture roles defined *OR*role descriptions are very generic and not tied to specific architecture requirements.  ||  Emerging: Formal architect titles given to senior IT resources, roles may start being defined.  ||  Advanced: Only data and application architect roles are formalized, generally focused on defining application or project level solutions - Documented architecture skills are used for recruiting and to shape training programs.  ||  Differentiated: Architects serve key roles on projects and are mostly interchangeable.  ||  Best In Class: Enterprise architect role visible within enterprise and tied into arch governance models.

items.control_description: 18. What is the level of collaboration both inside the architecture community as well as outside with business and technology clients of the organization?
items.remarks: Basic: Architects work as independent practitioners and collaborate little or none among themselves.  ||  Emerging: There is some collaboration within the architecture group along similar or related domains. No formal collaboration processes exist.  ||  Advanced: There is a formal process to solicit input within the architecture community. Upstream and downstream customers are brought into these sessions on an ad-hoc basis as needed.  ||  Differentiated: There is a formal process to solicit input within and outside of the architecture community. Upstream and downstream partners attend regular sessions with architecture.  ||  Best In Class: There is a formal process to solicit input within and outside of the architecture community. Business and IT partners regularly reach out to the architecture organization to keep them informed in a proactive manner.

items.control_description: 19. What is the level of industry specific and technology centric skill sets of the members of the architecture group ?
items.remarks: Basic: Heavy reliance on external resources to provide architecture guidance and direction; arch skills tied to specific platforms or products.  ||  Emerging: Breadth and depth of arch skills vary widely; no formal architecture curriculum exists for the architect career path  Little or no assessment or monitoring of skills inventory is performed.  ||  Advanced: Architecture skills are defined for specific roles within a work area, the skills required by each role, and the depth of knowledge required to fulfill the role successfully  Skill specialization begins (going beyond application and data), including network and security infrastructures, integration, and operations.  ||  Differentiated: IT training curriculum includes specific Architect paths; job descriptions exist; architects enriched through extracurricular activities  Critical architecture skills are measured through periodic surveys  Architects recognized as more than technical skills, skill definitions for roles include generic skills, business skills, enterprise architecture skills, project management skills, general knowledge skills, and technical IT skills.  ||  Best In Class: Industry-recognized experts in areas of architecture with reputation extending to partners and competitors; fostering architecture culture internally.

items.control_description: 20. Is there an ingrained cultural component to the architecture group that allows individuals to feel as part of a larger purpose and positively reinforces communication, collaboration & a 'can do' mentality?
items.remarks: Basic: Little or no influencing culture ingrained in architecture organization. Work is undertaken for the sake of doing work; resources have no alignment to company mission or vision.  ||  Emerging: Some influencing culture ingrained in Architecture organization. Some communication channels exist but used on ad hoc basis. No formal sense of community.  ||  Advanced: Influencing culture is ingrained in architecture organization. Communities exist and are used occasionally as formats for discussion. Some alignment of resources to company mission and vision.  ||  Differentiated: Influencing culture is ingrained in Architecture organization. Communities exist and are used frequently as formats for discussion. Strong alignment of resources to company mission and vision. General "Can Do" attitude persists across the organization. Architects frequently assisting other teams be successful.  ||  Best In Class: Influencing culture is ingrained in architecture organization. Communities exist and are used frequently as formats for discussion. Strong alignment of resources to company mission and vision. General "Can Do" attitude persists across the organization. Architecture group is consistently dedicated to assisting other teams be successful, on behalf of helping the company meet its objectives.

items.control_description: 21. How well developed are processes and means to share knowledge within the architecture community & beyond?
items.remarks: Basic: Little knowledge sharing or “cross-pollination” among architects  ||  Emerging: Some collaboration around vendor platform choices and technology direction.  ||  Advanced: Central repository used for collection and retrieval of architectural artifacts.  ||  Differentiated: High degree of knowledge sharing among architecture community.  ||  Best In Class: Full access to current and past artifacts and decisions; extends beyond organization to include partners.

items.control_description: 22. Is there a practice of developing business operations and technology blueprints that depict a to be architecture for business ops & IT architecture?
items.remarks: Basic: No plans exist to develop business driven target architectures and migrate to them. Limited management and / or organizational awareness of need to build plans to develop business driven target architectures One off architecture models created in isolation by various authors and used for very specific purposes.  ||  Emerging: Management awareness of need to develop blueprints  Roles and responsibilities defined, and blueprint planning work underway  One time Herculean effort produced comprehensive model that once provided value but which was never kept up to date.  ||  Advanced: Enterprise architects have published multiple iterations of the blueprint to coincide with the launch of major IT efforts. Project plans exist to mobilize and deliver the initiative defined by the blueprints. Process for maintaining and updating blueprints is operational. Resource requirements and availability are assessed  Cost / benefit assessment of the initiatives identified in blueprints is completed.  ||  Differentiated: Architecture Blueprinting is a recurring IT process and priority is given toward efforts to maintain its accuracy  Blueprints are periodically reviewed and updated  Blueprinting is integrated with portfolio management activities.  Blueprints include architecture risk assessment  Portfolio Management is adjusted based on the feedback received and lessons learned from updated IT architecture. Periodic reexamination of business drivers.  ||  Best In Class: Blueprinting process is ongoing incorporating insights from project work, technology innovation, and industry advances. Architecture implementation projects are continually sorted into prioritized order on implementation roadmap. Ongoing efforts to improve target architecture efforts, based on metrics, internal feedback and external best practices, supported by senior management. Continual alignment of migration strategies with business needs, investment and acquisition decisions.

items.control_description: 23. Is there a bottom-up practice of diagnosing business and application health that is used to drive changes in technology?
items.remarks: Basic: Minor or no consideration given to application landscape on a year Limited awareness of need to track and communicate desired and / or required changes to the application portfolio 0 year basis.  ||  Emerging: Some application health assessments occur in pockets in the organization periodically. Outcomes may OR may not be incorporated into discussions with the Business.  ||  Advanced: Application health assessments are formally defined , and are conducted in some areas on a regular basis Informal discussions with the business take place around business health, as health relates to need for technology.  ||  Differentiated: Application health assessments are formally defined, are repeatable and conducted across the organization  Business health assessments occur to some degree  Health assessments influence the planning cycle  Outcomes are measured on a regular basis.  ||  Best In Class: Both application and business health assessments are formally defined, are repeatable and conducted across the organization. Health assessments influence the planning cycle. Outcomes are measured on a regular basis. Ongoing efforts to incorporate health assessments with blueprinting efforts.

items.control_description: 24. Is there a process and resources dedicated to the development of reference architectures for different business, problem & technology domains?
items.remarks: Basic: No plans exist to develop reference architectures. All development work is solely projectoriented. Limited management and / or organizational awareness of need to build plans to develop reference architectures.  ||  Emerging: Management awareness of need to develop plans to build reference architectures  Roles and responsibilities defined, and planning work underway.  ||  Advanced: Implementation and migration strategies exist to achieve the reference architectures. Highlevel implementation plans exist, including a highlevel list of projects required.  ||  Differentiated: Active efforts underway to develop and implement reference architectures  Migration strategies are periodically reviewed and updated  Implementation plans are developed in alignment with architectural investment decisions  Architecture risks are identified and managed.  ||  Best In Class: Ongoing efforts to improve reference architecture implementation efforts, based on metrics, internal feedback and external best practices, supported by senior management. Continual alignment of migration strategies with investment and acquisition decisions.

items.control_description: 25. Does the architecture group create guiding principles and other technical guidance documents that help developers & ops to standardize architectures, designs & technology decisions?
items.remarks: Basic: No guiding principles are defined. Guiding principles are not used to drive decision making processes at all. Little management awareness of the value of architecture principles.  ||  Emerging: Guiding principles are defined based on executive's personal beliefs  Some ground rules (i.e., implicit guiding principles) have been established and used to drive decisions.  ||  Advanced: Guiding principles are defined based on each subject area's specific goals and objectives. Architecture areas are actively using guiding principles to drive recommendations.  ||  Differentiated: Guiding principles intended to drive business and technology collaboration are in place  Guiding principles are defined based on a common set of IT goals and objectives. The linkages between IT general guiding principles and specific technology area's principles are well established  IT are actively using common guiding principles to drive decision making processes. Principles are also used to guide business and IT joint decision making processes.  ||  Best In Class: Architecture principles undergo periodic review and revision to ensure alignment to overall IT and business principles, informed by metrics, internal feedback and external best practices. Guiding principles are defined based on a common set of company business goals and objectives. The traceability is well defined entire company is using the common set of guiding principles to drive all decisions.

items.control_description: 26. Is there a governance process and how broad is the focus of the governance?
items.remarks: Basic: No governance in place  ||  Emerging: Governance focuses on technology standard compliance and architecture documentation completeness  If Blueprints exist, they are used as baseline for projects only (no Future State).  ||  Advanced: Governance expanded into architecture quality and blueprinting compliance. Blueprint Architecture Diagrams used in reviews.  ||  Differentiated: Architecture governance integrated with SDLC and other IT Strategy planning processes.  Architecture health monitoring & tracking .Active SWAT activities responding to key architecture issues.  ||  Best In Class: Blueprints guide strategic enterprise architecture and IT investment decisions. Capability focused architecture decisions.

items.control_description: 27. Is there a formal and documented set of processes that describe how governance functions are executed throughout the project implementation and technology decision process?
items.remarks: Basic: No formal process in place. Enterprise architects have no visibility into project architecture.  ||  Emerging: Gate review structure applied to projects. Architecture governance conducted as separate processes  Outside of specific review there is ongoing, but informal dialog between architects and project team; no penalty for varying from Blueprint.  ||  Advanced: Corrective action focus. Job aids have been produced for governance use. Governance checklist is also available. Architecture Issue Escalation path clearly defined and executed.  ||  Differentiated: Exception Management / standards and waivers process is used to improve architecture development process.  Architecture process metrics are used to optimize and drive business linkages.  Business involved in the continuous process improvements of IT architecture.  ||  Best In Class: IT Governance fully integrated into corporate governance. Governance is part of everyday architecture processes; not just gate reviews. Outputs of governance are regularly reviewed for further process improvement. Projects require architects sign off before proceeding; new project insights are regularly fed back into blueprints (governance is two-way). Feedback on architecture process from all operating unit elements is used to drive architecture process improvements.

items.control_description: 28. Are there established and agreed upon metrics that inform management about the effectiveness and value of the governance process in place?
items.remarks: Basic: .  ||  Emerging: Metrics for standard compliance and architecture documentation completeness.  ||  Advanced: Architecture quality metrics and blueprinting compliance metrics tracked and reported.  ||  Differentiated: Metrics captured to monitor implementation governance processes  Monitor reusability metrics  Architecture risk is measured and monitored on a regular basis  Business Alignment Metrics in decisions (delivery of business value).  ||  Best In Class: Technology value metrics integrated into corporate reporting.

items.control_description: 29. Are there established organizational bodies that perform the governance functions (such as review boards, steering committees, etc.)?
items.remarks: Basic: Ad-hoc reviews as informal governance.  ||  Emerging: Crossdiscipline architecture review team.  ||  Advanced: Formal architecture review board in place.  ||  Differentiated: Active SWAT activities responding to key architecture Issues.  ||  Best In Class: Architecture governance board becomes part of overall corporate governance body.

items.control_description: 30. Are there any tools available that support the execution, reporting and metrics of the governance function?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: No tools in place  ||  Emerging: Spreadsheets and other adhoc tracking of issues.  ||  Advanced: Repeatable governance manual. Formal repository to track documentation.  ||  Differentiated: Reporting tools in place to produce consolidated metrics dashboards.  ||  Best In Class: Integrated enterprise wide corporate governance tools and reporting capabilities.

items.control_description: 31. To what level and with what regularity do projects get assigned architects that will support the project through its lifecycle?
items.remarks: Basic: No formal project architect position in place. Architecture work done informally by other staff members.  ||  Emerging: Project architect role defined.  Focus is on initial high level design.  ||  Advanced: Project architect role expanded into overall technology leadership on the project.  ||  Differentiated: Project architecture quality metrics formally defined, tracked and reported.  Corrective actions take to improve the architecture quality.  ||  Best In Class: Rotational programs in place to enable different architects to play different roles across the pool to remove "ivory tower" perception.

items.control_description: 32. To what level are IT architects involved in project delivery?
items.remarks: Basic: Little investment. No involvement in project.  ||  Emerging: Some investment.  Cursory involvement in project, but not enough to ensure major risks and/or dependencies are identified.  ||  Advanced: Investment.  Involvement in project. Risks and dependencies are identified, but no solution is suggested.  ||  Differentiated: High level of investment.  Risks and dependencies are identified but also guidance is provided around finding a solution.  ||  Best In Class: Admirable dedication. Risks and dependencies are identified but ongoing guidance and solution discussions provided to work through challenges together.

items.control_description: 33. How well are architects in tune with the main execution drivers at different stages of the process?
items.remarks: Basic: Poor awareness of core customer needs, both upstream and downstream.  ||  Emerging: Some awareness of core customer needs, both upstream and downstream.  ||  Advanced: Awareness of majority of customers' needs, both upstream and downstream.  Some minor chasms may exist with primary partners.  ||  Differentiated: Awareness of majority of customers' needs, both upstream and downstream.  Some minor chasms may exist between secondary or tertiary partners.  ||  Best In Class: Full, fluid integration between architecture and all of its customers, both upstream and downstream. Open dialogue between teams ensures challenges can be proactively addressed.

items.control_description: 34. To what level are reviews in the pre coding stage part of the SDLC?
