items.remarks: Basic: No process exists for formal review of project architectures and guideline compliance before a project implementation starts.  ||  Emerging: Some projects get architecture guidance and informal reviews by architects based solely on relationships and perceived needs of a party without any criteria as to what project type should be reviewed.  Outcomes are not formally documented.  ||  Advanced: Some projects get reviewed based on size, complexity and visibility in the architecture community.  Reviews are somewhat informal but guided by checklists.  Recommendations may be incorporated and informal waivers may be granted.  ||  Differentiated: Every new implementation project is reviewed; structure and process of reviews is somewhat formal.  A checklist exists but there is no formalized process to grant waivers or resolve disparate views on architectural compliance.  ||  Best In Class: Every new implementation project and major maintenance project undergoes a formal project review. Non compliance will lead to re-architecture or an accepted waiver process. There is a formal process to document and resolve disparate views and arrive at a consensus architecture.

items.control_description: 35. To what level are reviews in the pre release (post coding) stage part of the SDLC?
items.remarks: Basic: No process exists for formal review of project architectures and guideline compliance before a project moves into production state.  ||  Emerging: Some projects get architecture guidance and informal reviews by architects based solely on relationships and perceived needs of a party without any criteria as to what project type should be reviewed.  Outcomes are not formally documented.  ||  Advanced: Some projects get reviewed based on size, complexity and visibility in the architecture community.  Reviews are somewhat informal but guided by checklists.  Recommendations may be incorporated and informal waivers may be granted.  ||  Differentiated: Every new implementation project is reviewed; structure and process of reviews is somewhat formal.  A checklist exists but there is no formalized process to grant waivers or resolve disparate views on architectural compliance.  ||  Best In Class: Every new implementation project and major maintenance project undergoes a formal project review. Non compliance will lead to re-architecture or an accepted waiver process. There is a formal process to document and resolve disparate views and arrive at a consensus architecture.

items.control_description: 36. Is there a formal Innovation function?
items.remarks: Basic: Skunk works projects are common; new technology crops up in isolated pockets in the architecture.  ||  Emerging: IT primarily looking to vendors to drive the introduction of new technologies and set standards.  ||  Advanced: IT is coordinating ongoing technology exploration efforts setting specific goals and publishing results to wider audience.  ||  Differentiated: Technology research projects are actively tracked and monitored with results being folded into future state blueprints.  ||  Best In Class: Solid tech research efforts prompt new business ideas and help drive evolving corporate strategies.

items.control_description: 37. What is the level of dedication of research and innovation activities?
items.remarks: Basic: Research and innovation is rare but if done is done in resources' spare time, on a completely ad hoc basis.  ||  Emerging: Research and innovation is done consistently in pockets, informally.  ||  Advanced: Resources spilt time informally between project activities and research & innovation activities.  ||  Differentiated: Resources split time formally between project activities and research and innovation activities.  ||  Best In Class: There is an official organization dedicated to research and innovation activities.

items.control_description: 38. Do facilities and equipment exist to execute research and innovation projects on a dedicated environment?
items.remarks: Basic: No dedicated space exists; minimal or no equipment.  ||  Emerging: Dedicated space exists but equipment is minimal.  Activities are limited to white paper research.  ||  Advanced: Equipment and space exist but only basic innovation activities can be undertaken.  ||  Differentiated: Equipment and space exist.  Moderate innovation activities can be undertaken (partial collaboration with IT stakeholders).  ||  Best In Class: Equipment and space exist. Advanced innovation activities can be undertaken (full collaboration with business and IT stakeholders; incorporation of cutting edge technology).

items.control_description: 39. Is there a structured process to gather and communicate the effectiveness of research and innovation activities?
items.remarks: Basic: Metrics are not defined; data for likely metrics is not captured.  ||  Emerging: Metrics are not defined; data for likely metrics is being captured.  Reports are not utilized.  ||  Advanced: Metrics are defined; data for metrics is being captured.  Manual reports are generated.  ||  Differentiated: Advanced metrics are defined; some data for these metrics is being captured.  Some reporting is automated.  ||  Best In Class: Advanced metrics are defined, data is captured and information is reported on. Reporting is automated. Revenue/profit is correlated to innovation driven business capabilities.

items.control_description: 40. What is the depth and span of metrics that are collected about the performance and value of the architecture group?
items.remarks: Basic: Usually no metrics in place. No formal tracking in place. No reports available.  ||  Emerging: Some basic metrics are in place. Metrics are tracked in adhoc tools such as spreadsheets. Reporting is often done manually.  Adhoc reports produced. Historical analysis not always feasible.  ||  Advanced: Metrics for key processes are defined.  Formal tools are in place to systematically track metrics. Historical data available for analysis.  Historical trend reports are produced.  ||  Differentiated: Metrics used to measure both business and technology capabilities and qualities.  Tools available to consolidate data from various metrics repositories into single report, automatically.  Customized dashboard and reports available for various constituencies.  ||  Best In Class: Continuous improvement processes in place to refine metrics tracked and reported. Single metrics repository in place to track all metrics. Architecture metrics reporting fully integrated into overall IT metrics reporting.

items.control_description: 41. How well defined are the processes of ongoing communication between different business and IT stakeholders to inform & solve issues?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Minimal focus on communication / stakeholder relationship development.  ||  Emerging: Occasional interaction between stakeholders and architecture, but messaging is not always inclusive of all correct parties.  ||  Advanced: Interaction with stakeholders on regular basis through informal channels. Occasional communication out to stakeholder groups. Messaging is usually consistent across all relevant parties.  ||  Differentiated: Training (all modes) available at time and point of need Organization wide process for integrating and managing the knowledge content configuration.  ||  Best In Class: Company now has the ability to translate internal knowledge into innovation inputs.

items.control_description: 42. How well defined are career progression, levels, expectations and training programs both inside & outside the company that allow architects to progress in their career in a defined manner?
items.remarks: Basic: Managers explicitly push for training.  ||  Emerging: Start to emphasize the needs for knowledge management.  ||  Advanced: Managers recognize role in, and encourage, knowledgesharing.  The organization is able to see a link between KM processes and results.  ||  Differentiated: Training (all modes) available at time and point of need. Organization wide process for integrating and managing the knowledge content configuration.  ||  Best In Class: Company now has the ability to translate internal knowledge into innovation inputs.

items.control_description: 43. How well defined are processes that deal with capacity planning, work assignment, oversight and performance management?
items.remarks: Basic: No view into available capacity. Resources are staffed on a first come, first serve basis. No conscious alignment to most appropriate investments.  ||  Emerging: Minimal view into available capacity.  Resource assignments are made by asking questions instead of hard data (e.g., visibility into capacity and/or strategic alignment).  ||  Advanced: Basic view into available capacity exists. Skills needed / available are sometimes an input into making resource assignment. Resources are sometimes assigned to higher priority initiatives.  ||  Differentiated: Formal relationship exists between role, skill sets and career path.  Resource capacity is usually aligned to appropriate portfolio investment.  Career path and opportunities are clearly defined.  ||  Best In Class: Available resource capacity is leveraged for optimal portfolio investment. Career path and opportunities are clear and in practice and tied directly to role and skill set.

items.control_description: 44. Is there a budget?
items.remarks: Basic: A budget exists, but forecast is not tracked. Annual planning process not able to leverage historical architect time.  ||  Emerging: Forecast is tracked occasionally.  Annual planning process not able to leverage historical architect time.  ||  Advanced: Forecast is consistently tracked.  Annual planning process is not able to leverage historical architect time.  ||  Differentiated: Forecast is consistently tracked.  Annual planning process is occasionally able to leverage historical architect time.  ||  Best In Class: Forecast is consistently tracked. Annual planning process consistently leverages historical architect time.

items.control_description: 45. Are processes and templates used for enterprise architecture?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Processes are ad hoc and informal, processes followed may not be consistent. There is no unified architecture process across technologies and lines of business.  ||  Emerging: The basic EA Program is documented  Processes are planned and tracked  The organization is beginning to reuse methods for capturing critical EA information.  ||  Advanced: The lifecycle architecture processes have been defined and documented  Generic architecture processes are being customized for uses by agencies, departments, etc.  Process models have been prepared  Templates are used to ensure the capturing of information is consistent.  ||  Differentiated: The organization captures metrics to measure the effectiveness of the EA processes and templates  Corrective action plans are put in place when deficiencies in templates and/or procedures are identified  Meetings are held regularly to review modifications to the EA Framework.  ||  Best In Class: The lifecycle processes are being followed and have become second nature to the organization. Captured metrics are used to identify inefficiencies in EA processes and templates prior to notification of issues. Organization works with other states to share ideas for improvements to EA processes and templates.

items.control_description: 46. Is there adherence to published standards, processes and other EA elements & the processes?
items.remarks: Basic: The need for compliance to standards has been identified. Compliance is informal and unstructured. Compliance cannot be measured effectively, because processes are not consistent across areas and / or projects.  ||  Emerging: The organization has begun to develop a compliance process to ensure that projects and enhancements are consistent with EA standards.  ||  Advanced: A formal EA compliance process is well defined and is an integral part of the EA lifecycle processes. The EA compliance process is followed consistently throughout the enterprise. A business case is required for variance from the EA standards.  ||  Differentiated: Compliance to the EA standards has become common practice throughout the enterprise  Quality metrics associated with the business cases are captured  The compliance process is reviewed and updated when deficiencies or enhancements to the process are identified.  ||  Best In Class: Information gathered during the compliance process is used to proactively identify updates to the EA standards and / or framework. Architecture metrics are used to drive continuous process improvements in the business cases. The organization works with other states to share ideas for improvements to the compliance process.

items.control_description: 1. To what extent is contract management formalized within the organization?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: No formal contract management framework or process in place.  ||  Emerging: Contract management happens on an ad hoc basis and to inconsistent standards. Limited development of contracting strategies. Procurement has no involvement in ongoing contract management.  ||  Advanced: Basic contract management processes documented and in place supported by a formal contract management structure and contracting models. Not fully integrated with the SRM and / or sourcing strategy. Contract management is performed by business managers with very limited Procurement involvement.  ||  Differentiated: Formal contract management framework integrated with the sourcing strategy. Clearly defined contract management roles and responsibilities. One size fits all approach with limited guidance on different contract models and differentiated levels of contract management. Contract service delivery and administration for some major contracts managed by professional contract managers. Contract management tends to operate independent of procurement or with limited procurement support.  ||  Best In Class: Formal contract management framework integrated with the SRM and sourcing strategy. Clearly defined contract management roles and responsibilities, contracting models, processes and differentiated contract outputs (obligations) based on contract / relationship type. Contract service delivery, relationship, administration and risk for key suppliers managed on a routine basis by professional contract managers in procurement or with procurement support.

items.control_description: 2. What is the current state of a contract lifecycle management system?
items.remarks: Basic: No contract lifecycle management system (CLM), paper-based contracts stored manually or electronic contracts stored on hard drive.  ||  Emerging: Inconsistent usage of CLM, system capability not fully utilized.  ||  Advanced: CLM system being used consistently and contract information available for ordering process.  ||  Differentiated: Contracts in the CLM system are supplemented by catalogs available for punch out at ordering time.  ||  Best In Class: CLM system is integrated with RFX / e-auction system to pre-populate relevant information into the contract.

items.control_description: 3. What is the current usage of standard contract templates?
items.remarks: Basic: No usage of standard contract templates.  ||  Emerging: Contract templates exist with limited or inconsistent use.  ||  Advanced: Contract templates have been standardized and are consistently used across the business.  ||  Differentiated: Contract templates have been designed to integrate with CLM.  ||  Best In Class: Contract templates have been designed to integrate with CLM and are automated with continuous improvement to promote high usage in system.

items.control_description: 4. How effective have efforts been to drive contract coverage?
items.remarks: Basic: Contracts in place covering less than 25% of suppliers. No central visibility of contracts or regular communications of contract information. Very few, if any, corporate agreements exist. Procurement tends to be local. No attempt to report on levels of compliance with process or contracts.  ||  Emerging: Contracts in place covering 2550% of suppliers. No regular communication of contract information. Corporate agreements in place for some enterprise wide requirements. High levels of maverick buying outside these agreements. Staff and management openly dispute value and shop around for 'better' deals.  ||  Advanced: Contracts in place covering 5075% of suppliers. Contract information is communicated sporadically. Information on contracts is periodically updated on the corporate intranet but evidence is that few users regularly access this information. Maverick buying persists in categories where corporate agreements exist (<20% of spend).  ||  Differentiated: Contracts in place covering 7585% of influenceable spend. Updated contract information is regularly communicated to the business and easily accessible online (push and pull). 7080% of spend with contract suppliers is through contract terms. Some maverick buying persists in categories where corporate agreements exist (<10% of spend).  ||  Best In Class: Contracts in place covering >85% of influenceable spend. Updated contract information is regularly communicated to the business and easily accessible online (push and pull). >80% of spend with contract suppliers is through contract terms. Minimal maverick buying in categories where corporate agreements exist (<5% of spend).

items.control_description: 5. What is the level of compliance with preferred suppliers (i.e. is maverick buying a problem)?
items.remarks: Basic: Non compliance and maverick buying are widespread across the organization. Procurement's ability to consolidate spend with preferred suppliers is non existent. Management in some areas actively encourage staff to purchase outside these agreements.  ||  Emerging: Compliance to preferred supplier agreements is generally poor. There is limited support for procurement's attempts to mandate use.  ||  Advanced: Compliance to preferred suppliers is variable. In some categories or business areas it is very good but in others there is evidence of recurring non compliance.  ||  Differentiated: Compliance to preferred suppliers is high. There are occasional issues with maverick buying but these are not persistent.  ||  Best In Class: Compliance is automated and non-preferred supplier spend is immediately flagged. Compliance to preferred suppliers is very high. Cases of non compliance are very rare and normally have business justification.

items.control_description: 6. To what extent are sustainability criteria included in contract management?
items.remarks: Basic: No formal sustainability criteria in contracts or contract management framework.  ||  Emerging: Contract management incorporates sustainability criteria on an ad hoc basis and to inconsistent standards. Limited development of sustainability in contracting strategies. Little or no sustainability considerations in ongoing contract management..  ||  Advanced: Basic sustainability considerations (e.g. only up to tier 1 suppliers) included in some contracts and contract management processes. Not fully integrated with the SRM and/or sourcing strategy. Contracts are managed by business managers with limited sustainability knowledge or access to appropriate technical expertise.  ||  Differentiated: Formal contract management framework is integrated within the sourcing strategy and considers a range of sustainability considerations beyond tier 1 suppliers. An approach and guidance exists specifically for managing sustainability in contracts. Contract service delivery and administration for some major contracts managed by professional contract managers with some sustainability knowledge.  ||  Best In Class: Contract service delivery and administration for some major contracts managed by professional contract managers with very good sustainability knowledge and focused on leading sustainability practices in the industry.

items.control_description: 7. To what extent does procurement actively manage supplier numbers?
items.remarks: Basic: No evidence that procurement is aware of need for supplier rationalization despite very high numbers of suppliers. Supply base is growing aggressively year over year with new suppliers added constantly.  ||  Emerging: Procurement recognize that supplier numbers are too high but there is no evidence of procurement attempting supplier rationalization in last 3 years. Supply base is strongly growing ear on year.  ||  Advanced: Procurement aware of need to rationalize suppliers. Some evidence of efforts to reduce supplier numbers over the last three years but no current activity in progress. Supplier numbers widely recognized as too high. Supply base is still growing strongly year over year.  ||  Differentiated: Supplier rationalization initiatives have made some progress in reducing numbers of active suppliers but procurement believe there is more work to do. Procurement have performed reviews of transaction volumes to identify opportunities to reduce the supplier tail but this is not regularly repeated. Supply base is still growing year over year but net increase is small.  ||  Best In Class: Supplier rationalization initiatives have succeeded in reducing numbers of active suppliers to a point where procurement believe they have the optimal number of suppliers. Through automated dashboards, procurement performs an annual review of transaction volumes to identify opportunities to reduce the supplier tail. Request for a new supplier is flagged in the system and requires workflow approval to onboard.

items.control_description: 8. How are suppliers stratified for oversight and management?
items.remarks: Basic: No differentiation or visibility into suppliers.  ||  Emerging: Informal definition for "alliance partner" or top tier; no preferred vendor list.  ||  Advanced: Three to four tiers of relationships; specific criteria for becoming a top tier supplier.  ||  Differentiated: Differentiated strategies for supplier tiers; visibility and integration of top tier suppliers.  ||  Best In Class: All suppliers categorized into a supplier tier, system visibility and tracking of all suppliers within dashboards; but efforts focused on top tier suppliers.

items.control_description: 9. To what extent does the organization have a defined strategy and approach for managing strategic suppliers?
items.remarks: Basic: All suppliers are treated the same - the supply base is managed on a purely transactional basis with no partnerships or alliances in place.  ||  Emerging: There is no formal SRM strategy which differentiates supplier management based on supplier strategic importance. Management of supplier relationship is based on business stakeholders and is not consistent usually defaults to "top 23 spend suppliers". The organization does not have a single view of its strategic suppliers.  ||  Advanced: SRM strategy includes a view of different relationship types with processes, objectives, governance arrangements, KPIs and continuous development requirements partially defined. Governance currently only operates within procurement. Procurement is taking the lead on developing a process but there is limited business recognition of the strategy, process or procurement's responsibilities in this area.  ||  Differentiated: Strategic suppliers are defined, and aligned, across all the businesses. SRM strategy includes clearly defined relationship types linked to differentiated objectives, governance arrangements, KPIs and continuous development plans. Governance operates across the organization/business units for strategic suppliers. Executive sponsorship of individual strategic relationships through a designated owner within each organization.  ||  Best In Class: Strategic suppliers are defined, and aligned, across all the businesses. Clear cross-functional alignment and lead / support roles defined across the organization in terms of supporting strategic supplier negotiations / discussions, with Procurement in lead. Formalized SRM strategy includes clearly defined relationship types linked to differentiated objectives, governance arrangements, KPIs and continuous development plans. Governance operates across the organization for strategic suppliers. Automated dashboards pulling in operational performance and performance to contract terms supports discussions.

items.control_description: 10. How mature is your vendor selection process?
items.remarks: Basic: Not mature, select vendors solely based on relationships.  ||  Emerging: Limited controls in place when selecting new vendors. Must consider three suppliers and ensure meet some qualitative requirements.  ||  Advanced: Formal vendor selection process in place that procurement follows.  ||  Differentiated: Formal vendor selection process in place that the entire organization follows.  ||  Best In Class: The entire organization utilizes technology to host competitive bids to select suppliers based on costs as well as qualitative requirements which are all scored through technology system.

items.control_description: 11. How is supplier performance measured?
items.remarks: Basic: Little or no understanding of supplier performance. No formal performance measurements in place.  ||  Emerging: Supplier performance management guidelines have been defined but these are not integrated with SRM strategy and are not differentiated. Collection of performance data is infrequent and requires manual data collection and manipulation. In most cases the organization relies on suppliers to provide performance data.  ||  Advanced: Supplier performance metrics are measured and able to be put into dashboards with minimal manual manipulation. Metrics are accurate and not questioned.  ||  Differentiated: Supplier performance management process in place with links to SRM strategy. Guidance provided as to governance model (metrics reviewed, frequency of reviews, who is at reviews, level of improvement being sought within the type of relationship, etc.). Up to date performance data used to populate the dashboard / review materials. Heavily automated metrics pull and dashboard development.  ||  Best In Class: Automated scorecard in place, incorporating up to date metrics. Structured supplier performance management process in place with differentiated levels of activity based on segmentation of suppliers (aligned with SRM strategy) and governing metrics used. Frequency of reviews and level of improvement being sought within the relationship. Basic performance data captured for all contract suppliers on a regular basis and available to procurement. Summary level performance data is accessible to relevant stakeholders and to key suppliers.

items.control_description: 12. To what extent has the business implemented a supplier development program?
items.remarks: Basic: No defined supplier development / improvement program. Suppliers receive little briefing or feedback. Little information sharing.  ||  Emerging: Service issues raised on an ad hoc basis when considered significant. Areas for improvement identified by buyer, little progress in completion.  ||  Advanced: Regular review meetings between suppliers and procurement to identify improvement opportunities. Often reactive to specific issues. Suppliers have limited access to organization's assistance.  ||  Differentiated: Multifunctional teams meet to discuss issues and opportunities with suppliers on a regular basis. Specific targets / time scales set and monitored. Regular exchange of information. Regular supplier seminars held. Supplier development resources linked to category strategy and focused efforts on strategic / new suppliers.  ||  Best In Class: Pro-active supplier development program implemented. Evidence of benefits realized. Supplier is proactive in seeking out improvement opportunities. Suppliers receive regular feedback and communication (e.g. through conferences, seminars and newsletters).

items.control_description: 13. To what extent are planning schedules / forecasts shared with suppliers?
items.remarks: Basic: Suppliers receive schedules infrequently or not at all. There is a low level of accuracy. Schedules are out of date. There is no consideration of supplier’s capacity.  ||  Emerging: Longer term forecasts given but are subject to considerable change. Regular short term forecasts are provided to suppliers however, these are subject to frequent change.  ||  Advanced: Suppliers receive schedules subject to amendment but not always on a timely basis. Suppliers’ acknowledgments are checked.  ||  Differentiated: Contingency plans are in place. Suppliers receive mostly accurate schedules with few amendments.  ||  Best In Class: Up to date schedules / forecasts are shared with suppliers through real-time systems. Suppliers receive accurate and topical schedules. Long term capacity planning conducted with suppliers and supplier collaboration and visibility into demand is shared.

items.control_description: 14. To what extent does the organization learn from its supply market?
items.remarks: Basic: Procurement does not operate a two way feedback process.  ||  Emerging: Suppliers do have opportunities to provide feedback on the organization's supply management performance but data is not collated or acted on consistently.  ||  Advanced: Suppliers have opportunity to provide feedback on the organization's supply management performance as part of formal review process. Information gathered is collated and acted upon as key objective.  ||  Differentiated: Formal feedback process in addition to review of supplier technological capabilities and core competencies which are recognized and utilized where feasible.  ||  Best In Class: The organization utilizes supplier expertise in re-engineering in its procurement / supply chain processes as well as product development. Joint knowledge sharing objectives are in place with key suppliers.

items.control_description: 15. How is supplier feedback captured?
items.remarks: Basic: Procurement does not seek or collect supplier feedback.  ||  Emerging: Procurement does not seek supplier feedback in a consistent or structured fashion. Once feedback is collected, limited evidence of Procurement documenting or acting on feedback.  ||  Advanced: Collection of supplier feedback is ad hoc through contract review meetings. Some limited evidence of procurement management reviewing feedback to identify recurrent themes.  ||  Differentiated: Formal mechanism to gather feedback from suppliers at quarterly business reviews or preparing for contract negotiations. Procurement reviews feedback and acts on proposed feedback.  ||  Best In Class: Supplier councils are used to gather feedback from suppliers, identify improvement opportunities and provide improved communication through supplier relationship management tool.

items.control_description: 16. To what extent does procurement utilize technology to automate and streamline the complete supplier management lifecycle?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: No supplier management technology solution is available.  ||  Emerging: No elements of an automated supplier management solution are utilized but procurement is aware of the potential and has plans to trial use of available functionality.  ||  Advanced: There is limited use of supplier management automation (e.g., web based portal or online surveys). The supplier management functionality is not routinely available for Procurement use.  ||  Differentiated: The key elements of supplier management technology solution (see Level 5) have been deployed to support procurement, but usage is low or functionality is not enabled at an enterprise level. Functionality is not routinely used by procurement due to a combination of poor understanding of benefits, inadequate training and support and lack of management focus.  ||  Best In Class: Extensive use of supplier management technology across the enterprise that automates and streamlines the complete supplier management lifecycle, enabling self-service supplier registration, assessment, performance measurement, issue resolution and continuous improvement.

items.control_description: 17. How effective is procurement at supporting the planning for major projects, capital and new products & identifying strategies that maximize the value of third-party spend?
items.remarks: Basic: Procurement has no or very limited involvement in planning prior to a requisition or request for a contract being submitted.  ||  Emerging: Procurement's involvement in planning typically limited to ad hoc consultation on the supply market for a given commodity.  ||  Advanced: Procurement has a formal role in the demand planning process, including specific milestones for activities related to third-party spend. However, the process is inadequately defined in one or more areas such as: Clear roles and responsibilities are not in place between the business and procurement. Clear requirements have not been defined for the demand information required at various milestone. Performance metrics are not in place to track performance to planning milestones. Limited technology is in place to support the process, specifically the capture and analysis of demand information.  ||  Differentiated: Procurement has a formal role in the demand planning process, including specific milestones for activities related to third-party spend. However, the process is inconsistently implemented in one or more areas such as: Performance against milestones and other metrics is tracked, but not used to manage execution. Remediation efforts for missed milestones are not successful Technology does not readily support analysis across categories, sites or business units. Opportunities for strategic sourcing are not integrated into the portfolio planning process, affecting opportunities to aggregate demand and to effectively manage resource.  ||  Best In Class: An integrated planning process is implemented and consistently applied across the organization. Within this process: -Milestones for the planning of third-party spend are defined to ensure adequate lead time for aggregation of demand and strategic sourcing. Performance to milestones is managed closely, with an escalation process in place to remediate delays that affect third-party spend (e.g. minimize expediting charges). Technology is used to efficiently capture and analyze demand information and aggregate demand. The process is well-integrated with the portfolio planning process, specifically the ongoing development of upcoming procurement projects.

items.control_description: 18. How effective is procurement in translating demand plans for indirect spend into opportunities for sourcing, demand management & supplier management?
items.remarks: Basic: Procurement has no or limited involvement in planning prior to a requisition or request for a contract being submitted.  ||  Emerging: Procurement's involvement in the development of functional budgets for indirect spend is limited to ad hoc consultation on the supply market for a given commodity.  ||  Advanced: Procurement has a formal role in the development of functional budgets for indirect spend. However, the process is inadequately defined in one or more areas such as: Clear responsibilities for stakeholders and Procurement have not been defined budgeting/planning process standards and timing differ across sites or business units, making analysis of third-party demand prohibitive.  ||  Differentiated: Procurement has a formal role in the development of functional budgets for indirect spend. However, the process is inconsistently implemented in one or more areas such as: Visibility to demand for indirect spend is not readily accessible in functional budgets. Technology does not readily support analysis across categories, sites or business units. Opportunities for strategic sourcing are not integrated into the portfolio planning process, affecting opportunities to aggregate demand and to effectively manage resource.  ||  Best In Class: A formal process is implemented and consistently applied across the organization. Within this process: -Procurement takes an active role in working with stakeholders to analyze demand and identify projects that maximize value of third-party spend (e.g. sourcing, supplier management, or demand management). Future demand is aggregated across categories, sites, and business units and integrated into category strategies and management. Demand is communicated proactively to suppliers for all applicable categories. The process is well-integrated with the portfolio planning process, whereby all identified projects are integrated into the activity plan.

items.control_description: 19. How rigorously are consumption and compliance procedures applied to what was demanded & what was used?
items.remarks: Basic: There are no consumption policies in place.  ||  Emerging: Some application of demand management procedures. Primarily measurement of usage/volumes.  ||  Advanced: Consumption and compliance procedures are regularly reviewed. Target cost management is applied in key areas.  ||  Differentiated: Consumption and compliance procedures optimizing supply and demand are regularly reviewed and updated. Key measures are incorporated in some areas of the business. Improvements and benefits can be demonstrated.  ||  Best In Class: A total cost management approach is applied. Consumption and compliance procedures optimizing supply and demand are regularly reviewed and updated. Key measures are incorporated in business. Improvements and benefits can be demonstrated and tracked.

items.control_description: 20. How involved is Procurement in developing strategies to ensure the maximum value is received when contracting with vendors?
items.remarks: Basic: Procurement has no or very limited involvement in planning prior to a requisition or request for a contract being submitted.  ||  Emerging: Procurement’s involvement in planning typically limited to ad hoc consultation on the supply market for a given commodity.  ||  Advanced: Procurement has a formal role in the demand planning process, with the following areas being thought through, but not necessarily implemented: Roles and responsibilities & requirements. Performance metrics. Use of technology.  ||  Differentiated: Procurement heavily involved in the demand planning process, and is able to offer insight as to how the supply base can be used as an asset to influence quality, cost, or delivery.  ||  Best In Class: An integrated planning process is implemented and consistently applied across the organization, with defined milestones for the planning of third-party spend. Performance to milestones is closely managed. Technology is used to efficiently capture and analyze demand. Well-defined process integrated with new projects.

items.control_description: 21. To what extent are effective controls in place in the P2P process?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Delegated authorities and approval processes have not been consistently defined. Authorities have not been integrated into systems and are controlled offline. Use of PO's is rare. Most of the purchasing is by verbal commitment and manual approval of invoice. No workflow is used in the P2P process.  ||  Emerging: Delegated authorities and approval processes have not been standardized across the organization. Different systems apply different rules/controls across the organization.  Budget holders often require to approve the invoice before allowing payment (even on PO purchases). Use of POs and 3way matching is limited and payment performance is poor.  Limited workflow is used in the process.  ||  Advanced: Delegated authorities and approval processes have been defined but there is evidence of inconsistent application in systems across the organization.  Typically financial approval is required once only. Use of PO's and 3way matching is prescribed but there is widespread evidence of budget holders approving invoices without PO.  Workflow does not cover procurement intervention. Reliance on users to flag appropriate purchases for Procurement input offline.  ||  Differentiated: Delegated authorities have been defined across the organization and integrated in core Procure to Pay systems. Some evidence of inconsistency within non ERP buying channels.  Financial approval on a purchase is required once only  wherever possible approval is required before commitment and automated matching of orders, invoices and receipts is utilized to control payments.  Procurement intervention threshold managed through workflow. Threshold set across the board rather than by category.  ||  Best In Class: Delegated authorities and approval processes are clearly defined, integrated into systems and consistent across the organization. Compliance is enforced. Financial approval on a purchase is required once only wherever possible approval is required before commitment and automated matching of orders, invoices and receipts is utilized to control payments. Flexible workflow used to trigger. Procurement intervention on non contract purchases according to business rules defined by category (e.g. value thresholds).

items.control_description: 22. To what extent have order processing tasks been automated?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Use of Purchase Orders is rare. Verbal requests placed with suppliers. Different processes and suppliers by location. Purchase approval is retrospective and based on budget holders signing invoices.  ||  Emerging: Paper requisitions created and converted into PO's centrally.  Standard PO's used for all PO purchases. Invoices received and checked against POs before being sent for signature/approval by budget holders.  Frequent purchases without PO. Budget holders approve paper invoices retrospectively..  ||  Advanced: Automated replenishment systems used to enable automatic reordering of stock items based on predefined minimum stock levels.  Manual order processing intervention required to convert online requisitions to purchase orders.  No use of service POs. Standard PO's used for all PO purchases.  ||  Differentiated: Automated replenishment systems to enable automatic reordering of stock items based on predefined minimum stock levels.  Automatic conversion of approved requisitions to PO's for contract purchases.  Manual order processing intervention is managed through workflow but there is no ability to tailor it by category or supplier.  Some limited use of service POs. Suppliers do not have access to systems to complete timesheets.  ||  Best In Class: Automated replenishment systems to enable automatic re-ordering of stock items based on predefined minimum stock levels. Automatic conversion of approved requisitions to PO's for contract purchases. Manual order processing intervention limited to exceptions and managed through flexible business rules and workflow which allow it to be varied by category, supplier, and relationship type. Service POs used with service entry sheets for complex service purchases. Suppliers have access to complete own timesheets in purchasing systems.

items.control_description: 23. How are buying channels managed for the needs of different purchases?
items.remarks: Basic: Basic buying channels are available (PO and invoice approval) but are poorly defined and inconsistently used across the organization. There is no evidence of Procurement actively managing buying channels. There is significant use of verbal ordering and manual invoice approval with only limited use of purchase orders.  ||  Emerging: Basic buying channels are available (PO and invoice approval) with processes and policies defined to support these. The Procurement function has attempted to mandate the use of PO's for all purchases but no PO invoices still account for a large volume of purchases. No PO invoice approval is manual (no workflow).  ||  Advanced: The organization has begun implementing a range of buying channels (moving away from a one size fits all approach based on the use of POs) but progress to date is limited. Some use of purchasing cards and T&E cards as well as no PO invoice approval for some purchases. There is some lack of clarity around usage guidelines and controls, leading to sub optimal arrangements and usage.  ||  Differentiated: It has been recognized that a one size fits all approach with PO's is counterproductive. A range of clearly defined and appropriately controlled buying channels is available or being implemented in major corporate locations: e.g. purchasing cards, T&E cards, eprocurement (catalogue and non catalogue), framework orders, MRP orders, invoice approval workflow etc. In other locations purchasing options tend to be limited.  ||  Best In Class: It has been recognized that a one-size-fits-all approach with PO's is counter-productive. A consistent range of clearly defined and appropriately controlled buying channels is available across the organization to support different transaction types: e.g. purchasing cards, T&E cards, e-procurement (catalogue and non catalogue), framework orders, MRP orders, invoice approval workflow etc.

items.control_description: 24. To what extent does a strategy and toolset exist for managing low value transactions efficiently?
items.remarks: Basic: No evidence of knowledge of purchasing card as a procurement tool. There is no strategy for maximizing processing efficiency on low value purchases. Purchase cards are not used for low value purchases.  ||  Emerging: Procurement are aware of Purchase Cards but do not currently have any plans to introduce them. The same purchasing process is used for high and low value orders. There is no strategy for maximizing processing efficiency on low value purchases.  Purchase Cards are not currently used.  No clear usage strategy or guidelines are in place for high volume, low value purchases and for low volume, low value purchases.  ||  Advanced: The organization has begun to develop a strategy for low value purchases.  The organization has begun to implement Purchase Cards but they are not available in all areas.  Purchase Card usage is low and inconsistent. The business is unclear on what they should be used for and there is resistance from some budget holders.  ||  Differentiated: A strategy exists for driving processing efficiency on low value purchases but does not cover the full scope of transactions.  Purchase Cards have been implemented for high volume, low value purchases but there is no clear approach for managing low value, low volume purchases.  Purchase Card usage is on target with the level planned in the original strategy and business case.  ||  Best In Class: A clear strategy exists for maximizing processing efficiency on low value purchases whilst maintaining appropriate control, spend visibility and VAT reclaim potential as appropriate. Purchase cards have been implemented for specific types of low value purchases. Clear usage strategy / guidelines are in place for high volume, low value purchases and for low volume, low value purchases. Purchase card usage has reached or exceeded the level planned in the original strategy and business case. Opportunities to extend usage within the strategy revisited at least annually.

items.control_description: 25. What is the process for receiving goods and services?
items.remarks: Basic: Suppliers deliver on adhoc basis. Inefficient goods receipt processes. Paperwork intensive.  ||  Emerging: Selected suppliers have fixed nominated periods.  Inefficient goods receipt processes. Paperwork intensive.  ||  Advanced: Services are formally received by originator. All suppliers have fixed nominated delivery periods.  Goods receipting is poor with frequent errors and majority of goods receipts only processed after invoice has mismatched.  ||  Differentiated: Goods receipts automated via bar coding  standard format with all suppliers. Standard containers.  Service receipting discipline is inconsistent across the business. Recurrent issues with receipts only processed after invoice have mismatched.  ||  Best In Class: Supplier transmits delivery documentation in advance by EDI. Line-side supply. Goods receipt processed on same day as goods physically received. Service receipting is disciplined.

items.control_description: 26. How are payment terms managed?
items.remarks: Basic: Payments frequently and deliberately withheld to assist cash flow. High occurrence of supply stoppages due to poor payment. Early payments are common. Payment terms typically driven by suppliers. Large numbers of different payment terms exist in systems. No consistent approach or policy. Payment performance is not reported as a KPI even for Accounts Payable.  ||  Emerging: Payments sometimes deliberately withheld to assist cash flow. High occurrence of supply stoppages due to poor payment.  Frequent occurrences of invoices paid early.  Payment terms typically driven by suppliers. Large numbers of different payment terms exist in systems. No consistent approach or clear policy.  Payment performance is reported by Accounts Payable but there is limited evidence of actions to improve performance even with the A/P function.  ||  Advanced: Payment performance is variable. Business functions typically uninterested in payment performance until suppliers escalate it.  Large numbers of different payment terms exist despite clear policy on standard terms. Control on new payment terms is not effective.  Payment performance is measured at a corporate level only (i.e. not measured across business units/divisions). No attempt to report BU performance or to engage BU's to improve performance.  ||  Differentiated: Payment performance is variable. Business functions typically uninterested in payment performance until suppliers escalate it.  Rationalized and consistent set of payment terms used across the organization. Standard terms used except where agreed with Procurement and Finance.  Payment performance is measured and reported across business units/divisions but there is little evidence of joint action being taken to address issues.  ||  Best In Class: Invoices always paid to terms (not early). Early payment discounts incorporated into payment terms. Good payment performance recognized as key to developing productive supplier relationships. Prompt payment recognized as good practice by all functions. Rationalized and consistent set of payment terms used across the organization. Standard terms used except where agreed with procurement and finance. Payment performance measured and reported across business units / divisions and actions taken by business units and corporate functions to address issues jointly.

items.control_description: 27. How effective are support mechanisms to maximize compliant purchasing?
items.remarks: Basic: Not applicable  ||  Emerging: No use of online catalogues or eProcurement.  Contract pricing not maintained in purchasing systems. No use of source lists. Process dependent on users correctly identifying pricing before creating requisition/order.  There is no designated support mechanism for ordering. Users tend to rely on more experienced colleagues in their department.  ||  Advanced: No use of online catalogues or eProcurement.  Contract pricing maintained in purchasing systems for some supplies. No use of source lists.  There is no designated support mechanism for ordering. Users tend to contact Order Processing teams or buyers with questions.  ||  Differentiated: Catalogues (including pricing) in eProcurement system for simple indirect goods. No use of contracts in ERP for other requirements.  Use of source lists for some non catalog able requirements.  There is a Procurement Help Desk to assist requisitioners when they need assistance with ordering supplies.  ||  Best In Class: Widespread use of system pricing for contract items (either in online catalogues or as ERP contracts). Use of source lists in purchasing systems to maximize use of preferred vendors. There is a procurement help desk to assist requisitioners when they need assistance with ordering supplies.

items.control_description: 28. How well are procurement policies and procedures understood internally?
items.remarks: Basic: General procurement policies or guidelines have not been defined. Informal rules are driven by business unit management locally. Major variations in internal processes and no evidence of effort to drive standardization.  ||  Emerging: Procedures not generally shared with the business or integrated with other guidelines.  Non compliance is a major issue right across the organization.  ||  Advanced: Policies & procedures available in policy documents but not always accessible. Employees outside Procurement are often unaware of them or how to access them.  Low levels of non compliance with policy & procedures can be found all across the organization.  ||  Differentiated: Policies & procedures easily accessible on the corporate intranet.  Compliance is generally high but there are persistent issues in certain areas.  ||  Best In Class: Policies and procedures easily accessible on the corporate intranet and widely understood. Integrated with induction training for all relevant staff. High levels of internal compliance with policy and procedures across the organization.

items.control_description: 29. Are procedures in place for code of ethics, gifts and hospitality, disclosure of interests and fair dealing?
items.remarks: Basic: No procedures and no evidence of plans to develop any.  ||  Emerging: Work is underway to develop procedures but not yet complete. No evidence that procurement has plans to actively monitor compliance.  ||  Advanced: Clear procedures in place but there are known gaps. Plans in place to monitor compliance but no action taken yet.  ||  Differentiated: Comprehensive procedures documented but not well communicated. Compliance monitoring designed but rarely applied.  ||  Best In Class: Clear, comprehensive procedures in place and widely communicated. Compliance monitoring operational.

items.control_description: 30. Are minimum standards enforced through the contracting process to manage supplier risk?
items.remarks: Basic: Procurement does not participate in any formal, structured qualification process. Basic financial checks should be conducted on new supplier requests but suppliers are frequently added to the supplier database without these checks being completed.  ||  Emerging: No formal qualification process is in place in Procurement. Some buyers will conduct risk assessments during sourcing but there is no consistent approach.  Qualification limited to basic financial viability checks required by Finance on all new vendors.  ||  Advanced: A formal supplier qualification and risk assessment process has been developed as part of the sourcing process. However, application is variable. There is some evidence of risk assessment and planning for certain critical categories / suppliers. Supplier qualification / accreditation includes an assessment of supply security and regulatory compliance as well as financial viability. Reputational and sustainability risks are not routinely covered.  ||  Differentiated: Procurement conduct a standard, robust qualification of suppliers as part of the strategic sourcing process on all goods/services. A further risk assessment and risk management plan is required as part of the supplier selection decision and subsequent implementation.  All new suppliers must go through rigorous checks prior to being made available for use. Checks include financial risk but also commercial, supply chain, CSR, regulatory and sustainability risks  Different levels of qualification are required depending on the level of risk associated with the type of supplier  Formal accreditation process in place for high risk suppliers. Accreditation relies on self certification by suppliers.  ||  Best In Class: Procurement conduct a standard, robust qualification of suppliers as part of the strategic sourcing process on all goods / services. A further risk assessment and risk management plan is required as part of the supplier selection decision and subsequent implementation. All new suppliers must go through rigorous checks prior to being made available for use. Checks include financial risk but also commercial, supply chain, CSR, regulatory and sustainability risks Different levels of qualification are required depending on the level of risk associated with the type of supplier. Formal accreditation process in place for high risk suppliers supported by the use of supplier audits.

items.control_description: 31. How is compliance monitored and managed?
items.remarks: Basic: Little or no compliance monitoring takes place. Procurement do not know level of leakage from agreements. No consistent monitoring or process compliance. Levels of non compliance are high. Frequent purchasing outside buying channels e.g. use of no PO invoices. Accounts Payable still process non compliant invoices. No attempt to report on levels of compliance with process or contracts.  ||  Emerging: No consistent monitoring or process compliance. Levels of non compliance are high. Frequent purchasing outside buying channels e.g. use of no PO invoices. Accounts Payable still process non compliant invoices.  Procurement produce periodic reports to identify off contract and non contract spend. No mandate or management support to take effective action.  ||  Advanced: Process compliance is controlled through internal monitoring and controls but non compliant invoices will still be paid. Levels of non compliance are stable.  Procurement produce periodic reports to identify off contract and non contract spend. There is limited evidence of successful action by Procurement to address issues.  ||  Differentiated: Process compliance is controlled through internal (audits) and external controls (no PO, no Pay policies). Non compliance is limited.  Standard reports are produced monthly to identify off contract and non contract spend. Procurement seek to engage business stakeholders to drive action but with varying success.  ||  Best In Class: Process compliance is controlled through internal (audits) and external controls (no PO, no Pay policies). Non compliance is minimal. Standard reports are produced monthly to identify off contract and non contract spend and shared with business units / divisions. Effectiveness of actions taken jointly monitored by procurement and business.

items.control_description: 32. To what extent is supply risk actively assessed and monitored?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: Not Applicable  ||  Emerging: There is no formal process for risk management.  No predictive monitoring in place  Contingency plans are not in place even for critical requirements  No evidence that risk plans are created  Procurement relies on tip-offs from business stakeholders or suppliers to identify potential risks.  ||  Advanced: Risk management guidelines are in place for Procurement but there is limited evidence of a consistent approach.  Procurement actively involved in qualification of new suppliers but there is limited evidence of proactive or regular risk assessment and monitoring of existing suppliers by Procurement  Isolated examples of good practice for certain categories and suppliers.  Procurement does not consistently measure or report on supply risk  Some isolated examples of contingency plans to cover supply shortages on critical requirements are to be found.  Risk logs and plans are sometimes created but there is limited evidence that these are actioned.  ||  Differentiated: A risk management approach has been defined for Procurement which lays out Procurement responsibilities Risk monitoring and ongoing assessment in place for critical suppliers only Some evidence of structured attempts to monitor market information to identify potential risks Cross functional risk assessment & planning for critical supplies/suppliers. No evidence of joint planning with suppliers Category teams report risk status (qualitative assessment) Contingency plans in case of supply shortage in place for most critical requirements but not all. Quality of plans is inconsistent. Extent of follow through on risk plans varies from category to category.  ||  Best In Class: Detailed risk management processes have been rolled out across procurement, supported by best practice templates, training and tools. Risk monitoring requirements are defined by category and supplier according to exposure. Procurement lead periodic risk assessment exercises involving business stakeholders. Procurement routinely monitor industry news and information sources (e.g. rating agency reports) for changes to supplier or market conditions. There is evidence of joint risk assessment and monitoring with critical suppliers. Quantitative risk metrics in place. Supply risk KPI's included in CPO dashboard Complete contingency plans exist in case of supply shortage for critical requirements; plans identify alternate suppliers and alternate manufacturing and design specs evidence that risk plans are used to drive. Procurement efforts to mitigate and manage risks on an ongoing basis.

items.control_description: 33. How well do the procurement policies and procedures integrate sustainability considerations?
items.remarks: Basic: No policies or processes on how to incorporate sustainability considerations into procurement decisions  ||  Emerging: Sustainability considerations are embedded in policies or included in standalone policies. However, not all material sustainability risks/opportunities are considered.  Procedures do not include sustainability considerations.  ||  Advanced: Sustainability considerations are embedded in existing procurement policies or as standalone policies. All material sustainability risks/opportunities are considered.  Procedures include sustainability considerations to a limited and inconsistent extent.  ||  Differentiated: Sustainability considerations are embedded in policies or included in standalone policies. All material sustainability risks/opportunities are considered.  All relevant procedures for direct Procurement integrate sustainability/sustainability considerations however they are not applied consistently across the business units.  ||  Best In Class: All relevant procedures for direct procurement integrate sustainability / sustainability considerations and are applied consistently across the business units.

items.control_description: 34. To what extent are sustainability risks to supply managed?
items.remarks: Basic: Sustainability risks are not considered in supply chain risk assessments.  ||  Emerging: Some sustainability risks e.g. water scarcity, climate change, considered but on an ad hoc basis and in response to immediate threats. No formal process for managing sustainability risks.  ||  Advanced: Risk management guidelines include a number of sustainability risks.  Some isolated examples of short term plans to mitigate sustainability risks to supply, on critical requirements are to be found.  Risk logs and plans are sometimes created to mitigate sustainability risks but there is limited evidence that these are actioned.  ||  Differentiated: An approach to manage sustainability risks has been defined for procurement which lays out procurement responsibilities; sustainability risk also applies to natural disaster planning for key suppliers / plants plans, mainly short-term (15 years) to manage sustainability risks in place for most critical requirements but not all. Quality of plans is inconsistent.  Extent of follow through on risk plans varies from category to category.  ||  Best In Class: Clear sustainability risk assessment processes in place. Proactive and regular monitoring of risks in place (to include natural disaster risk for critical suppliers / plants). An assessment is repeated each year to identify critical suppliers and assess risk. Complete contingency plan including for the longer term (5 years +) exists in case of supply shortage for critical requirements. The plan identifies ways of working with preferred suppliers to mitigate sustainability risks to supply.

items.control_description: 35. To what extent are comprehensive category strategies in place for major spend categories?
items.remarks: [Rapid DOMA] Basic: The organization does not have a consistent view of its spend categories. No sourcing strategies are in place. Procurement have no involvement in sourcing decision making beyond administration of the formal RFP.  ||  Emerging: There is no evidence of strategies being developed at a spend category level. Local procurement activity is reactive to individual Business Unit/functional need rather than planned or coordinated across enterprise. Central Procurement have had some success in coordinating activity for some enterprise wide indirect requirements. Sourcing decision making still handled by the business in most cases with no Procurement involvement. Sourcing strategies are not formally documented. Procurement involvement is typically limited to tender and negotiation strategy.  ||  Advanced: Category sourcing strategies are in place only for a small minority of direct and indirect categories.  Procurement category teams tend to develop sourcing strategies as part of the strategic sourcing process being applied at subcategory level but there is little evidence of alignment with an overarching category strategy.  Limited or inconsistent consideration of a wide range of sourcing levers. Limited consideration of the wider supply chain opportunities.  Category strategies owned by Procurement are infrequently revisited and there is limited evidence that they are shaping the way Procurement manages its daytoday activity.  ||  Differentiated: Category sourcing strategies are in place for most areas of major direct spend. This is less well developed in areas of major indirect and capex spend. Some portfolio analysis considered.  Strategies show evidence of consideration of a wide range of sourcing levers. Limited consideration of the wider supply chain opportunities.  Category strategies tend to be owned by and understood in Procurement but understanding of stakeholders outside Procurement is inconsistent.  ||  Best In Class: Advanced and differentiated category sourcing strategies are in place for all major categories of indirect, direct and capital spend, based on comprehensive portfolio analysis. Portfolio is regularly reviewed with supplier and industry input and all sourcing levers are considered. Category strategies address opportunities across the broader supply chain. Alternative supply sources are developed in conjunction with current suppliers for key purchases. Category strategies are communicated within Procurement and to all key stakeholders for important categories.

items.control_description: 36. To what extent is category spend data available and consumable?
items.remarks: Basic: Minimal to no application of sourcing levers…suppliers dictate new pricing each year with minimal pushback.  ||  Emerging: Basic sourcing levers (best price evaluation, global sourcing, volume consolidation) are evaluated ad-hoc and applied only to these categories.  ||  Advanced: Basic sourcing levers are formally evaluated and applied to most categories. Advanced sourcing techniques are being applied to some categories.  ||  Differentiated: Each category is assessed for sourcing lever applicability; execution incorporates advanced supplier interactions focusing on total value.  ||  Best In Class: A tailored set of advanced sourcing techniques is applied in combination to each key category to achieve the next level of value year-on-year.

items.control_description: 37. To what extent do strategies for major spend categories consider specific sustainability risks and opportunities?
items.remarks: Basic: No understanding of total cost.  ||  Emerging: Some visibility into costs, limited category spend data is available.  ||  Advanced: Some category spend data is available, limited focus on reducing cost.  ||  Differentiated: Complete visibility into costs; focus on continually reducing total cost of doing business.  ||  Best In Class: Visibility into total costs and ability to manage; process for quantifying procurement risk trade-offs.

items.control_description: 38. How well are category economics understood?
items.remarks: Basic: No sourcing strategies are in place for specific categories. Supply chain sustainability risks and opportunities have not been considered.  ||  Emerging: Supply chain sustainability risks and opportunities have been considered but not at the category level.  ||  Advanced: Sustainability risks and opportunities have been identified for some but not all spend categories, but are not integrated into procurement decision making.  ||  Differentiated: Sustainability risks and opportunities have been identified for all major spend categories but not integrated into procurement decision making.  ||  Best In Class: Sustainability risks and opportunities have been identified for all major spend categories and are integrated into procurement decision making from specification, through to evaluation and contract management).

items.control_description: 39. How well leveraged is the global supply base?
items.remarks: Basic: No understanding of supplier economics and visibility to cost and process.  ||  Emerging: Some understanding of supplier economics practices, no benchmarking capabilities with peers.  ||  Advanced: Moderate understanding of supplier economics practices.  ||  Differentiated: Extensive understanding of industry economics, limited benchmarking with peers. Extensive use of outside benchmarks.  ||  Best In Class: Content rich supply market analysis tools; common continuous benchmarking approach real-time updates as to changes in underlying economics (automated feeds of commodity price changes, how it will impact pricing).

items.control_description: 40. Material and service standardization
items.remarks: Basic: Current suppliers only are considered for new business; supplier benchmarking rarely occurs and only considers cost.  ||  Emerging: New suppliers are sought out to complement the current suppliers, but limited to similar geography / capabilities; Supplier benchmarking occasionally occurs and focuses mainly on cost, with minimal quality considerations.  ||  Advanced: New diverse suppliers are sought out regionally / nationally to complement the current suppliers; supplier benchmarking does occur, with focus on cost but also quality & delivery considerations.  ||  Differentiated: Alternative suppliers are sought out globally to reduce cost and secure supply. Supplier benchmarking regularly evaluates suppliers with equal weight to capabilities, cost and quality considerations.  ||  Best In Class: Sourcing actively searches for suppliers globally that can lead company to new innovations and capabilities. Supplier benchmarking regularly evaluates suppliers with equal weight to capabilities, cost and quality considerations.

items.control_description: 41. How well integrated are supply chain requirements into supplier selection and management?
items.remarks: Basic: Supply chain requirements not considered.  ||  Emerging: Basic supply chain requirements understood and reflected in supplier discussions and management.  ||  Advanced: Supply chain requirements are fully understood and incorporated into. Sourcing decisions and codified into terms and conditions.  ||  Differentiated: Supply chain requirements incorporated into contracts and supplier performance management process within Sourcing.  ||  Best In Class: Supply chain requirements incorporated into contracts and supplier performance management process across the enterprise.

items.control_description: 42. How is supplier diversity incorporated?
items.remarks: Basic: Goal for diversity but no managed approach to meeting goals.  ||  Emerging: Diversity tracked against target but limited effort to locate suppliers or force primes to subcontract.  ||  Advanced: Efforts made to include diverse suppliers within supply base and making sourcing decisions. Diversity considered a differentiator when making sourcing decisions.  ||  Differentiated: Considerable effort to identify and use diverse suppliers; willing to pay premium for diversity.  ||  Best In Class: Advanced strategies in place to achieve diversity targets such as prime / subprime and certification assistance.

items.control_description: 43. How important is complexity to product development and lifecycle cost management?
items.remarks: Basic: Product and design complexity not recognized as a material cost driver.  ||  Emerging: Recognized as a cost driver and limited informal measures in place to control.  ||  Advanced: Procurement is linked to product development process, no suppliers decisions made without procurement's approval.  ||  Differentiated: Procurement / category management has a voice in product development process.  ||  Best In Class: Category strategy a key part of global platform and module strategies (where step design changes occur). Procurement personnel with appropriate technical skills fully embedded within product development process.

items.control_description: 44. What is sourcing's role in complexity management?
items.remarks: Basic: Sourcing "buys what they are told to buy".  ||  Emerging: On an ad hoc basis, sourcing identifies redundant and complementary parts and works to standardize off one.  ||  Advanced: On a frequent basis, sourcing works with the supply base to determine streamlined materials options.  ||  Differentiated: Sourcing works with the product engineering / design teams to ensure "Design for Sourcing / DFS" is incorporated into any decisions.  ||  Best In Class: Sourcing has the technical skills to help shape product design and ensure widest possible supply base options can be leveraged (e.g., minimize the "specing in" of hard to source / expensive parts).

items.control_description: 45. How important is Specification development?
items.remarks: Basic: Limited recognition of variability in specification as a source of material costs. Wide variety of specs exist.  ||  Emerging: Recognized as a cost driver and limited informal measures in place to control.  ||  Advanced: Standard material specification based on common, cost effective materials, limited supplier direction.  ||  Differentiated: Procurement is able to show impact of different specification options for key categories / cost areas, helping to shape design decisions and long-term impact.  ||  Best In Class: Category team play an active role in ‘designing in‘ specifications for new products in line with category strategy.

items.control_description: 46. How is sourcing embedded within NPI / advanced engineering?
items.remarks: Basic: Engineering interfaces with suppliers independent from production sourcing.  ||  Emerging: Approved vendor list used for new quotes, but limited competitive sourcing within the AVL / new suppliers.  ||  Advanced: Preferred suppliers selected based on competitive quote.  ||  Differentiated: Preferred suppliers engaged during development based on best total cost and value.  ||  Best In Class: Supplier selection coordinated with current category strategy while not constraining innovation.

items.control_description: 47. How well integrated are suppliers into the product development process?
items.remarks: Basic: Suppliers considered as a black box – either as a source of component or an extension of mfg capability.  ||  Emerging: Limited informal teaming occurs with suppliers, unstructured and rare.  ||  Advanced: Suppliers engaged to help develop new products, but on an ad hoc basis and limited to select categories.  ||  Differentiated: Preferred suppliers engaged during development based on best total cost and value.  ||  Best In Class: Risk sharing partners performing integrated design for strategic products.

items.control_description: 48. How well integrated and coordinated are Design Cost Reduction (DCR) efforts?
items.remarks: Basic: Engineering focus is on new product; value engineering does not exist except for quality improvement.  ||  Emerging: VA/VE understood but only pursued on an ad hoc basis, usually targeting a self-evident opportunity.  ||  Advanced: Value add / value engineering (VA / VE) practices established within function.  ||  Differentiated: Cross functional DCR work teams assemble on a project basis.  ||  Best In Class: Cross functional DCR management process with governance, metrics, targets – linked to company product strategy.

items.control_description: 49. What joint supplier cost reductions programs are in place?
items.remarks: Basic: Suppliers cost reduction captured only via competitive bid.  ||  Emerging: Suppliers given cost reduction targets / requirements periodically.  ||  Advanced: Improvement commitments negotiated up front, and suppliers participate with OEM upon request.  ||  Differentiated: Active two way participation on an established cadence.  ||  Best In Class: Joint cost reduction process with key suppliers fully embedded and enables lead development and pipeline management.

items.control_description: 50. How integrated are suppliers into Design Cost Reduction (DCR)?
items.remarks: Basic: Suppliers assist on an ad hoc basis.  ||  Emerging: Improvement commitments negotiated up front, and suppliers participate with OEM upon request.  ||  Advanced: Suppliers participate in DCR.  ||  Differentiated: Suppliers work with DCR teams and are a source for many improvement ideas during DCR sessions.  ||  Best In Class: Suppliers fully embedded and proactively provide cost reduction ideas -whether through us of improved technology, processes materials, etc..

items.control_description: 51. How structured is the sourcing process?
items.remarks: Basic: No strategic sourcing process in place.  ||  Emerging: Strategic sourcing done during periods of fiscal austerity with 3rd party support.  ||  Advanced: Strategic sourcing process in place, with adherence to a structured 9-step sourcing process.  ||  Differentiated: Strategic sourcing process is well understood and done on a regular schedule tied to contract renewals.  ||  Best In Class: Strategic sourcing done proactively based on market trends and internal considerations.

items.control_description: 52. How does sourcing strategy drive performance?
items.remarks: Basic: No sourcing strategy; purchasing power is not leveraged.  ||  Emerging: Sourcing strategy focuses on cost reduction.  ||  Advanced: Sourcing strategy focuses on improving total cost of ownership, to include cost, quality, delivery.  ||  Differentiated: Sourcing strategy is fully aligned to the corporate strategy and helps achieve integrated results across the organization.  ||  Best In Class: Sourcing strategy drives competitive advantage by leveraging supply markets globally and increases overall value of final product.

items.control_description: 53. What are the sourcing decision-making criteria?
